owocnik: Two different forms of Abortiporus biennis can be found: a "normal"-looking one, with a brown cap 5–15 cm in diameter and a white hymenophore, which when damaged turns from reddish to reddish-brown, and a form with an irregular, "interrupted" shape, made up of irregular white pores (1–3 per mm), which exude a reddish liquid (guttation) and turn reddish-brown when damaged.
In this latter form, as the fungus grows, it often engulfs sticks and blades of grass, as some species of the genus Hydnellum do.
Fruit bodies overlapping each other, surface rough, hairy.
podobne: Daedaleopsis confragosa also turns red, but it is harder, the shape of the fruit body is more regular, and it occurs on branches and trunks.
Abortiporus biennis may resemble a small Grifola frondosa or Meripilus giganteus, but both of these species do not turn red (the latter turns from grey to black).
Loweomyces fractipes is very similar, with a single cap and a lateral stalk, but it does not turn red, and the pores are well defined and smaller (4–5 per mm).

kapelusz: Ovoid when young, later hemispherical, convex, flat in the mature fruit body.
Surface bare, silky-shiny, white to cream in colour.
Turns yellow when pressed.
spod: Free, crowded.
In young fruit bodies white, and they remain white for quite a long time.
With time grey-brown with a fleshy tinge, finally chocolate-brown and even black-brown.
They never have a pink tinge.
trzon: Height 5–15 cm, thickness 1–3 cm.
Shape cylindrical, thickened at the base, at first solid, then tubular, easily breaking away from the cap, with a large hanging ring at the top.
Turns yellow when pressed.
miazsz: Soft and flexible, white, sometimes yellowish in old fruit bodies.
Taste insignificant, smell of aniseed.
podobne: There are many similar species of Agaricus.
Among the aniseed-smelling Agaricus, Agaricus silvicola is similar, but its gills stay red-pink for a long time.
Agaricus xanthodermus turns yellow when pressed (like the whitish Agaricus species), but smells of carbolic acid.
Among the large Agaricus species, Agaricus campestris is similar.

kapelusz: Diameter 10–25, at first almost spherical, then successively egg-shaped, hemispherical, flat-arched, finally spread out.
Surface light ochre covered with appressed small scales in colours from rusty brown to red-brown.
spod: Crowded, at first whitish, then pink-salmon, finally chocolate-brown.
Edges lighter.
trzon: Height 10–20 cm, thickness 2–3 cm, cylindrical, with a bulb at the base, usually hidden in the ground, hard, breaking off, at first solid, then hollow.
Surface coloured from white to ochre-yellow, yellow-brown when pressed.
Ring large, hanging, whitish-yellowish on the upper side, yellowish-rusty and hairy on the lower.
miazsz: Thick, soft, at first whitish, then yellowish-rusty, with a pleasant smell of aniseed or almonds.
podobne: Agaricus langei is distinguished by a long stem with blood-red flesh and an indistinct smell.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–10 cm, white, grey-white to brownish.
Skin from radially fibrillose to adpressed scaly.
spod: They do not reach the stem.
In young specimens they are whitish, later pink, finally dark brown.
trzon: Height 3–8 cm, thickness up to 3 cm, cylindrical, solid.
It has a distinct ring.
Colour white, below the ring sometimes scaly.
miazsz: Reddening slightly, with a faint, pleasant smell.
podobne: Agaricus bisporus can be confused with the poisonous Agaricus xanthodermus, but also with the edible Agaricus campestris and Agaricus arvensis.
Of all these species, Agaricus bisporus has the thickest, most fleshy cap.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–10, even 15 cm, hemispherical when young, flat in older specimens, even with a sunken centre.
The margin extends beyond the gills and remains inrolled for a long time.
Surface smooth and dry, sometimes cracking into patches.
It is whitish and does not change colour when rubbed.
Sometimes there are remnants of the veil on its margin.
spod: Crowded, narrow and free.
At first they are pale pink, then chocolate-brown, finally black-brown.
Edges white-flocculose.
trzon: Short and thick, cylindrical with a narrowed base, solid and hard.
Surface smooth or woolly, whitish.
It has a massive, double ring coloured from white to light ochre.
miazsz: Hard and very compact, white, not changing colour when damaged, or turning slightly pink.
It has a pleasant, almond smell and a nutty taste.
podobne: Agaricus bisporus, occurring mainly in cultivation and sold in shops.
In natural habitats it is fairly rare, and its wild-growing form is darker, brownish and has a detachable ring.
However, the most reliable way to tell these species apart is microscopic examination; A. bitorquis has 4-spored basidia, and A. bisporus 2-spored ones.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–11 cm, closed and almost spherical in young specimens, later hemispherical, finally flatly spread out.
Margin scaly-cracked, surface silky-fibrous, at the top there are sparse, adpressed brown scales.
When pressed it changes colour to yellowish or brownish (older specimens).
Cap colour at first white, later grey-ochre.
In mature mushrooms, especially in dry weather, the upper surface of the cap cracks and deep furrows and small fields form on it.
The skin can be easily peeled off the whole cap.
spod: Crowded, free at the stem.
Only in very young, still closed fruit bodies are they white, then they turn pink and darker with age; chocolate-brown to black-brown.
In old fruit bodies they become violet-black from the spores.
trzon: Height 4–8 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, cylindrical, solid, easily breaking off from the cap, with a white membranous ring at the top.
Surface smooth, white, brown in older specimens.
The ring is not very persistent and disappears in older specimens.
The upper part of the stem is often pinkish from the flesh showing through.
In older fungi the stem is darker, brown or rusty brown.
miazsz: White, or watery pink; when cut it turns pink in places.
Above the gills and in the stem under the gills the flesh often has a grey tint, and in the stem base orange.
Taste pleasant, smell slightly mushroomy.
podobne: Amanita virosa and some other Amanita.

However, the danger of confusion exists only in the case of very young, still closed fruit bodies of the field mushroom, which still have white gills, but these very quickly become pink, then darker and darker.
Amanitas always have white gills and a stem surrounded by a volva.
Agaricus arvensis.
A common species, often growing outside forests.
On the stem it has a ring with small scales, it has an aniseed or almond smell and pale grey-pink gills at maturity
Agaricus bitorquis.
However, it always has a bare cap and a double ring on the stem.
Edible.
Agaricus bisporus.
Distinguishing young specimens may be difficult, the place of origin may help (Agaricus bisporus comes from cultivation), they can be reliably distinguished by microscopic examination.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–10 cm, bell-shaped or hemispherical in young specimens, later arched, flat in older ones.
Surface dry, in colour from dark brown to ochre, densely covered with cinnamon-brown adpressed small scales of a fibrous structure.
Sometimes (rarely) a form with a light-coloured cap occurs.
spod: Crowded, narrow, free, grey-reddish in young specimens, dark brown in older ones.
Gill edges paler.
The white and membranous partial veil persists for quite a long time.
trzon: Height 5–12 cm, thickness 1–2 cm.
When pressed it turns red, later becomes darker (brown).
It is white with a protruding ring at the top, cylindrical, bulbously thickened at the bottom, solid when young, then tubular, easily breaking off from the cap.
miazsz: White, turning red when cut.
Taste good, smell indistinct.
podobne: There are several species of Agaricus with a brown cap.
Agaricus xanthodermus is similar.
It is distinguished by the smell of carbolic acid and the yellowing base of the stem.
In the rare Agaricus porphyrizon the flesh turns yellow when damaged, and it also has a slightly different cap colour.

kapelusz: At first hemispherical, later opening umbrella-like, 6 to 14 cm in diameter, white, fairly fleshy, with a faint, blunt umbo, the top from silky to delicately fibrillose, or even fibrillose-villose.
Sometimes it is white-cream, sulphur yellow or ochre-yellow in colour.
Turns yellow when pressed.
spod: Free, very closely spaced, whitish in young individuals, later grey-red, and finally dark red to black-brown.
trzon: Height 5–10 cm, width 1.5–3 cm, shape slender, cylindrical, narrowing slightly towards the top, above the ring silky fibrous.
Above the bulb mostly bent and characteristically widened at the base, with a very thin, hanging ring, edged on the underside with leathery warts.
miazsz: White in the cap, very thin, with a cavity near the stem.
Turning yellow when cut or crushed.
It smells pleasantly of aniseed.
wysyp: Spores elliptical, smooth, measuring 6–7.5(8) × 4–5.5 µm, without a germ pore.
podobne: The young, conically closed fruit bodies of this fungus can be confused with the deadly poisonous Amanita virosa, but in the Amanita the skin of the cap does not turn yellow after damage.
The final clarification is given by the base of the stem, which in the poisonous amanitas is provided with a volva.
Agaricus arvensis – its gills never have a pink tinge.
Agaricus xanthodermus differs in its carbolic (phenol) smell, and its flesh turns strongly yellow when damaged.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–12(15) cm, entirely white and convex, skin silky, often cracking radially, sometimes covered with delicate small scales and may have a light beige colouring at the top.
The skin on the cap turns yellow under pressure.
spod: Fairly thin, at first in the colour rose, pinkish-whitish and its shades, with time changing to chocolate-brown.
trzon: Up to 10–12 cm tall, entirely white, slender, passing into a bulb in the lower part, turning chrome yellow under pressure.
Stem sometimes hollow inside (see the photo).
Ring hanging, on the underside with a characteristic edge running all around.
miazsz: White, after cutting it takes on an intense yellow colour, when rubbed at the base it turns chrome yellow.
In smell it resembles carbolic acid or ink, and during cooking this smell increases in strength.
Very unpleasant in taste.
wysyp: The spore-shedding period falls in the months from July to October.
podobne: This mushroom is most easily confused with Agaricus arvensis.
The feature that distinguishes them is the smell of the flesh.
Agaricus sylvicola and Agaricus sylvaticus are also similar.
Both the smell and the taste distinguish this Agaricus from other edible Agaricus species.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–11 cm, shape hemispherical in young fruit bodies, later convex, flattened in older fruit bodies.
Sometimes it has a faintly marked umbo.
It is slightly hygrophanous.
Margin of the cap with hanging remains of the veil.
At first it is even, but in older fruit bodies torn and lobed.
Surface in colour from cream-white through cream-yellowish or cream-rusty to cream-brownish.
In young fruit bodies it is smooth, but later usually cracks into patches.
spod: Fairly crowded, up to 7 mm wide, sinuately notched at the stem.
At first they are whitish, with time increasingly darker, finally olive-brown.
trzon: Height 8–12 cm, thickness up to 1 cm, cylindrical, sometimes bent.
It has a membranous, non-persistent ring, a remnant of the veil.
Surface white, fibrillose, at the base there is a white, felty coating of mycelium.
miazsz: White or cream, flexible in the cap.
Young fruit bodies have a cucumber-mealy smell and a mild taste, older ones have a musty smell and a bitter taste.
wysyp: Spores egg-shaped or ellipsoid, measuring 12–13 × 6–7.5 μm.
podobne: The cracked Agrocybe is most easily recognised by the cap cracked into small fields (but this occurs only in middle-aged fruit bodies), and by remnants of the veil hanging from the cap.
Similar to it are, among others:
Agrocybe praecox.
It is more delicate, has darker fruit bodies, and its cap does not crack into small fields.
It is also more bitter and has smaller spores,
some species of Agaricus, but they have a shorter and thicker stem and their gills quickly become black-brown.

kapelusz: Diameter 1–4 cm, shape hemispherical in young fruit bodies, later convex, in older fruit bodies almost flat.
Colour yellowish to yellow-brown, surface smooth, slightly sticky when wet, sometimes with whitish remains of the veil at the margin.
spod: Attached or slightly decurrent, moderately broad, at first cream, then brown, sometimes rusty brown.
In young fruit bodies often completely covered by the veil.
trzon: Height 2–4 cm, thickness 1–2 mm, shape cylindrical or slightly narrowing towards the base, straight, sometimes bent.
Surface dry, smooth under the cap, otherwise finely fibrillose, of the same colour as the cap.
miazsz: Without taste or with a mealy taste, without smell.
podobne: Field cap species are difficult to distinguish.
Agrocybe pediades shows variability in colouring and in spore morphology.

It is characterised by the presence of a partial veil, but this is so short-lived that it can be seen only in very young fruit bodies, the size of the rubber on a pencil, and this feature lasts only a few hours, after which the veil disappears without trace.
Under the action of KOH its cap changes colour to red or pink, which does not occur in other species of Agrocybe.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–8 cm, in young fruit bodies hemispherical, then arched, finally almost flat, sometimes with a depressed centre.
It is hygrophanous.
Surface smooth, in colour yellowish, cream-white, ochre or brownish.
At the margin usually remnants of a whitish veil.
spod: Notched, crowded, at first whitish, then grey-white, clay-brownish or dirty brown.
trzon: Height 4–9 cm, thickness 4–9 mm, cylindrical, hollow inside.
Surface bare, in colour from whitish to ochre-cream.
Base with white rhizomorphs.
Ring membranous, drooping, disappearing only in older fruit bodies.
miazsz: Soft and whitish in the cap, brown in the stem.
It does not change colour after damage.
It has a faint, mealy smell and a mealy-bitter taste.
podobne: Agrocybe praecox is morphologically variable and difficult to distinguish from similar species.
Agrocybe dura also grows in spring.
It is paler and has a humped, more fleshy, non-hygrophanous cap, which usually cracks in dry weather.
It is also characterised by harder flesh without a mealy smell.
Agrocybe paludosa is also similar, but it grows in other, damp habitats and is rare.
It has a slender shape, a stem up to 4 mm thick, a persistent ring, a thin cap with a slightly wrinkled margin, brown spores and occurs in damp habitats.
Under the microscope the gill edges are sterile, filled mainly with club-shaped cheilocystidia.

owocnik: Diameter 2–10 cm.
In young individuals almost spherical, later bowl-shaped with bent margins, in older ones almost flat, roundish, lobed and bent, with wavy margins.
Stem absent.

The inner spore-bearing layer, in which the spores are formed, is smooth, in colour from yellow-red through orange to cinnabar-brown-red; the outer side is delicately velvety, in colour from whitish to pale yellow-ochre.
miazsz: Very thin, brittle and watery.
It is white-grey in colour, taste and smell faint, when crushed the smell is pleasant.
podobne: Sarcoscypha austriaca has a more intense colour (scarlet-red) and grows only in early spring.
Melastiza chateri is smaller and has a black-spotted margin of the fruit body.
Caloscypha fulgens has an orange-yellow fruit body, with the inside of the cup grey when young, later orange, and delicately granular on the outside.
It grows in early spring in mountain coniferous forests.
Pulvinula constellatio has disc-shaped or cushion-shaped fruit bodies.

kapelusz: Diameter 8–20 cm, at first almost spherical, later flat-arched, flat in older specimens.
Surface smooth and bare, sometimes with remnants of the veil.
Cap margin distinctly striate, colour bright orange to red-orange, later fading to golden yellow and pale yellow.
spod: Free and crowded, at first pale yellow in colour, later golden yellow.
trzon: Height up to 16 cm, almost cylindrical, with a slightly thickened base surrounded by a white volva in the form of large lobes.
At first solid, later hollow like a tube.
It has a large, yellow, hanging ring.
miazsz: White, golden-yellow only under the skin.
Taste and smell indistinct.
podobne: Amanita crocea.
It is lighter and has a scaly stem.
Amanita muscaria, which differs in the darker colour of the cap, white gills and white stem.

kapelusz: Fleshy, 5–10 cm in diameter, pale yellowish, less often yellowish-green, at first semicircular, later flat.
On its surface there are a few patches of various sizes.
When young the whole cap is surrounded by a veil.
During the growth of the fruit body it is torn apart.
From the lower part the ring on the stem forms, from the upper part the patches on the cap, which are often washed away during rain.
spod: On young fruit bodies white, on older ones yellow-white, crowded, not attached at the stem.
trzon: Thin (1–2 cm) and tall (5–15 cm), cylindrical, easily separating from the cap.
It is white or yellow-white, tapering towards the top.
On the bulbous base of the stem there is a short volva up to 4 cm thick with ragged, uneven edges.
There is a yellowish ring on the stem, hanging down in mature specimens.
miazsz: White, brittle, with a mild taste and a smell of raw potatoes.
Does not change colour when broken.
podobne: It is very similar to Amanita virosa and to the green Amanita, also called the death cap (Amanita phalloides).
Both of these species are deadly poisonous.
It is especially easy to confuse Amanita citrina specimens whose cap patches have been washed off by rain.

kapelusz: Ochre-orange to yellow-orange, 6–15 cm in diameter, at first semicircular-ovoid-bell-shaped, with age convex to spread out and with an umbo, surface sticky when wet, smooth and velvety when dry, usually without remnants of the veil, margin distinctly striate up to 1/3 of the radius.
spod: Cream, fairly crowded, broad, free.
trzon: Cylindrical, height 10–15 cm, thickness 1–2.5 cm, slightly narrowing towards the top; surface with yellow-orange flocks on a white background.
At the stem base a persistent and solid volva, membranous, white on the outside, yellowish on the inside.
miazsz: White, thin, without smell, mild, indistinct taste.
wysyp: Spores spherical or almost spherical, size: 11–12.5 × 9–10 µm
podobne: Possible confusion with Amanita caesarea, which also has a similar yellow-orange colour, but that species does not occur in Poland.
It can also be confused with Amanita fulva, which forms smaller fruit bodies and has a cap of a pale orange colour.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–10 cm, strongly spherical when young, later arched, finally flat.
Young specimens are covered with a white veil, which tears into shreds as the fungus grows.
The cap in the centre is ochre with a salmon tint to light leather colour, paler at the margins.
Edges sharp and crenate.
spod: Broad, free, with fringed edges.
trzon: Height 8–12 cm, width 1–2 cm, cylindrical, solid when young, later hollow.
It is white and has a white, hanging ring.
Bulb small and deeply embedded in the ground.
miazsz: Thin and white (yellowish only directly under the skin).
Taste musty, smell indeterminate.
podobne: It is easy to tell apart from other Amanita species, because it has a relatively long stem, a small bulb buried deep in the ground and white remains of the volva on the stem.
Similarly coloured is Amanita gemmata, and weakly coloured forms of Amanita muscaria are also similar.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–15 cm, at first hemispherical, then slightly convex to spread out.
Colour grey-brown or brown-ash.
The cap is covered with paler, white-grey patches.
Sometimes after rains the patches are absent.
spod: Densely arranged, white, not attached at the stem.
trzon: Height 6–15, exceptionally up to 20 cm, thickness 2–3 cm.
It is cylindrical, easy to break off, and has a whitish, large ring, notched at the top.
At the base it has a large and pointed bulb up to 4.5 cm wide, without a separate volva.

A characteristic feature of this bulb, distinguishing it from Amanita pantherina, is the presence on it of several warty rims (in Amanita pantherina the bulb is smaller and has several rows of rings).
miazsz: White, and under the cap skin it has a grey tint.
Smell earthy, taste indistinct or similar to radish.
wysyp: Spores broadly ellipsoid and smooth, measuring 8–10 × 5–8 μm.
podobne: Amanita pantherina, Amanita rubescens and Amanita porphyria.

kapelusz: Diameter from 3 to 10 cm, at first bell-shaped conical, later arched with a small umbo, finally flatly spread out without an umbo. It is distinctly striate at the margin, bare, smooth, usually without remnants of the veil, slimy-sticky in wet conditions, light brown, orange-brown, finally red-brown.
Sometimes there are greyish remnants of the veil on the surface.
The skin can be peeled off the whole cap.
spod: Moderately crowded, not attached to the stem, white or pale grey.
trzon: Height 8–15 cm, diameter 0.8–1.2 cm, cylindrical, tapering upwards, smooth, without a ring, tubular in older specimens, white to ochre-brown.

The base of the stem is surrounded by a membranous, loose volva with features characteristic of this species; it is membranous, attached at the bottom, free at the top, loose, reaching up to 1/4 of the height of the fruit body.
Its colour ranges from white to ochre-brown.
miazsz: The flesh is watery and whitish, brittle, thin, smell indistinct, taste sweetish.
podobne: Amanita crocea, which forms larger fruit bodies and has a cap of a vivid orange colour.
Amanita vaginata.
It usually has greyish shades, but there are varieties with colouring very similar to the rusty-brown Amanita.
They differ by the volva

kapelusz: Diameter up to 11 cm, semicircular when young, later arched, finally almost flat.
Cap margins striate, skin straw yellow, lemon, ochre-yellow, usually covered with whitish patches.
It fades in old age.
The white patches on the cap are easily washed off by rain, so they are often absent.
spod: White, crowded, not attached to the stem.
trzon: Height up to 14 cm, thickness up to 2 cm, white or yellowish, usually covered with standing white scales.
On young specimens a narrow, white ring is present, in older ones it disappears.
Bulb at the base of the stem covered by an attached volva.
miazsz: White, with a mild taste and faint smell.
podobne: Amanita excelsa.
It has a striate ring, and the base of the stem is not surrounded by a volva,
Amanita rubescens.
It has no volva, its flesh is wine-red, and the ring is striate on top.

kapelusz: Diameter up to 11 cm, semicircular when young, later arched, finally almost flat.
Cap margins striate, skin straw yellow, lemon, ochre-yellow, usually covered with whitish patches.
It fades in old age.
The white patches on the cap are easily washed off by rain, so they are often absent.
spod: White, crowded, not attached to the stem.
trzon: Height up to 14 cm, thickness up to 2 cm, white or yellowish, usually covered with standing white scales.
On young specimens a narrow, white ring is present, in older ones it disappears.
Bulb at the base of the stem covered by an attached volva.
miazsz: White, with a mild taste and faint smell.
podobne: Amanita excelsa.
It has a striate ring, and the base of the stem is not surrounded by a volva,
Amanita rubescens.
It has no volva, its flesh is wine-red, and the ring is striate on top.

kapelusz: Diameter up to 20 cm.
In very young specimens spherical, then hemispherical, with time low-arched, and in older specimens flat and slightly depressed in the centre.
Surface smooth, delicately crenate near the margin in older specimens.
At first it is covered with a whitish veil.
After it is torn, white or white-yellow patches remain on the cap.
In wet weather it is sticky.
spod: White or pale yellowish, bellied, crowded, free.
trzon: Height up to 20 cm, thickness up to 3 cm.
It is cylindrical, easily broken off, solid when young, then hollow.
Colour white or yellow, it has a hanging, white (sometimes yellowish) ring.
Base bulbous, surrounded by several rows of roll-like thickenings and without a distinct volva.
miazsz: White, brittle, does not change colour after damage, without smell and with a mild taste.
podobne: Amanita regalis – has a brownish colour of the cap skin, yellow dots and margin of the ring, and grows only under spruces

Amanita caesarea – it has a paler, orange-yellow cap without spots, a yellow stem and gills, and the stem bulb is surrounded by a volva; it occurs in warm broadleaved forests mainly in southern Europe and it is there that accidental consumption of the fly agaric (Amanita muscaria) most often occurs
Russula xerampelina and other red Russula species have a plain stem without a ring and other decorations, and a smooth cap
Amanita junquillea – is sometimes confused with yellow varieties of Amanita muscaria, but it is smaller and has a different structure of the stem.

inne: It occurs in Europe, in mixed forests on calcareous soils, and is very rare.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–12 cm, spherical when young, then becomes convex and flat.
Colour: brown-grey, brown or brown-yellow, in mountain areas it may be black-brown.
On the surface covered with white patches.
The skin on the surface is easily peeled off.
A characteristic feature making it possible to distinguish it from similar species of Amanita (the grey spotted amanita and the blusher) is that the cap margins are clearly striate.
spod: Crowded, white, free at the stem and not fused.
trzon: Height 5–15 cm and thickness 1–2 cm, white, at first thick and massive, then slender, cylindrical, hollow inside.
It is wider at the bottom and has a bulbous, relatively small swelling with several rows of small rolls (a characteristic feature making it possible to distinguish it from similar Amanita species).
Under the cap there is a smooth, membranous ring, which disappears in older mushrooms.
miazsz: Completely white, brittle, does not change colour after damage.
Mild in taste, sweetish-insipid, with a faint smell reminiscent of radish or raw potato.
wysyp: Spores smooth, broadly ellipsoid, measuring 9–12 × 7–9 μm.
podobne: It is often confused with Amanita rubescens and Amanita excelsa, which are edible fungi.
The main features allowing them to be distinguished are the smooth ring (in these two species it is grooved) and the different shape of the bulb.
Also similar is Amanita franchetii, but it differs in the yellow ring on the stem.
Moreover, characteristic of Amanita pantherina is the striation of the cap at the margins, and of the blusher the reddish tinge and the darkening of the flesh after damage.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–15 cm, hemispherical when young, then bell-arched, finally spread out.
Skin smooth, not striate at the margin, consisting of adhering and radially arranged fibrils.
Colour white-greenish, olive-greenish, grey-green, brown-green, usually paler at the margin, sometimes yellowish.
In the sun, and in older specimens, the colour is faded.
The skin is easily peeled off and white remnants of the veil often occur on it.
trzon: Height up to 15 cm, thickness up to 2 cm.
It is cylindrical, ending at the base in a bulb up to 4 cm in diameter.
The bulb is surrounded by a tall, whitish, spreading volva.
Colour of the stem whitish with a yellowish-greenish tinge.
It has a distinct, hanging ring, coloured from white to yellowish.
Above the ring the stem is smooth, below the ring there are delicate scales, sometimes forming a zigzag pattern.
miazsz: White, does not change colour when broken.
In young specimens the flesh has a mild smell, in old ones it smells slightly of potatoes.
Taste pleasant.
spod: Crowded, white, in old specimens with a slight yellowish-greenish tint.
In young specimens they are invisible, because they are covered by a whitish veil.
podobne: Inexperienced mushroom pickers sometimes confuse it with Tricholoma equestre, Russula virescens, Amanita citrina, Amanita submembranacea, and also other species of Amanita.
Young, weakly coloured specimens can also be confused with button mushrooms (Agaricus).

kapelusz: Diameter 4–9 cm, in young individuals bell-shaped to arched, then quickly flattening out.
Margin blunt, without striations, cap surface smooth, bare with delicate, embedded fibrils, usually with patchy remnants of the veil.
Colour grey-brown or grey-violet.
In dry weather it is shiny, in wet weather slippery.
spod: White, of uneven length, crowded and free at the stem.
trzon: Height 8–13 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, cylindrical, narrowed in the upper part.
Solid on young fruit bodies, later hollow inside; on older ones grey-brown with a violet tinge.
Ring hanging, disappearing in older specimens.
Base bulbous with a large volva standing away from the stem and torn, usually darker than the stem.
miazsz: Brittle, white, fairly thin.
It has an unpleasant smell of rotting potatoes and a taste of radish.
wysyp: Spores spherical, smooth, 8–10 μm in diameter.
podobne: Sometimes Amanita excelsa is similar, but it does not have a protruding bulb, and is also larger and fleshier.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–25 cm, at first bulbous and surrounded by a veil, later hemispherical, then increasingly spread out.
Surface dry, shiny, liver-brown in colour, darker at the top, covered fairly regularly with concentrically arranged ochre-yellow patches.
At the cap margin of older specimens it is striate.
spod: Free, densely arranged, white, later cream-yellowish.
In young specimens covered by a yellowish veil.
trzon: 8–20 cm high, 1.5–3.5 cm in diameter, cylindrical, brittle.
At the base it has a bulb with several rows of rings covered with warts (remnants of the veil).
Surface smooth, white or yellow-white, with a distinct yellowish ring.
miazsz: Yellowish-brown under the cap skin, with a mild and faint taste.
It does not change colour after damage.
podobne: Amanita excelsa.
It has a brown-grey cap without yellow patches, white gills, and a crenate white ring.

kapelusz: Flesh-reddish, pale reddish, brown-reddish or light brown with a reddish tinge, up to 15 cm in diameter.
Surface dry, covered with brown-pink patches of various sizes, semicircular in young specimens, then spread flat.
spod: White when young, later with a pinkish bloom, up to 12 mm wide, adnate or decurrent, fairly crowded.
When damaged they change colour to brownish-reddish.
trzon: At first whitish, later brown-reddish, bulbously thickened at the base, up to 15 cm high, surrounded by remains of the volva in the form of irregular rolls.
It is equipped with a striate ring.
miazsz: White, fleshy, turning reddish when damaged, brittle, without smell, with a mild taste.
wysyp: Spores smooth, broadly ellipsoid, measuring 6–7 × 8–10 μm
podobne: It is sometimes confused with the poisonous Amanita pantherina and with Amanita excelsa.
Characteristic of the blusher are a pinkish tinge, reddening of the flesh after damage and the lack of distinct striation on the cap.
Moreover, Amanita pantherina has a folded volva at the base of the stem.

kapelusz: Diameter up to 20 cm, at first convex, later spread out, depressed in the centre, margin sharp.
Surface cream-white to pale grey, covered with patch-like scales of the same colour or darker.
They are soft and delicate, hanging from the cap margin.
This Amanita can reach very large sizes, so that in cap size it resembles the parasol mushroom (Macrolepiota procera), but in weight it exceeds it 2-3 times.
spod: White-cream, crowded, bulging.
trzon: Height up to 15 cm, thickness up to 5 cm, base bulbously thickened, deeply embedded in the substrate, slightly widening towards the base, hard, stem solid.
Ring cream, thick.
miazsz: White, thick in the fruit body, smell faint, resembling old ham.
podobne: They are easily confused with amanitas with a bulbous base, e.g. Amanita virosa.
The most similar is Amanita echinocephala.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–8 cm, ovoid-bell-shaped when young, later arched, finally flat with a small, blunt umbo.
Edges sharp and striate, grooved in older specimens.
Surface smooth, in colour from olive-brown to grey-brown, or yellow to red-brown.
In the centre there is usually a large grey-white patch, a remnant of the veil.
spod: Free and broad, at first white, later cream.
trzon: Height 5–11 cm, thickness up to 1.2 cm, hollow and brittle, cylindrical, thicker at the bottom.
Surface the colour of the cap, covered in the lower part with white flakes.
Base surrounded by a membranous volva, at first white, later greyish.
miazsz: White, without smell.
Taste slightly nutty.
wysyp: Spores spherical or nearly spherical, measuring 10–14 μm.

kapelusz: Diameter about 5–10 cm.
White or cream in colour, with a smooth or slightly fibrous surface, on which remnants of the veil can occasionally be found.
The shape of the cap is at first oval or semicircular, in mature fruit bodies convex or flat.
The cap edge is smooth and pointed.
spod: Gilled, white.
Gills widely spaced, not attached to the stem, with smooth or flocculose edges.
trzon: Length approx. 7–10 (up to 12) cm, diameter approx. 1–1.5 cm.
Colour whitish to greenish, often with a zigzag pattern and a flocculose surface.
The stem is almost cylindrical, tapering slightly towards the top.
On the stem there is a white ring, hanging down, furrowed and often torn, above which the stem is smooth.
The stem base is bulbous, at its base there are remains of the veil (the so-called volva), yellowish in older fruit bodies.
miazsz: White in colour.
The smell of the flesh is sweetish and the taste nutty.
It does not change colour when treated with a solution of potassium hydroxide (in the variety Amanita verna var. decipiens, occurring in southern Europe, it turns orange-yellow).
wysyp: Spores roundish in shape, measuring 8–10×7–9 μm, white.
podobne: Agaricus sp., which immature fruit bodies with a white hymenophore resemble
Amanita citrina
Amanita gilbertii
an Amanita with a thick volva
Amanita virosa, which has a less conical cap and fruits in spring.

kapelusz: Diameter 6–10 cm, at first oval, later conical-bell-shaped, finally slightly convex.
Surface of the cap smooth, dry and silky, sticky in wet weather.
Colour white and pale yellow only at the apex.
It may turn yellow with age.
On the surface it sometimes has irregular large patches, sometimes it is without patches.
spod: White, crowded, sometimes with ragged edges.
Free at the stem.
trzon: Height: 8–12 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, cylindrical, narrowed at the top, with a bulbous base.
With age it becomes slender.
Surface with large fibrous scales.
On the stem a ring, which, however, may disappear in old specimens.
The bulbous base of the stem has a distinct, ragged volva.
miazsz: White, brittle, does not change colour when broken.
Taste mild, smell unpleasant, suffocating.
podobne: It may be confused with Agaricus species.
In very young Agaricus the gills are white, but later they turn pink, and in older ones they are chocolate-coloured, which distinguishes these fungi from each other.
Thus the danger of confusion concerns only very young Agaricus.
Moreover, the destroying angel (Amanita virosa) has a movable volva on the bulb of the stem, which Agaricus species do not have.
Very similar is Amanita verna, but it has a pure white cap and a smooth stem.
There is also a very similar white (albino) form of Amanita phalloides.
All three of these white amanitas are deadly poisonous.
White Volvopluteus species, e.g. Volvopluteus gloiocephalus, are similar, but they have pink gills and lack a ring and a bulb at the end of the stem.
It also differs in the place of occurrence – Volvariella species very rarely occur in forests.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–7 cm.
Young fruit bodies are arched with a clearly visible, blunt umbo, with time they become flat, finally concave in the centre.
Margin at first inrolled, later straightened, sharp and thin.
Surface smooth, bare.
It is hygrophanous; in dry weather it is pale ochre, in wet weather its colour is from grey-brown to olive-grey.
spod: Crowded and decurrent on the stem, first white, then yellowish.
trzon: Height 4–9 cm, thickness 8–18 mm, cottony and soft in the centre.
Base widened in a club-like manner and connected to the substrate by white mycelium.
Surface smooth, fibrous, white-grey, cream or light brown in colour.
miazsz: White, soft and watery.
It does not change colour after damage.
Without a distinct taste and without smell, at most with a faint smell of stale meal.
podobne: A characteristic feature of this white funnel cap species is the bulbously thickened base of the stem.
However, this feature is not always well developed, and then it is difficult to distinguish it from some other species of funnel caps.
Clitocybe nebularis is the most similar.
It is, however, larger and has harder and more sourish flesh.
Moreover, its gills separate easily from the cap when rubbed with a finger.
Clitocybe costata is also similar, but even its older specimens have a rolled-under cap margin, and moreover it is wavy.
It usually has no umbo and has more reddish-brown tints.

owocnik: Height 2–7 cm, diameter up to 3 cm, shape pear-shaped or club-shaped.
Surface rough, floury, very finely warty.
At the top there are small, long-persisting low spines.
Colour from whitish-ochre through grey-nut-brown to grey-ochre, the upper part of the fruit body usually brownish.
Endoperidium rough, as if mealy, brittle, with very fine warts.
It is coloured from white-cream to light brown, in young fruit bodies with a copper tint, in old ones it becomes matt, paper-like.
Only very young fruit bodies are white, they quickly change to a darker colour.
At the top it has a mound on which, in mature fruit bodies, a small opening forms through which the spores escape.
At first this opening is round, later it has increasingly ragged edges.
At the base of the fruit body there are whitish, fairly thick rhizomorphs penetrating the substrate.
miazsz: Divided into soil and subsoil.
The subgleba is finely chambered, white in young fruit bodies, grey-brown in older ones.
The gleba is of a similar colour, in older fruit bodies it becomes olive-brown and gradually passes into a clearly visible, elongated columella.
podobne: Because of the substrate, which is atypical for puffballs, this species is hard to confuse with other puffballs.
It is also characteristic that the fruit bodies are white only in very early stages of development; also characteristic are the thick, whitish, root-like cords of mycelium.
Lycoperdon perlatum, but it grows on the ground and is covered with spines.
Lycoperdon umbrinum also changes colour very early and has whitish mycelial cords (but thin).
However, it does not grow on wood but on the ground and has a different surface

kapelusz: Diameter 2.5–10 cm, conical in young specimens, later convex, finally flat.
Cap margin translucent, inrolled in young specimens.
It is hygrophanous, when wet it is in colour from pink-brown to flesh-brown, when dry it is paler.
On the surface it has concentrically arranged small scales and tufts of similar colour to the cap.
They are 1–1.5 mm long and usually persist for a long time on the cap surface.
spod: Attached or shortly decurrent, whitish in young specimens, then pale pink with rusty-red spots.
trzon: Height 4–10 cm, thickness up to 1.8 cm.
It is cylindrical with a bulbously widened base from which numerous rhizomorphs grow.
It has a woolly ring, sometimes fairly thick and persistent, with yellowish flocks on the lower side, but sometimes it disappears.
Surface of the stem of the same colour as the cap.
Below the ring numerous flocculose remnants of the veil, in colour from yellowish to orange-yellow, occur on it.
miazsz: White in colour, turning pink with age, with a mushroomy smell.
Taste at first mild, then irritating and unpleasant.
podobne: The yellowish honey fungus is confused with Armillaria mellea, Armillaria ostoyae or Armillaria tabescens.
In mushroom atlases until the 80s.
XX century: the yellow honey fungus was not distinguished and all these species were called by the name honey fungus.
Distinguishing individual species of honey fungus is difficult, and often impossible from mature fruit bodies alone.
From the mushroom pickers' point of view, however, not distinguishing these species is of no great importance, since all are edible.
The ringless honey fungus has no ring on the stem and is rare in Poland; the honey fungus occurs on dead broadleaved trees and has a cap with very fine fibrils, sometimes completely bare.
Armillaria ostoyae occurs only on conifers and has a cap with distinct tufts.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–13 cm.
First it is hemispherical, convex, later flattened.
Honey-yellow, honey-brown, olive-yellow when young, then olive-brown, dark red-brown.
Covered with fine red-brown, brown or blackish scales, which are darkest and densest in the centre.
In old specimens the scales often disappear and the cap is bare.
spod: At first whitish, later beige-pinkish, yellowish with brownish spots, decurrent, thin.
trzon: Height 8–18 cm, thickness 0.5–2.5 cm; yellowish, honey brown, red-brown, black-brown, paler at the top, slender, cylindrical, curved, with a widened, rough and darker base.
The stems of neighbouring fungi are often fused together.
It has a broad membranous ring of golden-yellow colour, which is covered with yellow tufts in its lower part.
miazsz: Whitish, pale flesh-coloured, does not change colour when cut, soft and fleshy in young fruit bodies, hard and bast-like in old ones (especially in the stem).
podobne: Mushroom pickers often do not distinguish Armillaria mellea from Armillaria ostoyae or Armillaria tabescens.
In older mushroom atlases the honey fungus (Armillaria mellea) was usually not distinguished from the dark honey fungus, or all three of these species were called honey fungus.
From the mushroom pickers' point of view, not distinguishing these species is of no great importance, since all are edible.
The opienka bezpierscieniowa (Polish name) has no ring on the stem and is rare in Poland; Armillaria ostoyae occurs only on conifers and has a cap with distinct tufts.
Inexperienced mushroom pickers may confuse the honey fungus with the poisonous Hypholoma fasciculare.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–8 cm, convex in young specimens, but quickly becomes spread out, and in older specimens concave.
Colour flesh-coloured or red-brown.
A characteristic feature is the presence on the cap of blackish-brown, fairly large scales reaching its margin.
spod: Fairly crowded, at first cream-white, then brown.
trzon: Height 4–12 cm, thickness up to 2 cm.
It is cylindrical, fibrous, club-shaped, solid and often curved.
In older specimens it becomes cottony and hollow inside.
Whitish in the upper part, rusty lower down and usually with remains of a whitish sheath and brown tufts.
Ring fairly thick, white in colour; on the underside and at the edges there are dark-coloured scales.
miazsz: White in colour, with age taking on a pinkish tinge, with a mushroomy smell and a mild taste.
wysyp: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, with droplets, measuring 7.5–10 × 5–7 µm.
podobne: Mushroom pickers often confuse Armillaria ostoyae with Armillaria mellea or Armillaria tabescens.
In older mushroom atlases the honey fungus (Armillaria mellea) was usually not distinguished from the dark honey fungus, or all three of these species were called honey fungus.
From the mushroom pickers' point of view, not distinguishing these species is of no great importance, since all are edible.
The ringless honey fungus has no ring on the stem and is rare in Poland; the honey fungus occurs on dead broadleaved trees and has a cap with very fine fibrils, sometimes completely bare.

owocnik: Bushy, 2–4, exceptionally up to 8 cm tall.

The little bush grows from one thick trunk, which branches repeatedly upwards into ever thinner twigs (as in a candelabrum). The last branching is widened in a cup shape, and several small outgrowths grow from the edges of the cup.
The branches are raised upwards and fairly crowded, so that the little bush is compact.
Colour from pale flesh through pale yellow to ochre-yellow.
In North America the fruit body reaches the dimensions: 4–13 cm in height and 2–10 cm in width.
miazsz: Flexible, coloured from whitish to light yellow.
When rubbed or damaged it turns brown.
Taste mild or slightly peppery, smell indistinct, sometimes resembling baked potatoes.

kapelusz: Diameter 10–35 cm, at first arched, then flat, finally funnel-shaped concave, always without an umbo.
Margin at first inrolled and delicately hairy, in adult specimens sharp and wavy-bent.
The record specimen had a cap 45 cm in diameter.
spod: Crowded, narrow, springy and deeply decurrent on the stem.
In young specimens white, in older ones leathery yellowish, finally brown.
They turn brown when pressed.
trzon: Height 5–10 cm, width 2–4 cm, hard, solid, fibrous.
At first white, then increasingly darker, finally dirty brown.
miazsz: Hard, in colour from white to cream-white, brown after drying, watery in older specimens.
Taste sweetish, smell of semen.
wysyp: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, 6–9 × 4–5.5 μm, weakly amyloid.
podobne: Infundibulicybe gibba.
It is also whitish and funnel-shaped, but much smaller, and its spores are non-amyloid and not ellipsoid, but stone-shaped.
Infundibulicybe geotropa.
It is funnel-shaped, but usually smaller with a taller stem.
Its spores are non-amyloid.
On the cap it always has a prominent umbo.

owocnik: It forms a thin, membranous, white, spread-out thallus with an indistinct margin and a smooth hymenophore.
It does not form fibres.
It forms sclerotia.

kapelusz: At first convex, never flattening out completely, reaching a diameter of 4–20 cm.
Surface dry, dull, reddish with a characteristic frill at the edge of the cap.
In young fruit bodies the colour of the cap is dark brown to cinnamon.
trzon: The stem reaches 7–15 cm, relatively long, resembling a Leccinum more than a Boletus, yellow or peach, strongly furrowed with a grooved surface.
miazsz: It has a pinkish tinge, and this colour does not change under the action of oxygen (oxidation).
spod: They are coloured from bright yellow to yellow-green.
Taste slightly sourish.

kapelusz: A medium-sized webcap.
Cap diameter (3) 4–8 cm, shape at first hemispherical, later convex, finally flat.
Margin sharp.
Surface dry, covered with fine, darker fibrils.
It is fleshy and not hygrophanous.
Colour from yellow-orange to reddish, paler when dried.
spod: Moderately crowded, fairly thick, up to 1 cm wide.
In young fruit bodies they are light yellow, later increasingly darker; yellow-brown, cinnamon-brown, rusty-brown.
Edges smooth.
trzon: Height up to 7 cm, thickness up to 1.5 cm, cylindrical in shape, slightly wider or bulbous at the base.
It is strong, solid.
Surface scaly or fibrillose with yellow remains of the veil, orange-yellow, reddish-brown at the bottom.
miazsz: Thick, fleshy.
In the cap it is yellowish in colour, in the stem saffron.
It is tasteless, but has an unpleasant smell, slightly similar to the smell of a cesspit.
podobne: Among the yellow webcaps the most similar are Cortinarius limonius and Cortinarius tofaceus.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–8 cm, at first hemispherical, then arched, finally flattened.
Surface bare, in young specimens remnants of a yellow cortina at the margin.
It is hygrophanous; in wet weather it is fox-red to orange-brown, in dry weather chrome, apricot-yellow or lemon-yellow with a darker top.
spod: Adnate, crowded, wavy, yellowish in young specimens, cinnamon or rusty brown in older ones.
trzon: Height 6–15 cm, thickness up to 1.5 cm, cylindrical, solid.
Surface colour from yellow to orange-yellow with yellow remnants of the cortina.
inne: Fairly thick, yellow or rusty yellow, rusty or orange at the base of the stem.
Taste and smell indistinct.
podobne: The species called zaslonak cytrynowozolty in Polish is characterised by a lemon-yellow or apricot-yellow cap, a chapped or wrinkled cap, and a fibrous or felty stem.
Cortinarius callisteus is similar, but it has a darker, more rusty-iron colour.
Cortinarius rubellus also has a similar colour when dry, but has a pointed umbo and sparser, darker gills.

owocnik: Diameter 2–10 cm, shape at first goblet-shaped, later cup-shaped, finally disc-shaped and spread out.
Sometimes it resembles an ear in shape.
The fruit body is bent and vein-like ribbed.
The upper surface is brown, dull, delicately suede-like, and sometimes frosted.
The spores are produced on the lower surface, which is red-brown and shiny, smooth, and in mature fruit bodies whitish from the spores.
In wet weather the fruit body is gelatinous and translucent.
In dry weather the fruit bodies may dry out and are then corky or horny, and their inner side takes on a colour from blackish-brown through brown-violet to blackish-grey.
However, after prolonged rain they soak up water again and regain their gelatinous consistency and springiness.
miazsz: Thin, gelatinous-springy, without smell, with a mild taste.
podobne: Auricularia auricula-judae can be confused with Auricularia mesenterica, which has a hairy, zoned upper surface.

inne: Gelatinous, soft, somewhat leathery; when dry hard and cartilaginous, attached flat; margin mostly spreading, pale, grey-brown and thickly hairy, on the underside grey to purple-brown; somewhat wrinkle-furrowed and ribbed.

kapelusz: Diameter up to 5 cm, shape flattened, kidney-shaped or semicircular.
It is hairy or felty and slightly zoned.
Cap margin paler.
Colour grey-brown to black. Specimens that have overwintered have a rather inconspicuous black-brown colouring and are often covered with green algae.
trzon: Lateral or eccentric, up to about 8 cm long.
Sometimes branched, brown-black in colour, hairy, thin.
spod: Up to 3 mm long, light, after a short time grey-brown, ending at the stem.
miazsz: From grey-brown to whitish, bast-like and elastic, without a distinct smell.
wysyp: Spores elliptical or egg-spherical, warty, colourless, 4–5.5 × 4–4.5 µm in diameter.

kapelusz: A small fungus with a cap diameter usually of 8–22 mm.
In young specimens the cap is hemispherical, then convex, finally flat, sometimes with a small knob in the centre.
Surface smooth, matt; when wet the gills show through slightly up to half of the cap diameter.
Margin straight, sharp and delicately, radially fibrillose.
spod: Narrowly attached to the stem or almost free, very crowded.
Colour whitish, in older ones with brown spots.
They are 1–2 mm wide and have smooth edges.
trzon: Height 1.5–5 cm, thickness 1–2 mm, of equal thickness, solid.
Surface densely and finely dusted with white granules.
In the upper part its colour is from pale cream to pale brown, in the lower part it is darker – pinkish-brown or yellowish-brown.
The stem is often rooting at the base, with white rhizomorphs and covered with white hairs.
miazsz: The same colour as the cap surface.
It has a faint mushroomy smell and taste.
podobne: On cones, 3 species of Strobilurus occur in Poland: Strobilurus esculentus, Strobilurus stephanocystis and Strobilurus tenacellus.
They occur mainly in spring.
Baeospora myosura is distinguished from them by a densely dusted stem, crowded gills, smaller size, mostly paler colour, and amyloid spores and thin-walled cheilocystidia.
Mycena strobilicola also occurs on cones.
It appears in spring.
It differs by a distinct smell of chlorine, a white, brittle stem and a more conical cap.

owocnik: Annual.
It is spread out flat, at first round in shape, thin and closely attached to the substrate.
Consistency fairly woody, surface at first white, then light yellow, finally yellow.
The outer edge remains white; through a lens it can be seen that it is shaggy.
Hymenophore spiny.
Spines conical, blunt, up to 5 mm long and 1–2 mm wide, of the same colour as the fruit body.
They have a rough, lumpy surface.
podobne: On wood there develop many similar species of fungi with a spread-out, spiny fruit body.
In the taxonomic diagnosis M.K.
Nobles emphasises that this species grows on bark and has a circular fruit body, but it can also grow on wood, and the circular fruit body is found only in young specimens.
Morphologically very similar are Hyphoderma setigerum and some other species of the genus Xylodon and Hyphodontia.
Also under the microscope it is difficult to tell apart some species of these genera.
It seems that a revision of these species is necessary.

owocnik: Annual.
A single fruit body is semicircular in shape, but also spread out or spread out and reflexed.
Fruit bodies often occur in large clusters, covering a stretch up to 5 m long.
A single fruit body is 2–10 cm wide and about 1 cm thick.
It is attached to the substrate sideways.
Usually the fruit bodies grow in groups, overlapping like roof tiles, one above the other.
Surface delicately velvety and wrinkled.
Colour from ochre-brown to grey-brown.
The marginal zone is distinctly paler, whitish, and only in older fruit bodies does it become grey-black.
spod: Tubular.
Tubes 4–6 mm long, clearly contrasting with the pale colour of the flesh.
They are separated from the flesh by a grey-blackish line visible on a transverse section of the fruit body.
After pressing, the tubes darken.
Pores rounded and fine; 4–6 per 1 mm.
Hymenophore colour from whitish to grey-dark brown.
miazsz: Whitish or cream, thin, leathery and elastic.
It has a faint, slightly sourish smell.
wysyp: Spores ellipsoid, flattened and narrowed on one side.
podobne: Similar is Bjerkandera fumosa.
It has thicker flesh and the hymenophore is not grey, but whitish-yellowish, turning only slightly brown on pressure.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–5 cm, at first closed, conical, later egg-shaped, finally spread out flat.
The margin of young fruit bodies is inrolled, the surface smooth, in colour from golden to egg-yolk golden.
In older fruit bodies the surface is slippery, pale yellow or olive-yellow in colour.
In older specimens the cap fades and becomes whitish, brownish only in the centre.
Older specimens have a clearly striate cap margin.
spod: Thin, moderately crowded.
In young fruit bodies they are coloured from whitish to clay yellow, in older ones ochre-rusty.
trzon: Relatively long compared with the diameter of the cap.
It is 5–10 cm long and 3–7 mm thick.
It is cylindrical, hollow inside, brittle.
Surface smooth, pale yellow, covered with a whitish bloom.
miazsz: Thin, yellowish, watery, without distinct smell and taste.

kapelusz: It is thick and sometimes wrinkled, and its diameter reaches 30 cm.
In young specimens it is semicircular, later flat-arched, finally flat.
Surface dry, at first suede-like, later smooth and bare, sometimes cracked.
Colour from dark brown through chestnut-brown to dark brown.
spod: They are up to 3 cm long and can be easily separated from the cap flesh.
In young fruit bodies they are white, cream, in older ones yellowish-olive, yellow-green, olive-green.
trzon: Height 5–12 cm, thickness 2–4 cm.
In young specimens the stem is usually swollen, thick, later club-shaped, cylindrical.
Surface pale brown-red with a characteristic dark brown net pattern.
miazsz: White, only brownish under the cap skin.
At first it is very hard, later it becomes softer.
It does not change colour in the air.
It has a mushroomy smell and taste.
podobne: Most similar is Boletus reticulatus, which grows in similar habitats and also has a reticulate stem, but this reticulum is more distinct and paler.
In addition it has a lighter cap (without chestnut-brown and blackish tinges).
Boletus edulis has a similar cap colouring to Boletus aereus, but it is paler, moreover its stem is not reticulate and it grows mainly under spruces.

kapelusz: It has a diameter from 6 to 25 centimetres.
In young individuals it is usually white, later sand-coloured.
With time it becomes light brown and dark brown.
It is rare for the cap of Boletus edulis to be carmine in colour.
The shape of the cap is at first smooth and semicircular, later more convex; old specimens are spread out like a cushion.
The cap surface is matt, may be wrinkled, in rain and in older individuals – it becomes smooth and sticky.
spod: Fine tubes, roundish in cross-section, 8 to 30 millimetres long.
They can be easily separated from the flesh of the cap.
Pores and tubes in young fruit bodies are usually white or cream.
In older individuals they are yellowish-olive, yellow-green and olive-green.
At the base the hymenophore is notched with a sinus.
Basidia measure 32–40 × 10–12 µm, club-shaped with 4 spores.
trzon: It is from 5 to 20 centimetres high and from 1.5 to 10 centimetres thick.
It is white, whitish-grey or sand-coloured.
In young individuals of Boletus edulis the stem is plump and deeply embedded in the ground, later it elongates and becomes club-shaped and barrel-shaped.
It has a delicate reticulum of whitish or light brown colouring, visible especially in the upper part of the stem.
miazsz: It is usually white, less often cream or sandy, reddish-brown under the skin.
In young individuals it is hard, and in older ones spongy.
It does not change colour in air or when sliced.
It has a pleasant smell, and the taste is described as nutty.
podobne: The king bolete is confused with other bolete species, until recently regarded rather as its varieties.
In Central Europe it is most easily confused with Boletus aereus, which looks almost identical to Boletus edulis.
The only feature that distinguishes these two species is the colour of the cap, which in Boletus aereus is much darker than in Boletus edulis.
The similar Boletus reticulatus usually has a cracked cap skin and a darker stem with a more distinct net.
In turn, Boletus pinophilus stands out by having both the cap and the stem reddish-brown.
In addition, Boletus edulis differs from Boletus pinophilus and Boletus reticulatus in the place where it most often occurs.
Boletus edulis is most often found under spruces, the pine bolete under pines, and Boletus reticulatus under oaks and beeches.
In North America the most similar species are: Boletus variipes, B. nobilis, B. barrowsii.

Boletus is sometimes confused with Tylopilus felleus, an inedible mushroom commonly found in Poland, which has a very bitter taste (when mixed with edible mushrooms it spoils all the flavour of the dish) and can cause stomach upset.
In the young stage the bitter bolete looks very similar to the porcini, but its tubes soon become slightly pink or take on a wine-red shade.
When touched the bitter bolete turns brown, in contrast to a bolete (Boletus), which does not change colour.

These fungi can be clearly distinguished by the stem, which in the bitter bolete is pale yellowish and covered with a darker, brownish, raised and palpable reticulum, much more distinct than in the porcini.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–30 cm, shape at first hemispherical, then flat-arched, finally spread out.
Surface delicately felty, usually uneven, bumpy or wrinkled, matt, sticky in rain.
It is red-brown in colour, sometimes with a purple or violet tinge.
spod: Tubular.
Tubes pale in young fruit bodies, in older ones gradually darkening to an olive-yellow colour.
trzon: Height 6–16 cm, thickness 3–7 cm, shape at first barrel-shaped, then egg-shaped, finally club-shaped, covered with a moderately distinct reticulum, whitish at the top, usually reaching the base where it is more brownish.
miazsz: In young fungi white (only red-brown under the skin), in older ones cream-white with a yellow tinge.
wysyp: Spores smooth, 14–18 × 5–6 μm, without a germ pore.
podobne: The pine bolete can be confused with edible species: Boletus edulis, Boletus reticulatus and with Boletus aereus, which grows under oaks and is a warmth-loving fungus.

kapelusz: Diameter up to 25 cm, in young specimens semicircular, smooth and dark brown, becoming spread out, cushion-shaped and lighter in older ones.
When it is dry for a longer period, small cracks can be seen on some older specimens.
spod: Up to 35–40 mm long.
In young fruit bodies white to grey-white, in older ones yellow-green to olive-green.
Sinuately notched at the stem.
Pores small, the colour of the tubes.
They do not change colour when pressed.
trzon: Thickness from 2 to 7 centimetres, height 8–25 cm.
Light brown or grey-brown.
Covered entirely with a raised reticulum (net), white when young to brownish in old fruit bodies, always paler than the stem.
In young specimens the stem is usually barrel-shaped, swollen, then club-shaped.
It is also sometimes cylindrical.
The mycelium at the base of the stem is white.
miazsz: White to cream, brownish under the skin, sometimes slightly yellowish above the tubes; does not change colour in the air.
Compact when young, spongy in older specimens.
Taste mild, nutty, smell pleasant.
wysyp: Spores smooth, ellipsoid-spindle-shaped and sometimes even cylindrical, without a germ pore, with extreme dimensions of 13–20 × 4–6 μm, but most often within the range 14–16 × 4.5–5.5 μm.
podobne: It can be confused with Tylopilus felleus.
This one, however, grows mainly in coniferous forests, has a very bitter taste and the reticulum on its stem is always darker than the stem itself.
It is also very similar to several other species of bolete, especially Boletus edulis or Boletus aereus.
Confusing it with them is of little importance from the mushroom pickers' point of view, since both these species are also edible.

owocnik: It is morphologically variable, but fairly easy to distinguish from similar species because of its parchment-like appearance.
It is flat, spread out on the substrate and closely attached to it, but with margins that bend away.
It is thin – 0.2–1 mm thick, but reaches a width and length of even several dozen centimetres.

The surface of young fruit bodies is white, smooth, later the margins bend more and more away from the substrate, and the surface of the fruit bodies becomes cream, pale yellowish, yellow-ochre, slightly reddish or greyish, irregularly reticulate or porous-pitted.
The wrinkles on the surface take a labyrinth-like shape.
Annual.
It is attached to the substrate by the side or by a distinctly narrowed base.
Fruit bodies grow singly or in a few clusters, in overlapping tiers.
A single one is 3–12 cm in diameter and 4–8 cm thick.
Shape semicircular, kidney-shaped, fan-shaped or bracket-shaped.
Margin sharp in young fruit bodies, sometimes slightly incised, rounded, thickened and darker in older ones.
Sometimes (rarely) the fruit body is spread out and reflexed.
The upper surface of the fruit body is smooth or mossy, usually uneven, hilly or warty near the base.
In young fruit bodies it is white, then cream, in older ones pale yellow-brown with darker spots and pits.
They form in places where the fruit body exudes drops of liquid.
spod: Tubular, located on the underside of the fruit body.
The tubes are 3–7 mm long, white to cream in colour and form only a single layer running obliquely downwards.
Pores round to maze-like in shape.
There are 3–4 of them per 1 mm.
In wet weather the tubes exude drops of colourless or white liquid.
miazsz: White, 5–15 mm thick.
In young fruit bodies fleshy and juicy, in older ones fibrous and bast-like.
After drying it becomes hard and brittle.
In taste at first weakly sourish, later burning and bitter.
Smell sharp and unpleasant.
podobne: There are many species of small-pored polypores, but the weeping one is easily recognised by several characteristic features:
in wet weather it exudes a white or colourless liquid, both from the hymenophore and on the surface of the cap,
the cap has an uneven, knobbly surface with pits left where the liquid has dried,
It has a characteristic smell similar to that of Heterobasidion.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–15 cm, hemispherical in young specimens, then arched.
Margin rolled under for a long time.
Colour light brown or grey-olive.
Surface suede-like.
spod: Long, sinuately notched at the stem, lemon-yellow in young specimens, darker – olive – in older ones.
Pores of the tubes round, fine, turning blue when crushed.
trzon: Height 7–14 cm, thickness 2–4.5 cm.
Strong and thick, at first barrel-shaped, then becoming cylindrical or club-shaped.
Yellow at the top, carmine-red at the bottom.
It is entirely covered with a net of delicate lines.
Under the cap it is white, in the centre red, at the bottom brown.
miazsz: Cream-coloured, pinkish near the stem base.
When cut it turns blue-green.
Taste bitter, smell faint, sourish.
podobne: Suillellus luridus is similar, but has orange-red tubes and does not have a red stem.
A similarly coloured cap is found in Rubroboletus satanas and Caloboletus radicans.

kapelusz: Diameter 8-15 (up to 30) cm.
Semicircular when young, then slightly flattened, of a pale, whitish-grey, grey-beige colour.
Cap skin suede-like, often cracked.
spod: Long, up to 15–30 mm, notched.
Light yellow when young, later lemon yellow, olive yellow with age, turning strongly blue when damaged.
trzon: Length up to 13 cm, diameter up to 18 cm.
Thickened in the middle part, narrowed at the bottom and ending in a point.
Buff-yellow, lemon-yellow, distinctly turning bluer in damaged places.
Coloured in the upper part, somewhat paler in the lower part.
Covered with a delicate reticulum visible only in its upper part.
miazsz: Firm, pale yellow, distinctly turning blue on cutting.
Smell unpleasant, at first mild, later distinctly bitterish.
podobne: Boletus calopus.
It is distinguished by a red-coloured stem without a rooting base and by flesh that turns blue less strongly.

kapelusz: Diameter 6–12 cm, in young specimens bell-shaped to conical, in older ones arched, finally flatly spread.
Cap not hygrophanous, thick-fleshed, usually with a small and blunt umbo, its margin is inrolled for a long time and often wavy.
Surface smooth, matt, whitish to cream in colour.
spod: Thin and crowded, notched with a tooth at the stem and adnate.
In young specimens whitish or cream, in older ones pale ochre.
trzon: Height 4–9 cm, thickness 1.5–4 cm, barrel-shaped in young specimens, cylindrical in older ones.
It is hard and solid, surface smooth, coloured from white to cream, often pale ochre in the lower part.
miazsz: Whitish, thick.
Taste mild, smell of fresh flour.
It does not change colour after damage.
podobne: Entoloma sinuatum.
It is more pinkish; the danger of confusion exists especially in young specimens, because the gills of both these species are white when young.
In older specimens of this species the gills become pink, and the spore print is also pink,
Inosperma erubescens.
It has a larger umbo on the cap, grows in forests and has a reddish tinge.

kapelusz: Diameter 6–10 cm, at first hemispherical, then arched, finally spread out flat and shallowly depressed, in wet weather slippery and shiny.
Surface intensely yellow with an olive tinge, orange-red in the centre, with brownish patches and radially arranged brown fibrils on it.
In young fruit bodies the cap together with the stem is surrounded by a whitish cortina.
spod: Broadly adnate, narrow, at first yellow with an olive tinge, then brown with an olive tinge.
trzon: Height 6–10 cm, thickness 1.3–2 cm, cylindrical, solid, with a wide bulb at the base reaching a diameter of up to 3.5 cm.
Surface sulphur yellow, covered with longitudinal fibrils of the veil, at first green-yellow, then changing colour from the spores to orange-brown.
miazsz: Whitish-yellowish, mild in taste, with the smell of dried dill or bread.
inne: NaOH colours the cap skin and flesh red-brown, Lugol's solution rusty-brown.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–8 cm, hemispherical when young, then flat, and even slightly concave in the centre.
Margin thin, straight, inrolled for a long time.
Surface smooth, very sticky and slippery, shiny and reddish when moist, silky when dry, yellow with red-brown small scales.
spod: Attached, crowded, thin, with short gills.
At first they are the same colour as the cap, later from the spores they become rusty-brown or ochre.
trzon: Cylindrical, longitudinally fibrillose with remnants of the veil.
Yellow mycelium often occurs at the base.
miazsz: Compact, golden yellow.
Smell indistinct, taste sweetish.
podobne: The most similar is Cortinarius elegantissimus / It may also be confused with Tricholoma equestre.

owocnik: Of the apothecium (cup) type, at first spherical, but then it splits unevenly forming a cup with wavy edges.
It is up to 5 cm in diameter.
Fruit bodies often grow close together and under pressure their natural circular shape is deformed; moreover, as it develops the cup becomes increasingly flattened.
Its inner surface is smooth, in colour from yellow to yellow-orange.
Outer surface fibrillose-rough and darker, dark blue in colour with a greenish-blue bloom.
Similar discolouration, but to a lesser degree, also occurs on the inner surface and on the mycelium growing from the apothecium into the soil.
Flesh brittle, cream, with a mild taste and no smell.
podobne: Much more common is Aleuria aurantia.
It also has an orange inner part of the cup, but the outer part is also orange and never has the dark blue and greenish-blue tones typical of Caloscypha fulgens.

owocnik: It is among the fungi that form the largest fruit bodies.
It produces impressive fruit bodies reaching 10–60 cm in diameter, circumference up to 135 cm, sometimes even more.
They are spherical or slightly flattened, and at the base they have a cord of white mycelium.
The peridium is thin.
The exoperidium of young fruit bodies is white and covered with a mealy bloom, with time it darkens and changes colour to pale ochre, finally to leathery brown.
The endoperidium is white, papery and during ripening also becomes increasingly darker: grey-yellowish, nut-brown and dirty brown.
After ripening the peridium splits in various places over the whole surface and the gleba is exposed.
At the base of the fruit body the gleba is poorly developed and mainly the subgleba occurs here; this is also where the fruit body splits last.
Gleba cottony, compact, denser towards the bottom.
In young fruit bodies it is white, as they mature it becomes golden-yellow, grey-yellow, finally olive-brown.
After the peridium splits and falls off, the gleba keeps its consistency for a short time, soon becoming powdery.
The subgleba is compact, difficult to distinguish from the soil.
podobne: There are many similar puffballs and earthballs, but the giant puffball is easy to distinguish thanks to its giant size.
One of the largest known fruit bodies, found in 1955 in northern Bohemia, was 46 cm tall, 212 cm in circumference and weighed 20.80 kg.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–8 cm, bell-shaped in young specimens, then broadly spread out, completely flat in old age, but not depressed.
In wet weather it is beige-yellow or yellow-brown, in dry weather it is from whitish to cream; older specimens become violet-grey from the gills showing through.
Young specimens are covered with a white, cobweb-like veil.
It disappears fairly quickly, remaining only at the margin, where it forms pale cream tufts.
This species, however, shows great morphological variability in the colour of the cap and the amount of its veil.
spod: In young specimens white, then grey-lilac, finally chocolate-brown.
They are often violet-grey in colour.
They are very crowded and have edges fringed whitish (this can only be seen with a magnifying glass).
trzon: Height 4–8 cm, thickness 2–3 mm.
It is cylindrical, longitudinally fibrous and very brittle.
At first it is whitish in colour and solid, then it becomes darker and hollow inside.
miazsz: Pale grey-brown, thin, brittle.
It has a faint mushroomy smell, taste indistinct.
podobne: There are many similar species of Psathyrella, for example Psathyrella piluliformis with a brown cap, but it may also be confused with the similar Lacrymaria lacrymabunda.

kapelusz: Diameter 1.5–4.5 cm, arched when young, later flat, finally funnel-shaped.
Sometimes it has a warty little umbo in the centre.
Surface when dry dull with adhering scales, when wet it turns black.
Colour grey-brown or grey, to violet.
spod: Broad and broadly adnate, slightly decurrent on the stem.
Colour white to cream-white.
When damaged they turn black after a while.
They are crowded and forked at the ends.
trzon: Height 3–10 cm, thickness 2–6 mm, cylindrical, solid and brittle.
Surface light grey-brown covered with longitudinal white fibres, darker in the upper part, felty at the base.
miazsz: Thin, whitish, without a distinct taste and smell.
When damaged it changes colour to light reddish.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–8 cm.
Arched and cushion-shaped in young specimens, with time flat, becoming funnel-shaped in older specimens.
At first it has inrolled margins, later it is bent in waves and lobed.
Skin yellow, but with a violet down, which in older specimens dries and takes the form of fine, adhering scales, especially in the centre of the cap.
spod: In the form of ridges deeply decurrent on the stem.
They are forked and connected by transverse anastomoses.
They are yellow-orange in colour, often with a pink tinge, and are wavy, which makes them resemble wrinkles.
trzon: Height 3–7 cm, thickness up to 2.5 cm, hard, yellow.
Shape cylindrical, in the upper part widening conically, passing smoothly into the cap.
miazsz: Pale yellow, springy and hard.
podobne: The most similar species is Cantharellus cibarius.
It differs in lacking the violet bloom on the cap and has less wavy and forked ridges.

kapelusz: Diameter 1–12 cm.
Button-like and round in shape in young fruit bodies, later convex with an inrolled margin, and in older specimens spread out, funnel-shaped and irregular.
Colour light yellow to orange-yellow.
Surface smooth, matt.
spod: In the form of irregularly and fork-like branched, thick ridges running far down the stem.
They are the same colour as the cap.
Often joined by anastomoses.
trzon: Height 3–6 cm, diameter up to 2.5 cm.
Colour of the cap, often of a paler shade.
Base narrowed, above it wider and passing gently into the cap.
Solid, hard and often bent.
miazsz: White or pale yellow in colour, of compact consistency, brittle, fibrous in the stem.
Smell fruity, spicy, slightly peppery.
Taste mild, sourish or slightly acrid.
wysyp: Spores measuring 7–11 × 4–6.5 µm, colourless, ellipsoid in shape, smooth.
podobne: Cantharellus amethysteus, whose cap is covered with felty, violet small scales (especially in young specimens).
It occurs mainly in the mountains under beeches and is rare.
Cantharellus friesii.
It is intensely orange and grows only in beech forests.
Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca, differing mainly in its thin and crowded gills and the darker, orange colour of the fruit bodies.
Mistaking the chanterelle (Cantharellus cibarius) for any of the other chanterelle species does not matter from the mushroom pickers' point of view, since they are all edible.
However, it is easily confused with the false chanterelle, which according to some authors is inedible, according to others poisonous.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–8 cm.
Arched in young specimens, then flat, finally funnel-shaped, fleshy.
Margin lobed, wavy, blunt, surface coloured from white to yellowish, often whitish or yellowish mottled.
spod: Ridged (phlebioid).
Ridges low and forked, deeply decurrent on the stem and of the same colour.
trzon: Height 3–7 cm, thickness up to 3 cm, hard, widening upwards and gradually merging into the cap.
Surface bare, smooth and of the same colour as the cap.
miazsz: Fleshy, whitish, not changing colour when damaged, with a slight spicy smell and a delicately burning taste.
wysyp: Spores ellipsoid with a hilar appendage, smooth, hyaline, with granules and guttules, 8–9 × 4.5–5 µm.
podobne: Cantharellus cibarius is usually smaller, has a very intense yellow colour and a fruity smell.
It prefers more acidic soils and lives together with a larger number of tree species: beech, birch, oak, spruce and pine.
Cantharellus amethysteus has various yellow colours with a violet to amethyst tinge.
It also prefers acid soils and occurs under deciduous trees, including oak, beech and birch, but sporadically also under conifers.
Cantharellus ferruginascens is more slender and its pressed places slowly change colour to rusty.

kapelusz: Diameter 10–40 cm.

Young ones almost flat with a rolled-under margin, older ones slightly funnel-shaped; covered with dark brown scales on a whitish to light brown background (looking from the centre outwards of the cap).
spod: Irregular, angular, white/cream pores, the smaller the farther from the stem, 1–2.5 mm in diameter, decurrent.
trzon: Most often lateral, short and stocky, with tubes passing smoothly from the cap to the stem.
At the top usually white or dirty flesh-coloured, at the bottom covered with brown-black or black down.
miazsz: White, with a weak taste and a mealy-cucumber smell.
It is juicy-fleshy, and after drying becomes light, corky and brittle.
wysyp: Spores oblong elliptical, smooth, measuring 10–13 × 4–5 µm.
podobne: Polyporus tuberaster.
Fruit body much smaller (up to 15 cm in diameter).
Cap funnel-shaped, stem central.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–10 cm, shape round or kidney-shaped, convex in young specimens, spread out flat in older ones.
Surface smooth and bare.
Cap margin sometimes wavy.
Colour in young specimens fawn-red or cinnamon, in older ones grey-yellow.
spod: Small, 0.1–0.2 mm in diameter and 0.5–1.5 mm long, running down one side of the stem.
They form only a single layer.
Pores at first white, brownish in older specimens.
trzon: Height 0.5–2 cm, thickness 0.5–1.5 cm.
It usually grows from the side.
In the upper part it is the same colour as the cap, whereas in the lower part it is black.
miazsz: White, with a faint smell and a somewhat bitter taste.
wysyp: Spores cylindrical or sausage-shaped, smooth, measuring 10–7 × 2–3.5 μm.
A species with fairly high morphological variability.
Individual specimens differ quite considerably in colour and in the shape of the cap.
In dry weather its development often stops, and the pores take on a brown colour.
podobne: Picipes melanopus.
It has a dark brown and suede-like cap,
Picipes badius has an entirely black stem.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–5, exceptionally up to 7 cm.
Cushion-shaped in young specimens, slightly flattened in older ones.
Skin smooth, orange-brown in colour.
In wet weather it is greasy.
spod: Fairly short, attached or slightly decurrent on the stem.
They are rusty-brown in colour.
The pores are darker, brick-brown in colour, with a coppery tint.
They are large, angular and have uneven edges.
trzon: Height 2–6 cm, diameter 0.4–1 cm.
It has the same colour as the cap, only in the lower part it is lighter (yellowish).
It is cylindrical, equally thick over its whole length, or slightly narrowed below, solid, sometimes slightly bent.
miazsz: Cream in the cap, yellow or lemon yellow in the stem.
It has a weak smell and an acrid, burning taste.
podobne: Suillus variegatus is similar in appearance, but is clearly larger and does not have such a burning taste.
The similar Boletinus cavipes is easily distinguished by its hollow stem and disappearing ring.
It has a somewhat bitter taste, but not as burning as the peppery bolete.

kapelusz: Diameter 46–130 mm, spherical in young fruit bodies, umbrella-shaped and grey in older ones, covered with fine scales of a colour similar to the cap skin.
In the centre a large patch of colour from brown to red-brown.
spod: White, free, fairly crowded, 1–7 mm away from the stem.
When damaged they turn red.
With age they become beige.
trzon: Height 80–190 mm, 7–13 mm thick, smooth, coloured whitish to light beige, ending in a bulb.
Ring movable, double.
miazsz: Whitish; when damaged it changes colour to red-yellow or orange, with age to red.
Smell earthy or mushroomy, taste unpleasant.
