miazsz: 2–6 cm thick, soft when young, fleshy, full of blood-coloured juice, flesh-red with marbled veins, with a pleasant smell and a sourish taste.
spod: 10–15 cm long, compact and dense, whitish, yellowish, later rusty-brown.
Pores fine, spherical, 0.2–0.3 mm in diameter.
trzon: Lateral, short, 2–4 cm long, barely noticeable.
wysyp: Spores egg-shaped, smooth, colourless, measuring 4–6 × 3–4 μm.

kapelusz: Diameter 1–7 cm, hemispherical in young fruit bodies, flat in older ones.
Yellow-orange, orange or yellow-brown, smooth, very slimy and shiny in wet weather.
spod: First whitish, later ochre-yellow, sparse, rounded and convex at the stem.
trzon: Height 5–10 cm, thickness 3–8 mm, cylindrical, hollow like a tube, central or lateral, often curved.
Ring absent.
Colour blackish-brown, lightened to yellow at the top.
Starting from the bottom more or less covered with brown suede.
miazsz: Elastic, fibrous in the stem.
White or cream, thin, not changing colour when cut.
Taste insignificant, smell pleasant, but indistinct.
podobne: The white spore print is very characteristic and definitely distinguishes the velvet shank from the fungi with which it may be confused: Galerina marginata, Kuehneromyces mutabilis or Hypholoma fasciculare.
All those mentioned have a darker spore print.
Also very characteristic of the velvet shank are the time of appearance of the fruit bodies, the suede-like dark stem and the copper-yellow colour of the cap.
Other species of the genus Flammulina are very similar to Flammulina velutipes; in Europe they include:
Flammulina elastica – differs in the shape of the gills and in microscopic features.
It occurs mainly on willows, less often on aspen.
Flammulina fennae – occurs mainly in summer and usually has a paler cap.
Flammulina ononidis – grows in meadows on the remains of spiny restharrow.
The poplar velvet shank – unlike the velvet shank – usually has a rooting stem.
It is also paler, occurring mainly on poplars.
Flammulina rossica – has a very pale cap, differs mainly in microscopic features.

kapelusz: It is up to 50 cm wide, at first bulbous, later hoof-shaped.
On the upper side it is covered with a hard, non-cracking crust.
In young specimens it is velvety, in older ones bare and matt.
In young specimens it is clay-coloured or red-brown, in older ones grey or blackish.
On the crust concentric rings are visible, which are zones of annual growth.
The cap margin is whitish and blunt.
spod: Arranged in many layers, 2–7 cm long.
At first they are pale orange, later orange-brown, finally ochre-brown.
They darken when pressed.
miazsz: Thickness 0.5–3 cm.
It is rusty brown, soft, corky-woody, in the cap it has a suede-like structure, at the point of attachment vegetative mycelium.
wysyp: In May and June it releases white, powdery spores.
podobne: Fomitopsis pinicola.
It has a more vivid growth zone (yellow or orange-red) and red-brown flesh.
Older specimens of it are morphologically difficult to distinguish, because they no longer have such a bright border.
These species can, however, be easily told apart with a match; in Fomitopsis pinicola the crust melts under high temperature, in Fomes fomentarius it chars.
Phellinus hartigii, but it grows mainly on firs.
Phellinus igniarius, but it grows mainly on willows.

owocnik: Width 5–20 cm, thickness 5–20 cm.
Young specimens have a bulbous shape, which with time changes to bracket-shaped or cap-shaped.
The outer surface is smooth, wavy, concentrically zoned.
It is coloured from grey to dark brown, the margin (growth edge) is paler; in colour from whitish to ochre-brown.
In older specimens the upper surface is often overgrown with algae, turning green.
spod: Tubular, rusty-brown in young individuals, grey-brown in older ones.
The tubes are 3–5 mm long and there may be many layers of them in the fruit body, but the differences between them are barely visible.
Setae absent.
miazsz: Yellow-brown, very tough, without a distinct taste or smell.
wysyp: Spores almost spherical, smooth, measuring 6-7.5 × 5–6.5 μm{.
podobne: Phellinus igniarius, but it grows only on deciduous trees, mainly on willows and poplars,
the so-called Formitoporia robusta.
It grows mainly on old oaks, often high in their crowns,
Fomitopsis pinicola.
It has a brighter growth edge; yellow or orange-red.
Phellinus tremulae, but it grows only on aspen.

owocnik: The fruit body is closely attached to the substrate, sometimes covers a large area and is matched in colour to the tree species on which it occurs.
At first it is flat, but every year it produces a new, cushion-shaped, dark spore-bearing layer, as a result of which it gradually becomes more and more convex, cushion-shaped.
It reaches a width of 2–30 cm and a thickness of up to 2.5 cm.
Fruit bodies usually occur singly, less often in groups of two or three.
They have a surface in colour from cinnamon-rufous to chestnut-brown.
The margin of the fruit body is clearly delimited from the substrate, in young specimens fluffy felty.
spod: Tubular, brown in young individuals, grey-brown in older ones.
The tubes are 5–6 mm long and up to 10 layers of them, one on top of another, may occur in the fruit body.
The pores are so small that they are not visible to the naked eye.
They have oblique mouths, slightly mouldy.
In the hymenium there are few and poorly developed bristles, sometimes none at all.
miazsz: Dark, reddish-brown; very bast-like and tough.
podobne: Phellinus laevigatus has a cracked surface covered with nodules and warts, and a grey to grey-black colour.
Phellinus conchatus is dark brown and often overgrown with mosses.

owocnik: Perennial fruit body, hard and woody – a typical bracket fungus.
It occurs singly, or in groups in which neighbouring fruit bodies sometimes fuse together.
A single individual is hemispherical, hoof-shaped or knobbly, reaching a width of up to 30 cm and a thickness of up to 20 cm.
It is attached to the substrate sideways.
Upper surface uneven, sometimes distinctly hilly, usually cracked and broadly, concentrically zoned.
At first delicately velvety or felty and yellow-rusty, then bare and ever darker – dark rusty, olive, grey-brown to almost black.
Margin blunt, broad, rounded, slightly wavy and always lighter – yellow-rusty.
spod: Tubular, brown in young individuals, grey-brown in older ones.
Tubes (2–) 3–5 (7–) mm long, slightly paler than the flesh.
They form many layers, clearly separated by thin layers of trama.
Pores round and very fine, 0.15–0.25 mm in diameter, 5–6 per 1 mm.
At first they are yellow-brown, then dark brown or light cinnamon and often mossy.
Old pores often become overgrown with brown mycelium.
Smell weak, taste indistinct.
miazsz: Very hard and woody, weakly zoned, turning black under the action of KOH.
It is up to 8 cm thick, with a silky sheen, colour at first yellow-rusty, then rusty-cinnamon.

kapelusz: Annual fruit body 10–30 cm in diameter, attached sideways to the trunk and narrowed at the point of attachment.
On the upper side grey-whitish to brownish, covered with a matt, cracking and peeling skin.
Shape hemispherical or cushion-shaped.
spod: They are 1.5–5 (exceptionally up to 8) mm long, white in young specimens, straw yellow in older ones.
Pores round.
The tubes of mature fruit bodies can easily be separated from the flesh of the cap.
Taste astringent, slightly bitterish
miazsz: White, uniformly compact on a cross-section, non-fibrous, bast-like.
After drying it becomes corky.
wysyp: Spores cylindrical and comma-shaped with a sharply ending base, measuring 5–7 × 1.5-2 µm.
They have a smooth surface and usually two oil droplets (guttules) inside.

owocnik: A bracket fungus with a perennial fruit body attached sideways to a tree (living or dead).
Width reaches 40 cm, thickness up to 15 cm.
Young specimens have a flattened fruit body, older ones – thicker, hoof-shaped.
Older fruit bodies covered with a hard grey-brown skin with a paler growth zone.
During great heat the skin melts.
Growth zone: in young ones whitish, orange to cherry-coloured, in older ones darker and narrower.
spod: On the underside of the fruit body there are several layers of tubes up to 8 mm long in each layer, cream to yellowish in colour.
With age the underside of the fruit body becomes brown.
Tube pores round, regular.
The hymenophore turns cream-coloured when crushed, or on old fruit bodies.
However, the age of the fruit body cannot be determined from the number of tube layers, because within a year it can produce from one to several of these layers.
miazsz: Wood-coloured or lemon-yellow to yellow-brown, turning slightly pink when damaged.
It is bitter in taste.
wysyp: Spores smooth and colourless, elliptical or oblong-egg-shaped, measuring 6–8 × 3–4 μm.
podobne: Rhodofomes roseus with smaller fruit bodies (up to 8 cm wide) in colour from dirty pink through purple-pink to almost black.
Older fruit bodies of Fomitopsis pinicola become grey and very similar to Fomes fomentarius.

They can be distinguished by the colour of the pores (yellow in Fomitopsis pinicola), the growth zone (brown in the hubiak (Fomes)) or by the match test: in the hubiak (Fomes) the skin under a lit match only chars, in Fomitopsis pinicola it melts.

owocnik: It is perennial, reaching an age of up to 10 years.
It attaches to the substrate by its side and has a varied shape.
It may be semicircular, shelf-shaped, sometimes cushion-shaped, spread out with a turned-back margin, or irregular.
Width 5–25 cm, thickness 2–6 cm, margin of the fruit body sharp.
Surface bare, wavy and usually unzoned, only at the margin there is slight zoning.
Colour light brownish, similar to the colour of wood.
spod: Gilled, labyrinth-like.
Gills not layered, flexible and thick, 2–5 cm long, cream-brown in colour.
miazsz: Colour from cream to brown, corky and flexible.
After drying it becomes very light.
podobne: Daedaleopsis confragosa has a similar, maze-like hymenophore, but forms a thin, zoned fruit body with a very sharp margin.

owocnik: A bracket fungus with a perennial, durable fruit body, usually attached sideways to the tree.
Width reaches 8 cm, thickness up to 3 cm.
Fruit bodies usually occur in groups of several, sometimes growing together.
They are hemispherical or hoof-shaped, sometimes bracket-shaped, in which case their hymenophore runs down onto the substrate.
Surface uneven, warty, delicately hairy in young specimens, bare in older ones.
Sometimes it is cracked.
It is concentrically furrowed.
At first it is grey-pink in colour, then increasingly darker – from purple-brown to black.
The margin is paler (pinkish) and sterile (without hymenophore), sharp in young specimens, blunt and wavy in older ones.
miazsz: Hard, corky or woody, when torn it has a flocculose-fibrous structure.
It is indistinctly banded.
When raw it is salmon-pink in colour, after drying dirty flesh-coloured.
spod: Tubular, at first white-pink in colour, later dirty flesh-coloured.
Darkens when pressed.
The tubes are 5–7 mm long and form many indistinct layers.
The tube pores are angular and small; there are 3–4 (exceptionally up to 5) pores per 1 mm.
Each of them is 0.1–0.3 mm in diameter, and the pore walls are thick.
In the older layers these pores are overgrown with white mycelium.
The hymenophore has a faint mushroomy smell and a bitter taste.
podobne: It is easy to distinguish from other bracket fungi because of the pink colour of the hymenophore and flesh.
A pink hymenophore is also found in Leptoporus mollis and in the so-called Rhodonia placenta, but their fruit bodies are not woody, they are annual and soft.
They can also be easily distinguished by the match test; the surface of the rosy conk melts in the flame of a match, whereas the ones listed above only char.

owocnik: Most often crust-like and rather weakly attached to the substrate.
Sometimes, especially on vertical trunks, it forms something like caps – numerous, slightly bent-back folds, which on the outer side are yellowish-brown in colour.
Shape very variable; irregular, knobbly or bracket-shaped, often overlapping like roof tiles.
Surface in colour from whitish to yellow-brown.
Margin white and usually wavy-bent.
spod: They are up to 5 mm long and whitish.
Pores round to angular in shape and 0.2–0.4 mm in diameter.
On average there are 3 pores per 1 mm of length.
miazsz: White, elastic and corky.
Taste and smell indistinct.
podobne: If the margins of the fruit bodies are not bent back, distinguishing this species from other similar ones is difficult.

kapelusz: Diameter 1.5–5 cm, at first hemispherical, later convex, finally flat.
It usually has a blunt, broad umbo.
It is strongly hygrophanous; when dry it is from pale beige to yellow-ochre, in wet weather it becomes ochre-brown or red-brown.
When drying it becomes paler from the top.
In wet weather radial striation is visible, in dry weather the striation is invisible.
spod: Slightly bulging, broadly adnate and notched with a tooth at the stem.
Their colour is at first ochre-brown, later rusty brown, the gill edges are paler.
trzon: Height 2–8 cm, thickness 0.1–0.6 cm.
Cylindrical, hollow inside.

It has an impermanent annular zone, above which it is ochre in colour and mealy-dusted, below it is brownish in colour and covered with longitudinal, silvery-white fibrils, at the base darker (in colour from olive-brown to black).
miazsz: Pale ochre in the cap, umber-brown in the stem.
Taste and smell mealy with an admixture of radish.
wysyp: Spores elliptical, with a rough or wrinkled surface, measuring 7–11 × 4–6 μm.
podobne: It can easily be confused with Kuehneromyces mutabilis, which is an edible fungus.
It differs in its cinnamon-coloured gills and in the presence of black-brown scales on the stem below the ring.
Flammulina velutipes is also similar.
This one, however, has a dark stem without a ring.

kapelusz: Perennial, hoof-shaped or semicircular, 10–30 cm in size, 4–10 cm thick.
It is attached by its side.
The cap on its upper surface is matt, red-brown, in older specimens brown-black.
Its surface is strongly wavy and knobbly, sometimes with distinct zones.
Margin of the cap rounded and pure white.
Skin hard, does not allow itself to be dented with a finger.
spod: Small, round, white, turning brown when pressed.
On older specimens they become brown.
Tube length 10–15 mm.
miazsz: Chocolate-brown or chestnut-brown.
It is fibrous, corky and hard.
It is several times thicker than the length of the individual tubes and has distinctly marked growth zones.
podobne: Ganoderma pfeifferi Bres.
Fruit body unzoned, copper-red or rusty purple in colour, and the pores yellowish with time.
It grows on deciduous trees, mainly on beech.
Ganoderma resinaceum Boud.
Fruit body brick-red or almost black and sometimes shiny.
Grows on deciduous trees, mainly on oak.

kapelusz: Perennial, hoof-shaped or semicircular, 10–50 cm in size, 1–5 cm thick.
It is attached by its side.
Cap on the upper surface of a colour from red-brown to brown-grey.
It is covered with a hard crust with a strongly zoned, wavy and knobbly surface.
It is often covered with a thick, rusty-brown layer of spores, which not only fall downwards but, because of air turbulence, also settle on the upper surface of the fruit body.
The cap margin is pure white, knobbly and flattened.
Surface smooth, sometimes slightly shiny, but without a lacquered coating.
spod: 5–10 mm long, round, white, turning brown when pressed.
On a cross-section they form several layers, which are separated by a thin intermediate layer of brown colour.
Urn-shaped galls of the fly Aganthomyia wankowiczi often occur on the pores.
So far the galls of this fly have not been observed on any other species of fungus.
At the places where these insects feed, galls may form on the hymenophore.
miazsz: Fairly soft, elastic, whitish in young fruit bodies, later cinnamon-brown to dark brown.
It darkens when pressed, and turns black with KOH.
Taste bitter, slightly burning.
podobne: Ganoderma adspersum.
It differs by a thicker fruit body, darker, red flesh and larger spores.
It is resistant to feeding by insect larvae.
Ganoderma pfeifferi.
It has a hoof-shaped fruit body (but sometimes also flat), unzoned.
Grows on beech.

owocnik: Annual, bracket type, reaching a size of 3–18 × 5–22 × 14 cm.
It consists of a stem and a cap.
Cap laterally attached, flat, semicircular or kidney-shaped.
Upper surface shiny, as if varnished, even in young fruit bodies, wavy, uneven and knobbly in older ones, coloured from brown to black.
The outer edge, being the zone of active growth, is at first white to cream in colour, in older specimens brown.
Stem conical, often flattened, irregularly bent, 1–10 cm long and 0.7–4 cm thick.
It is mostly lateral, rarely central, shiny like the cap, and brown to black in colour.
Context in the cap and stem at first whitish to cream in colour, then pale brown, soft and corky, up to 3.5 cm thick.
When dry it is light.
Hymenophore tubular, whitish in young fruit bodies, then cream, finally brownish.
Tube layer up to 2.5 cm thick and coloured from light brown to cocoa, separated from the stem by a groove.
Pores 3–4 per 1 mm.
podobne: The brown-black lacquer bracket is related to Ganoderma lucidum.
It differs from it by a more massive fruit body, the brown-black colour of the cap surface, paler context and broader spores with a rough surface.
Moreover it grows mainly on the wood of conifers, whereas Ganoderma lucidum grows mainly on broadleaved trees.

kapelusz: 8–25 cm in diameter, flat, semicircular or kidney-shaped.
At first light, lemon yellow, with age it fairly quickly changes colour to yellow-red, later darkens to purple, purple-brown, finally red-blackish.
Surface uneven, usually furrowed.
Margin of the fruit body narrow, wavy, white or straw yellow in colour.
The most characteristic feature of this species is the glossy, as if varnished, surface.
trzon: Eccentric or lateral, of irregular cylindrical shape and covered with nodules.
It may be up to 15 cm long and up to 2 cm thick, it has a colour similar to the cap and is also glossy.
There are, however, forms without a stem, attached sideways, or with only a rudimentary stem.
spod: They usually form one layer, more rarely two or three.
They are 2–20 (30) mm long.
Pores small, round, at first whitish, then cream, brown with age.
There are 4–5 of them per 1 mm.
They turn brown when touched.
miazsz: Spongy, white, ochre just above the tubes, indistinctly streaked, without any specific taste or smell.
podobne: Ganoderma carnosum, whose fruit bodies are darker in colour and grow on conifers.
Formitopsis pinicola.

owocnik: Perennial, bracket type, large, reaching a diameter of up to 45 cm.
It is attached to the substrate sideways, sometimes there is only a rudimentary stem.
Shape semicircular or kidney-shaped.

Surface smooth, shiny or matt, weakly grooved, yellowish in young fruit bodies, covered with a thin resinous layer, in older ones darker and darker – brick-chestnut, dark red-brown, and finally almost black.
When dried it is often cracked.
Margin blunt, thick, in colour from whitish to cream.
Hymenophore tubular.
Tubes 5–20 mm long, usually forming only one layer, more rarely 2–5 layers.
Pores small, circular, 2–2.5 per 1 mm.
podobne: The pale-fleshed Ganoderma may be confused with Ganoderma pfeifferi, which has a similar resinous crust on the upper surface of the fruit body, but is distinguished by its dark brown or umber context and broader spores.
Ganoderma lucidum has a paler context, without a darker zone above the tubes and does not have a resinous crust, as a result of which it is much more shiny (even in older specimens).
It is also distinguished by its spores.

owocnik: When young spherical, sometimes slightly flattened. 1–4 cm in diameter, entirely covered with a thin layer of mycelium.
The outer covering splits to half the height of the fruit body into 6–12 triangular non-hygroscopic lobes, which spread out star-like and hold a thick layer of mycelium with the substrate.
Opened fruit bodies reach 4–9 cm in diameter.
The arms of fresh specimens are brown-grey or dark grey, when dry paler, greyish or coffee-coloured.
Inner envelope inversely pear-shaped, taller than wide, set on a distinct, short and thick neck.
A distinct apophysis at the base of the inner veil.
Apical opening flat or slightly raised, fringed, without a small disc, but with a paler circular area.
Interior of the fruit body black-brown.
podobne: The crowned earthstar can be confused with Geastrum pectinatum, whose spherical head is comb-like furrowed at the bottom.

owocnik: Spherical, sometimes slightly flattened, up to 2 cm in diameter.
In mature specimens the outer covering splits into 7–8 (up to 10) arms arranged in a star shape, which spread open and bend downwards.
The arms are fleshy, at first white-ochre, then beige to light ochre.
Developed fruit bodies reach a diameter of 2 to 8 cm.
The inner envelope of the fruit body is of the same colour as the arms, 1.5–2 cm in diameter, sessile, without a neck.
The opening at the top (peristome) is flat or slightly raised, fringed without a collar.
The inside of the fruit body is dark, grey-brown.
podobne: Geastrum fimbriatum can be confused with Geastrum rufescens, which differs in its reddish flesh and larger fruit bodies.

owocnik: Young ones have the form of the so-called "egg", of a characteristic, onion-like shape and 3–5 cm in diameter.
Its surface is light brown, darker with age, sometimes slightly pinkish.
The egg is partly sunk in the ground and furrowed before it bursts.
The exoperidium splits halfway into 5-8 fleshy arms, which spread out like a star.
Fruit bodies developed in this way reach a diameter of 5 to 18 cm.
The inner side of the arms is smooth, light or dark brown, sometimes with a reddish tinge, usually cracked in various ways.

At the same time as the exoperidium splits, the ochre-grey fleshy layer, about 3 mm thick, splits right at the base of the fleshy arms, its edges detach from the fibrous layer and form a neck-like collar surrounding the inner layer (endoperidium).
Sometimes this collar remains only in the form of a disc.
The endoperidium is more or less spherical, sometimes slightly flattened, 2–4 cm in diameter, parchment-like, sessile and without an apophysis.
At first it has the same colour as the fleshy layer, later it becomes ochre-brown.
It opens through an opening in the upper part in the centre.
The margin of this opening (peristome) is low, slightly raised and fibrous.
The columella reaches to half the height of the endoperidium.
The gleba is brown.
podobne: Smaller fruit bodies can be confused with Geastrum fimbriatum or Geastrum rufescens.
The gwiazdosz potrojny (Polish name), however, is fairly clearly distinguished from other species of earthstars by two features: large size and the presence of a collar.

owocnik: Spherical, slightly flattened, conically bulging at the top, 2–5 cm in diameter.
Entirely surrounded by a layer of ochre-brown to reddish-brown mycelium, which also grows through particles of soil.
The outer covering (ectoperidium) splits from the top to the middle of the fruit body into 5–6 (up to ten) triangular, unequal arms, which spread open and then bend under the fruit body.
When dried they may bend back again and cover the endoperidium once more.
Developed fruit bodies reach a diameter of 3–8 cm.
The arms are at first flesh pink, later red-brown, covered with fine cracks after drying.
Inner covering (endoperidium) up to 3 cm in diameter, roundish, slightly bulging at the top, pale ochre to brownish, sessile, although in dried fruit bodies a small neck may appear.
The apical opening (peristome) with an uneven, fringed margin, flat, without a collar.
The columella is fairly persistent, reaching at least to the middle of the endoperidium.
Gleba brown.
podobne: Geastrum rufescens can be confused with Geastrum fimbriatum, whose fruit bodies are smaller and whose flesh does not turn red.

owocnik: Closed when young, roundish, slightly raised at the top, 1.5–4 cm in diameter.
Surface covered with remains of the substrate of the mycelium.
The outer covering splits down to the middle into 6-10 triangular arms, which spread open and then curl under, as a result of which the fruit body takes on a star shape.
With the arms bent back it reaches a diameter of 4–6.5 (9) cm.
Inner covering strongly flattened, pale, in young fruit bodies covered with a spongy bloom.
At the base a distinct apophysis with a sharp edge directed downwards.
Neck distinct, 0.4–0.6 cm high.
The apical opening (peristome) is up to 0.5 cm tall, at first covered with a mealy bloom, later crested, with 16–20 notches, surrounded by a rim or without a rim.
podobne: The striated earthstar (Geastrum striatum) can be confused with Geastrum pectinatum, from which it differs in its apophysis.
In the striate earthstar the apophysis has a sharp edge directed downwards.
At the base of the endoperidium it forms a kind of collar.

owocnik: Thickness up to 3 cm, diameter up to 10 cm.
It is usually attached sideways and is semicircular, circular, spread out, sometimes ridged in shape.
Colour of the surface from red-brown to tobacco-brown, the outer, fresh growth zone is orange-yellow in colour.
It is wavy-grooved and zoned, bristly-haired when young, bare in older specimens.
spod: Variable; usually gilled, sometimes gill-and-pore or poroid.
Gills often connected by transverse anastomoses.
Colour from yellowish through orange and rusty to rusty brown.
miazsz: Thin, dark brown, leathery and elastic.
Taste mild or slightly bitter.
podobne: There are several similar species of earthstars.
Gloeophyllum abietinum has a darker colouring (without yellow and orange tones) and loose, thick gills.
It grows only on the wood of conifers.
Gloeophyllum trabeum grows on both coniferous and broadleaved wood, but its hymenophore takes the form of labyrinthine or anastomosing gills.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–15 cm, bluntly conical in young specimens, later hemispherical, arched, finally flat and concave in the centre or even funnel-shaped.
Margin always inrolled.
Surface smooth and covered with slime (it dries out during drought).
Young fruit bodies are violet-grey, grey-brown, older ones chocolate brown, finally ochre.
Slimy remnants of the veil often hang from the cap margins.
spod: Distant, of different lengths, decurrent at the stem.
Whitish in young specimens, darker in older ones.
trzon: Height 2–5 cm, thickness up to 3 cm, cylindrical, solid, slippery.
It has a disappearing ring.
Surface whitish, yellow in places below.
Under the cap, remains of a slimy veil.
miazsz: Brownish under the cap, in the lower part lemon-coloured in places, otherwise whitish.
It has a mild taste and a faint smell.
podobne: Gomphidius maculatus, found under larches.
It differs somewhat in the colour of the cap (flesh-ochre to brown-flesh) and is covered with dark brown spots,
Chroogomphus helveticus.
It is not slimy and has an orange-brown to pink-violet fruit body.
Chroogomphus rutilus is not slimy and has a red-brown cap.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–6 cm, hemispherical in young specimens, later cushion-shaped, flat and depressed in the centre in older ones.
Cap margin inrolled for a long time.
In dry weather it is dry, in wet weather slippery.
Pink through grey-pink to bright red in colour.
spod: In young specimens they are covered by a slimy veil.
They are distant and thick with straight edges, decurrent on the stem.
At first they are white, later they turn grey-grey from the spores.
trzon: Height 2–5 cm, thickness up to 3 cm.
It is cylindrical and solid, has a fairly quickly disappearing and not very distinct ring.
Above the ring it is white, in the lower part yellow, the whole of it is slippery.
miazsz: Whitish in the cap, yellowish in the stem.
Taste and smell indistinct.
podobne: A characteristic species, easy to distinguish from other species.

owocnik: Annual, large to very large, 20 to 60 cm in diameter, bushy-branched, composed of many spatula-shaped caps growing from a common trunk.
Single caps tongue-shaped or semicircular, flat, 4–10 cm in diameter, thin, brittle, nut-brown, yellow-olive in colour.
Cap margins uneven, cut, radially wrinkled.
spod: 2–3 mm long, whitish, decurrent on the stem.
Pores small, about 0.5 mm in diameter.
miazsz: Thin, up to 0.5 cm thick, white, fleshy.
Smell pleasant, mushroomy, taste mild.
podobne: Polyporus umbellatus, whose fruit bodies are attached to the stalks centrally, and their colour is paler, whitish to pale ochre.
Meripilus giganteus, whose fruit bodies are much larger and wider, composed of larger caps.
Besides, it appears on many tree species, whereas Daedalea quercina occurs almost exclusively on oaks.

Bondarzewia mesenterica, which grows at the base of firs and is distinguished by large, angular and uneven pores, and its fruit bodies, as in the wachlarzowiec (Meripilus), are built of larger and more spreading caps.

owocnik: Height 5–12 cm, width 3–7 cm, spatula-shaped, tongue-shaped, funnel-shaped, often formed like a horn, narrowed below, often with a slit.
It is translucent.
Surface bare, in young fruit bodies coloured from orange to salmon-red, in older ones coral-red to reddish-brown.
The hymenium is on the inner side.
At first it is smooth, later ribbed-wrinkled or veined and often whitish from the spores.
trzon: Short, cylindrical or narrowed downwards, hollow, torn at the top.
Whitish colour.
miazsz: It is 2–5 mm thick, at first springy and cartilaginous, then gelatinous, and in older fruit bodies it dissolves.
At first it is orange in colour, with time it fades and becomes yellowish.
It is tasteless and has a pleasant smell.

kapelusz: Diameter 6–15 cm.
In young individuals hemispherical and suede-like, then convex and finally spread out.
Colour yellow-ochre, yellow-rusty, reddish, brown-orange, surface dry, covered with embedded scales of brown colour.
spod: Moderately crowded, slightly decurrent with a small tooth or attached.
At first they are cream-coloured, then light yellow-brown, finally rusty-brown.
trzon: Height 8–20 cm, thickness 1–3 cm, shape cylindrical, spindle-shaped, thickened at the bottom and often rooting.
It has a fairly persistent ring.
Above the ring it is smooth, only dusted, below the ring covered with brown, small fibrils and hairs.
Colour light yellow, darkening towards the base to reddish-brown.
miazsz: Hard, yellow.
It has a pleasant, mushroomy smell, but is bitter in taste.
podobne: A species that is hard to confuse.
It stands out among others growing on trees by its large size, as well as by its colour and the ring on the stem.
Older and small specimens may possibly be confused with Pholiota squarrosa.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–9 cm.
In young individuals it is hemispherical and has remnants of the veil at the margin, later it becomes arched, and finally flattened.
Margin of the cap not inrolled.
It often has a blunt umbo.
Surface delicately felty in young specimens, later almost bare, with small spots in places.
Colour rusty-orange, usually lighter at the margin (golden yellow), darker in the centre (brownish-red).
It is hygrophanous and slippery in wet weather.
spod: Notched with a tooth at the stem, broad.
Yellow in young specimens, later darker; yellow-rusty or orange-brown.
Contrary to the Polish species name, spots are not always present on the gills, especially in young specimens.
trzon: Height 3–8 cm, thickness up to 1.1 cm.
It is cylindrical, usually curved, at first solid, later tubular.
Yellow right under the cap, otherwise brownish or reddish-brown.
In young specimens there is a fibrous annular zone, later disappearing.
At the base there is white mycelium.
miazsz: Colour from pale to red-yellowish, and brown at the base of the stem.
Taste more or less bitter, smell indistinct.
podobne: According to Jan Holec, the rustgill G. sapineus (Fr.) Maire shows a great similarity to the small-scaled rustgill (G. penetrans (Fr.) Maire).
In some cases these species cannot be distinguished macroscopically and microscopic analysis of the hyphae of the cap skin is necessary.
In G. sapineus they are mostly 8–16 µm wide, thickly encrusted rusty-brown and often consist of swollen, short cells.
In G. penetrans they are 3–10 (–12) µm wide, less incrusted and composed of non-inflated cylindrical cells.
Moreover, G. sapineus produces fruit bodies in summer (mainly from June to August), whereas G. penetrans is mainly an autumn species (it produces fruit bodies especially from September to November)
There are many similar species growing on wood.
For mushroom pickers there is a danger of confusing it with the edible Kuehneromyces mutabilis.
On spruce wood grows Gymnopilus picreus.
It is smaller and more brightly coloured.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–12 mm.
Shape semicircular with a flat, or slightly depressed, top.
Surface smooth, flesh-coloured or reddish-brown.
Often the cap is wrinkled and faded, and its margin striate.
It shows a feature characteristic of Marasmius: in dry weather the cap together with the stem dry out and shrink so that they are almost invisible.
After rain it regains firmness and continues to grow.
spod: Distant, of different lengths, attached to the stem.
They are whitish or brownish in colour.
trzon: Thread-like, sometimes widened at the top, 2–6 cm high and 1 mm thick.
Surface smooth, shiny, black-brown, almost black at the top.
It is flexible, hard to tear.
Usually numerous hair-like projections resembling the stem, but without a cap, also grow from the substrate.
miazsz: Very thin, whitish in the cap.
No smell, taste mild.
podobne: There are many similar species of small mushrooms.
Some of them:
Gymnopus perforans, also called the 'cabbage' marasmius.
It is very similar and in addition also grows on the needles of conifers, often together with a similar needle-dwelling species.
It is easiest to tell apart by the unpleasant smell of rotting cabbage and the thicker stem
Marasmius rotula.
It grows on fallen twigs of deciduous trees.
It is distinguished by its gills; they are fused into a collar surrounding the stem.
Moreover it has a pale cap.

kapelusz: Diameter 1.5–6 cm, smooth and bare.
Colour pale ochre, red-yellow, yellow-brownish to red-brown.
It is hygrophanous; pale brown after rain, pale cream during drought and darker in the central part.
Bell-shaped when young, then flat.
Margin mostly not grooved, only in older specimens wavy and bent.
spod: Gills very crowded, thin and brittle, at first white, later ochre-cream.
trzon: Height 3–6 cm, thickness 2–4 mm, cylindrical, hollow like a tube, brittle.
Surface smooth and bare, colour ochre-brown (coloured similarly to the cap).
Base entwined with threads of mycelium.
When collecting it, delicate attached mycelial cords, white to yellowish, are often pulled out.
miazsz: Thin, whitish and watery.
Taste slight, smell indistinct.
Spore print white.
podobne: Marasmius oreades has an elastic stem, distant gills and grows in meadows and pastures.
Gymnopus hariolorum has a smell of rotten cabbage and a felty-bristly mycelium at the base of the stem
Gymnopus aquosus has a paler cap and a stem thickened at the base.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–10 cm, at first bell-shaped, later low-arched, finally flat with a low umbo.
Margin irregular.
Surface smooth, bare, pale reddish, red-brown, pale brown, sometimes with dark brown spots.
It is not hygrophanous; when wet the striation is visible only right at the margin.
spod: Very distant, folded, at first white-cream, often with rusty spots, then flesh-red, when mature dusted with white spores.
trzon: Height 6–15 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, spindle-shaped, thickened in the middle, bent, narrowing at the bottom, at first solid, then cottony inside.
Surface longitudinally fibrous, colour from pale brown to red-brown, darker at the bottom – brown-black.
The stems are deeply anchored in the substrate by a rooting stem base growing out of a black sclerotium of irregular shape.
miazsz: Springy, whitish to cream in colour, very hard in the stem, without distinct taste and smell.

owocnik: In habit they resemble basidiomycetes.
They consist of a head and a stem, hollow inside.
Height 5–12 cm, width 5–15 cm.
Shape irregularly spherical, strongly folded like a brain.
In the centre the head is hollow and interwoven, cream.
Surface in colour from yellow-brown through brown to chestnut-brown, and even black-brown.
The hymenial layer is on the outer surface of the head.
trzon: Short, irregular, dirty white, slightly thickened in the lower part.
It has irregular depressions over the whole surface.
In young specimens it is solid, in older ones hollow inside.
At first it is whitish, with time it acquires a violet-red tint.
miazsz: Cartilaginous, brittle, with an indistinct smell.
It is whitish and very brittle.
podobne: Gyromitra gigas is very similar.
It is rarer, produces larger fruit bodies, with a different shape of the head and usually paler colouring.
In addition, they differ in habitat: the giant false morel (Gyromitra gigas) grows in broadleaved and spruce forests.
A similar species is also Gyromitra fastigiata.
It has a colour similar to the giant false morel (Gyromitra gigas), but it is more slender, and its head has the shape of a bent disc.
It occurs on calcareous soils on rotting broadleaved wood, mainly beech.
It is the rarest of these 3 species, in Poland under partial protection.

It must be remembered, however, that the fruit bodies of Gyromitra gigas are not large straight away, and Gyromitra esculenta may have fairly light colours, which is why collecting Gyromitra is not recommended to beginners.
Inexperienced mushroom pickers also sometimes confuse it with the edible morel (Morchella esculenta).

owocnik: Diameter 5–15 cm.
It is irregularly, wavily or brain-like bent, with lobes bent down to the base of the stem or strongly fused with it.
Its colour is from pale olive-yellow to ochre-yellow, darkening as it matures.
Hollow in the centre, whitish.
trzon: White or pale ochre; thick, relatively short, narrowing towards the base, less often somewhat bulbous, wavy-furrowed, with a smooth surface; chambered and hollow inside.
It is from 1/5 to 1/4 of the height of the head long and often just as wide as it.
It passes smoothly into the head.
miazsz: White, waxy and very brittle, with a mild taste, without smell.
wysyp: Spores ellipsoid, with a finely warty surface, measuring 18–24 × 8–10 µm.
They are thickened at the ends.
podobne: Gyromitra esculenta is very similar.
It is much more common, smaller and usually darker in colour.

These features are not sufficient, however, to distinguish these species reliably; the fruit bodies of Gyromitra gigas are not large straight away, smaller specimens also occur among mature fruit bodies, and in Gyromitra esculenta similar, light-brown-coloured specimens occur.
These species can be reliably distinguished only by microscopic examination; in Gyromitra esculenta the spores are smooth and without thickenings at the ends.

owocnik: Irregularly folded with two, more rarely three or four, upward-directed, inverted cornet-shaped folds, giving it the appearance of a mitre; dark chestnut or red-brown.
In particularly favourable conditions the fruit body (head together with stem) can reach a height of even up to 20 cm, but as a rule it is much smaller.
trzon: White; usually of equal thickness at the top and the bottom, sometimes flattened, swollen at the top and somewhat folded and narrowed at the base; solid when young, later chambered and hollow.
miazsz: White, brittle, with an indistinct taste and smell.
podobne: Gyromitra esculenta is similar, but it has a more brain-like folded head and occurs only in early spring.
Gyromitra ambigua is almost indistinguishable macroscopically.
It is usually smaller, darker and has a violet-brown colouring, but certainty is given only by microscopic analysis.
It is very rare and under partial species protection.

kapelusz: Rusty or chestnut-brown, convex when young, flat or cushion-shaped in the mature fruit body.
The skin of the cap is at first suede-like, later bald, in drought it cracks into small fields.
spod: White when young, then yellowish, not turning blue when cut.
Pores small, round, white, then yellow.
trzon: Irregularly cylindrical, variously bent.
Surface bare, dry, red-brown.
Inside at first solid, then spongy, finally completely hollow or with empty chambers.
miazsz: White, not changing colour when cut, hard and firm when young, brittle in older specimens.
Taste slight, smell indistinct.
wysyp: Spores 7-10 × 4-6 µm in diameter, egg-shaped, smooth, almost colourless.

kapelusz: Diameter 3.5–12 cm.
Young fruit bodies arched, later cushion-shaped, finally flat.
The surface resembles suede, as it is covered with a thick fibrous layer of felt.
It is cream-coloured, straw yellow or sulphur yellow with a yellow-green tint.
Older fruit bodies fade and become whitish.
Dark blue spots appear where it is squeezed
spod: White or cream, at first adnate to the stem, then free.
When cut they turn blue.
Pores small, angularly rounded, at first white, cream with age, turning blue when touched.
trzon: Height 5–10 cm, thickness 1–3 cm.
It is irregularly cylindrical, thinner at the top.
At first spongy inside, later hollow, divided into chambers.
Surface bare in the upper part, otherwise felty, coloured the same as the cap.
It turns intensely blue where crushed.
miazsz: White or yellowish, quickly and intensely turning blue on the cut surface.
Taste slight, smell indistinct.
wysyp: Spores 8–15 × 4–6 µm, ovoid, smooth, pale yellowish.

owocnik: Semicircular, attached sideways to the substrate, spread out and bent back or cushion-shaped.
On the surface delicately velvety, later bare and wrinkled, red-orange with a brownish tinge at the base.
5–10 cm wide, 1–4 cm thick.
spod: Flesh colour.
Pores bright orange, at first circular, later of irregular shape.
miazsz: Fibrous, elastic, spongy, saturated with water.
Colour cream-orange to carmine.
Hard after drying, cream-brown.
Spore print:
Light straw-coloured.
podobne: Pycnoporellus fulgens, growing on conifers
Hapalopilus nidulans, which has ochre-coloured fruit bodies, grows on the wood of various trees, and its flesh turns an intense violet colour when treated with alkalis.

kapelusz: Stemless, attached to the substrate by its side.
A single one is bracket-shaped or shell-shaped, 4–12 cm wide and 2–4 cm thick.
Usually the fruit bodies grow in groups of several, often fusing together.
Sometimes they overlap like roof tiles or form rows.
The upper surface is felty in young fruit bodies, bare in older ones.
It is uneven, matt, unzoned, fairly soft and resembles pumice.
Colour from yellow-brown to cinnamon-brown.
spod: Tubular.
Tubes in colour from ochre-brown to cinnamon-brown and 0.5–1.5 cm long.
Pores angular, of the same colour, 2–4 fit into one millimetre.
With time they become elongated and uneven.
miazsz: In living fruit bodies juicy, fibrous, soft, when dry corky and brittle.
It has the same colour as the upper surface of the cap or slightly paler, and is faintly streaked.
KOH (like other hydroxides) colours it violet or grey-lilac.
It is tasteless and has a faint, slightly aniseed-like smell.
wysyp: Spores elliptical to cylindrical in shape, smooth, measuring 3.5–5 × 2–3 μm.
podobne: Hapalopilus croceus has a cream-orange or red-orange fruit body and is rare,
Lactiporus sulfureus.
It is intensely yellow and does not change colour under the influence of KOH,
Pycnoporus cinnabarinus is smaller and has a more intense (cinnabar) colour.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–8 cm, exceptionally up to 10 cm.
In young specimens hemispherical or bell-shaped with an inrolled margin, then spread out and wavy at the margins.
Colour cream, ochre or rusty-yellow, skin smooth.
In wet weather greasy or slimy, in dry weather only slightly sticky.
spod: Crowded and narrowly attached to the stem or completely free.
They have ragged margins and a grey-ochre colour.
In wet weather they weep, that is, they exude milky or almost transparent drops on the edges.
trzon: Height 5–10 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, cylindrical, with a fibrous surface, sometimes covered with small scales, especially in the upper part.
miazsz: Cream-white, darker in the lower part of the stem.
It smells of radish and is mostly bitter.
podobne: Hebeloma radicosum.
It has a distinctly rooting stem growing out of rotten wood.
Hebeloma sinapizans.
It has a much larger cap, coloured darker in the centre than at the periphery.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–11 cm.
In young specimens hemispherical with an inrolled margin, later low-arched, sometimes with a small, blunt umbo.
Cap surface slippery and smooth in wet weather, colour cream-ochre, dirty yellowish or ochre-brown, often with a flesh tinge.
spod: Crowded, notched, coloured from cream-brown to brown.
trzon: Height 3–9 cm, thickness 0.8–1.4 cm, fibrous, usually thickened to 2 cm at the base.
It is solid, with a flaky and scaly surface.
It is coloured from whitish to ochre, in the lower part it is brownish.
miazsz: Thick, fairly hard and not changing colour when damaged.
In taste at first mild, but after a while bitterish, smell sweet, cocoa-like.
podobne: There are many similarly coloured species of Hebeloma.
Correct identification of them without a microscope and knowledge of microscopic anatomical features is difficult.
Hebeloma sinapizans is similar, occurring mainly under beeches and oaks.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–12 cm.
Convex with an inrolled margin in young specimens, later flat, broadly spread in older ones, quite often with a small, blunt umbo.
Cap surface slippery and smooth, in young specimens white-cream at the margins, rusty yellow in the centre, in older ones darkening to red-ochre or dirty brown.
spod: Crowded, free or narrowly attached.
At first they are whitish or cream in colour, with time they darken to the colour of coffee with milk, finally becoming cinnamon-brown.
trzon: Height 4–10 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, cylindrical, fibrous with a bulb-like widened base (sometimes rooting).
In the upper part it is covered with whitish scales, which darken with time to a brown colour, in the lower part it is darker.
miazsz: Whitish, hard, thick, does not change colour when pressed.
In young specimens it is soft, in older ones hard.
It has a bitter taste and a smell similar to radish.
podobne: There are many similarly coloured species of Hebeloma.
Correct identification of them without a microscope and knowledge of microscopic anatomical features is difficult.
Hebeloma laterinum, for example, is very similar.
The common Hebeloma crustuliniforme is also smaller, and drops of milk, or spots left after its drying, often occur on its gills and the upper part of the stem.

owocnik: Of the apothecium type, consisting of a cup and a stalk.
Cup 2–12 cm in diameter, increasingly flat with age.

Upper (hymenial) surface yellow-brown to brown, bare and smooth, lower surface brown to yellow-brown, sometimes paler near the stem and delicately blurred near the edge, with forked whitish to brownish ribs that extend from the stem, sometimes almost to the edge of the cup.
Stem 2–9 cm high and up to 5 cm thick, wider near the cup, deeply ribbed with sharp (sometimes blunt) forking ribs, which also extend onto the lower surface of the cup.
Surface whitish to brownish and finely hairy.
Flesh without a distinct smell or taste.
podobne: The ribs occurring on the lower surface of the fruit body are of key importance for identification.
In the cup-shaped Helvella they extend not only on the stem, but also on the cup, sometimes almost to its edge.
Dissingia leucomelaena is similar, but its ribs do not extend onto the lower surface of the cap, moreover it has a less developed stem and it is often underground.
In Helvella queletii the ribs also do not extend onto the lower surface of the cap.
In Helvella costifera the ribs also continue onto the cap, but the cup-shaped Helvella differs from it in four features:
its ribs on the stem are generally rounded and blunt, not sharp,
has a grey cap,
the spores are somewhat smaller,
the pigment in the cells of its outer surface is found only in the cell walls, not inside the cells.

owocnik: This species is very variable in size.
Fruit bodies up to 8 cm high, consisting of a saddle-shaped bent cap and a stem.
The cap is 0.5 to 3 cm in diameter, 0.5 to 2 cm high, and usually consists of two lobes turned upwards.
Their fertile (hymenial) outer surface is grey-brown or black, the sterile inner surface is somewhat paler.
The stem is 3 to 8 mm in diameter and slightly thickened at the base, 4 to 8 cm long, grey-brown, usually with many shallow grooves.
podobne: Helvella lacunosa also has a grey-brown or black cap, but it can be easily told apart from the black Helvella species by its more massive and deeply furrowed stem.
Helvella elastica differs by a beige and less angular cap and a whitish stem.

owocnik: It is 2–10 (exceptionally up to 25) cm tall, with a marked head and stem.
The head is 2–5 × 2–5 cm in size, of irregular shape, lobed, irregularly folded, sometimes saddle-like concave.
The stem is 3–10 cm tall and 2–5 cm thick, distinctly furrowed, widened at the bottom.
Flesh thin, brittle.
Both the head and the stem are coloured from whitish through cream-yellowish to dirty ochre.
wysyp: Ascospores elliptical, smooth, colourless, measuring 19 × 11.5 μm (15–21 × 10–12 μm).
podobne: It has such a characteristic appearance that it is hard to confuse with other species.
Helvella elastica is somewhat similar, but has a smooth stem, without pits and ribs, is smaller and has a saddle-shaped head.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–7 cm, height 2–5 cm.
It consists of 2–3 bent lobes of irregular shape, whose lower margin is attached to the stem.
Outer surface smooth, bare, in colour ash-grey, grey, blue-grey, grey-black, often with brownish tinges.
The inner surface is also smooth, coloured from grey to soot-grey.
Often the outer surface is almost black.
trzon: Height 3–10 cm, diameter 1–3 cm.
It is hollow inside and has a narrowly club-shaped, cylindrical shape with longitudinal ribs, often also with deep pits.
Surface smooth, in colour from grey through grey-brown to blackish.
miazsz: Thin, brittle, whitish or greyish in colour.
Taste and smell indistinct.
podobne: Helvella atra is smaller and has a grey stem and a smoke-brown cap,
Helvella ephippium is smaller and is greyish or brown in colour.

kapelusz: At first almost spherical, later increasingly spread out, in the form of a round cup 2–4 cm in diameter.
Spores are produced on the upper, concave surface of this cup.
It is smooth, ash-grey, grey-brown, grey-black in colour.
The lower surface is grey-white and felty-hairy (just like the stem).
trzon: Height 1–7 cm, when mature usually longer than the width of the cap, thickness 1- 5 mm; more or less cylindrical, sometimes with cracks near the base.
Surface brownish (of a similar colour to the underside of the cap), whitish at the base, finely hairy, but almost bare in older specimens.
miazsz: Thin, whitish, with indistinct smell and taste.
podobne: There are several similar species of cup fungi that are difficult to tell apart, with cup-shaped caps, thin, non-ribbed stalks and hairy fruit bodies.
Helvella (the ash-grey elfin saddle) differs from them in its spindle-shaped spores; the spores of similar species, including Helvella cupuliformis, are ellipsoid.
However, this feature should be assessed with caution, because the spores of Helvella macropus are often ellipsoid when immature.

owocnik: Consisting of a cap and a stem.
Cap saddle-shaped, composed of three triangular lobes forming a pyramidal, more or less folded head.
Outer surface hairy, dark brown or blackish with indistinct purple tints, inner surface grey-white, with age it tends to darken or take on a brown-ochre colour.
Stem cylindrical, winding, usually widened at the base, finely striate, cartilaginous, elastic, hollow, smooth, without a distinct smell or taste.
podobne: Similar in colour is Helvella lacunosa, but it differs clearly in its stem, which is furrowed with deep pitted grooves, and also in its head, which is more complex and twisted.
Helvella atra is also similar, but it has a lighter colour, blackish-grey, a taller grooved stem of blackish-brown colour and smaller spores, 18-20 × 10-12 µm.
Helvella monachella can also be confused with Gyromitra infula.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–20 cm, at first hemispherical, later arched, cushion-shaped and sometimes almost flat.
Cream-grey in colour with a slight olive tinge when young, then cream-olive up to beige-brown in older fruit bodies.
The layer under the skin is brownish.
Cap skin at first felty, covered with fine threads, slightly frosted.
Older fruit bodies become bald and smooth in places.
Damaged or rubbed skin turns brown, and even takes on a ruddy-brown tinge.
It happens that during drought or heat it may crack.
spod: Tube pores small, first lemon yellow, golden yellow with age, in old specimens with a greenish or olive tinge.
They do not change colour when pressed, and turn slightly brown when dried.
Tubes 15–30 mm long, of the same colour as the pores.
When cut they do not change colour.
trzon: 50–180 mm long and 25–80 mm thick, at first pale yellow, yellowish-grey with age.
In the upper part, under the tubes, it often has a reddish or brown-reddish ring-like band, and sometimes at the base it is also flushed pinkish, reddish or covered with reddish spots.
Its surface is never covered with a reticulum (net); instead it is rough, granular to slightly fibrous, and becomes smoother with age.
Its texture is somewhat like that of Leccinum, and the furrows on the surface are slightly darker; they become distinctly darker when they dry out, e.g. during hot weather.
Shape of the stem at first plump and massive, then cylindrical, even spindle-shaped or club-shaped.
The mycelium at the base of the stem is white or whitish, sometimes slightly ochre.
miazsz: Whitish, whitish-yellowish to pale lemon; darker above the tubes – lemon, at the base of the stem even to yellow-brown.
It does not change colour when cut.
In the stem it is somewhat fibrous.
The smell is especially noticeable at the base of the stem.
It is unpleasant, medicinal, reminiscent of phenol or iodoform used in hospitals for disinfection.
The smell intensifies considerably during cooking.
Taste mild.
wysyp: Spores smooth, ellipsoid to spindle-shaped, measuring 10–16 × 4–6 μm, but usually within the range 11–14 × 4.5–5.5 μm.

kapelusz: Diameter 6–20 cm.
In young individuals it is hemispherical, later it stays convex for a long time, and only sometimes in older specimens does it become flat.
It is coloured from cream-ochre through cream-brown to reddish-brown.
Surface densely covered with a woolly veil, which with time becomes scaly.
In older specimens the scales remain only near the margin of the cap.
spod: Grey-beige when young, then dark grey-brown.
trzon: Height 3–8 cm, thickness 1–3 cm.
Usually the cap is attached to it centrally, but sometimes laterally.
It has a woolly ring, and is usually thickened at the base.
Its colour is slightly lighter than the cap, only at the base it is ochre-brown.
Above the ring it is whitish and smooth, below it is covered with woolly scales.
miazsz: Pale ochre-brown and bitterish.
podobne: Hemipholiota heteroclita (Fr.) Bon, but it has a chemical smell of gas and grows mainly on living birches and alders, rarely on poplar.
Pholiota squarrosa, but it does not grow high up on the trunks of living trees but at the base of the trunk, and it is smaller.

owocnik: It has an irregularly spherical or lumpy shape and reaches a length of up to several dozen cm.
At first it is white, later cream, finally ochre.
It attaches to the substrate by a stem from which grow numerous, repeatedly branching twigs, ending in a tuft of thin, long, hanging needles.
miazsz: Elastic and soft, with an unpleasant smell but mild in taste.
podobne: Hericium coralloides is very similar, growing mainly on beech, less often on silver birch and aspen.
The fundamental difference in structure is that in Hericium alpestre there are no spines on the branches; they are clustered in tufts at the ends of the branches.
They are hanging, longer than in the beech tooth fungus, and have sharp ends.
Moreover, the spores of Hericium alpestre are larger than the spores of Hericium coralloides,
Hericium erinaceus also has a fruit body covered with hanging spines, but they are not branched.

owocnik: Up to 30 cm in diameter, consisting of many shell-shaped, irregular and wavy lobes fused at the base on a common, thick stem.
The individual caps are arranged in tufts, sometimes overlapping like roof tiles.
Colour of young fruit bodies whitish-cream, later yellowish, finally yellowish-brownish or ochre.
kapelusz: Individual lobes shell-shaped, fan-shaped, 30–80 mm wide.
At first convex, then flat to slightly concave, wavy with age.
Their upper surface is covered with incompletely developed, sterile, non-erect spines or is warty.
Margin sharp, often wavy or inrolled.
spod: Spiny, spines crowded, vertical, whitish, 5–15 mm long, located on the underside of the lobes.
miazsz: The colour of the cap or slightly paler, soft, thick and fleshy, brittle when young, later somewhat fibrous-tough, and hardening in old age.
Smell pleasant, sweetish-fruity.
Taste mild.

owocnik: Irregularly oval, large, 10–40 cm in diameter.
It has a short stem branching into branches that reach a thickness of 3 cm in older specimens.
These branches end in tufts of soft, thin spines 1–2 cm long.
In young specimens the fruit body is pure white, in older ones it becomes creamy or cream-coloured.
miazsz: White, brittle and not changing colour when cut.
It has a faint smell and taste.
wysyp: Spores roundish-elliptical, hyaline, 3–5 × 3–4 μm in diameter.
They have a surface covered with small warts.
podobne: Hericium alpestre.
It occurs only on fir and it lacks spines on the branches; they are clustered in tufts at the ends of the branches.
They are hanging, longer than in Hericium coralloides and have pointed tips,
Hericium erinaceus also has a fruit body covered with hanging spines, but they are not branched.

owocnik: Spherical or cushion-shaped, sometimes thatch-like, 8–20 cm in size, but growing up to 30 cm.
In youth it is white, then white-cream, yellowish-blue, finally ochre-brownish.
It attaches to the tree by its side or by a bulbous part, which becomes woody in older specimens.
It is densely covered with spines 2–6 cm long and 1.5–2 mm thick (at the base).
The spines are whitish-yellow when young, later cream, in old age in colour from yellow-orange to grey-brownish.
miazsz: Fleshy, elastic, springy and slightly fibrous.
It is white, compact and perforated.
Taste sweetish, smell mushroomy.
wysyp: Spores very finely dotted, measuring 5–6 × 4–5 µm.
podobne: In Poland there also occur Hericium coralloides and Hericium alpestre, but they differ quite considerably in the shape of the fruit body and in the spines.

owocnik: Perennial, persistent, bracket-shaped, shelf-like, spread out and reflexed or irregular, often bent in waves.
It is attached to the substrate sideways or by its base.
Fruit bodies grow singly or several together, and then they may grow together at the bases.
Diameter 5–10 cm, colour reddish-brown to dark reddish-brown, in the central part also blackish-brown.
Growth margin white in colour.
Surface matt, forming a thin crust, often unevenly knobbly.
spod: White-cream, in older specimens also arranged in layers.
Pores fairly small, 0.2–0.4 mm in size, roundish and decurrent.
miazsz: Thickness 0.5–3 cm, light wood-coloured, fibrous-corky.
Smell sweetish.
podobne: In Poland there are also two other species of this root fungus: Heterobasidion abietinum, growing mainly on fir, rarely on spruce, and Heterobasidion parviporum, growing mainly on spruce, rarely on fir.
Neoantrodia serialis is also similar, but has paler, yellowish fruit bodies.

kapelusz: Diameter up to 5 cm, at first hemispherical, then convex, finally flat.
Surface dry, velvety, later smooth or finely cracked.
Colour ochre, yellowish-brown with or without an apricot tint, light brown, reddish-brown, yellow-brown to honey-brown, and usually paler at the margin.
spod: Pale yellow to yellow with an olive-green tinge.
When wounded they turn blue.
The pores are the same colour, and turn blue when injured.
trzon: Cylindrical, spindle-shaped or club-shaped.
Surface yellowish and usually almost entirely covered with very fine red granules, changing colour with age.
When damaged it turns blue.
miazsz: Whitish in the cap with a pinkish tinge under the skin.
In the stem yellowish and orange-brown at the base, sometimes with a few orange-red dots.
In the cap it turns blue after damage.
Taste and smell are indefinite.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–10 cm, hemispherical in young specimens, later spread out, finally flat.
Surface dry, suede-like, in dry weather sometimes cracked.
Colour at first intense carmine-red, later red, finally dull pink.
The skin cannot be separated from the flesh.
spod: 6–15 mm long, greenish-yellow, notched at the stem or slightly decurrent.
Pores at first from lemon-yellow to pale yellow in colour, later olive.
When pressed they change colour to blue.
trzon: Height 3–12 cm, thickness 4–2.5 cm, cylindrical in shape, often curved.
Surface light yellow, often flushed with red or with red spots.
miazsz: Yellowish, reddish only under the cap skin.
Turns blue when cut.
Without a distinct taste or smell.

owocnik: Of the apothecium type without a stem, at first cup-shaped, widening more and more during development and reaching a diameter of up to 3 cm.
Upper surface in colour from white to bluish-white and fairly smooth, lower surface brown and densely hairy, with hairs projecting above the rim of the cup.
Flesh brownish, brittle, without smell.
podobne: There are many fungus species with cup-shaped ground-dwelling fruit bodies, but Humaria hemisphaerica is easy to tell apart.
Other species of these fungi are either brightly coloured, or have smaller fruit bodies, or occur only on burnt ground.
Similar are species of the genus Jafnea, but they do not occur in Poland.

kapelusz: Diameter up to 4–10(15) cm, usually concave in the centre, colour whitish to pale orange.
Surface dry, bare and smooth, sometimes delicately mossy.
Shape variable, margin turned under and irregular.
A characteristic feature is its brittleness.
Fruit bodies often grown together in groups of several.
During drought the colour fades, becoming distinctly paler.
spod: Spines up to 6 mm long, crowded and sometimes slightly decurrent on the stem.
Colour whitish to pale orange.
Brittle, just like the cap.
On young fruit bodies they are short and pale yellow, and only later do they become longer and take on the same colour as the cap.
trzon: Height up to 7 cm, thickness 1.5–4 cm, usually eccentric, hard, solid, often irregularly bent.
Colour from white through cream to rusty-brownish.
wysyp: Spores colourless and smooth, almost spherical, measuring 6.5–9 × 5.5–7 μm.
podobne: Hydnum rufescens, which has a more intense colour, the boundary between the spines of its hymenophore and the stem is very clearly marked, and the spines are not decurrent on the stem.
Albatrellus ovinus, especially young specimens.
In hedgehog fungi spines are already visible in fruit bodies a few millimetres in size.

kapelusz: Diameter 1.5 to 5 cm, young – sharply conical, later broadly conical, at the margin may be lobed-wavy, in older fruit bodies flatly spread and radially cracked, always with a distinct umbo, sticky in wet conditions, radially fibrous during drought, yellow-orange, orange, red-orange, margin not striate.
spod: Free at the stem to very weakly attached, up to 8 mm wide, light yellow in young fruit bodies, then salmon-orange with a yellow edge, fading to lemon yellow in old specimens.
trzon: Height from 2 to 7 cm, diameter from 3 to 8 mm, cylindrical with a rounded base, hollow, sometimes longitudinally fibrillose, reddish, coloured the same as the cap, white at the base.
miazsz: The colour of the cap, pale yellow in the stem.
Taste and smell indistinct.
podobne: Among the yellow waxcaps in Poland occur: Hygrocybe citrinovirens, Hygrocybe chlorophana, Hygrocybe conica, Gliophorus psittacinus, Cuphophyllus russocoriaceus.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–5 cm, at first hemispherical, later spread out and usually with a blunt bulge in the centre.
It never becomes conical.
Surface bare, smooth, and slippery in mature fruit bodies.
Colour sulphur or golden-yellow, but it quickly fades.
Cap margins often striate.
spod: Broad, notched with a tooth at the stem, may also be attached or free.
Colour from lemon to pale yellow, paler on the edges.
trzon: Height 2–8 cm, thickness up to 1 cm, narrowed at the base, slimy and shiny in wet conditions, at first solid, later hollow.
Colour from orange-yellow to sulphur yellow.
miazsz: Thin-fleshed, light yellow, does not darken when squeezed.
Without a distinct taste or smell.
podobne: Hygrocybe quieta has a slightly darker cap with an orange top, and the gills are also slightly darker.

kapelusz: Diameter 2 to 5 cm, when young hemispherical, with age becomes arched, then almost flat.
Surface smooth, slippery in wet conditions, matt during drought, with closely appressed fine fibrils, margin sharp.
Colour red to scarlet red, fading with time to ochre-yellow.
Margin sharp, cap surface weakly grooved.
spod: Thick, broad, fairly crowded, broadly adnate and decurrent with a tooth, at first red-orange, then yellow-orange.
Gill edges yellow and smooth
trzon: Height from 4 to 6 cm, diameter from 5 to 8 mm, cylindrical, flattened, bent, base slightly narrowed, surface smooth, fibrous, hollow.
Colour scarlet red to orange-red, white towards the base.
It is brittle and hollow inside.
miazsz: Thin, brittle, watery, red-orange in the cap, taste mild, no smell.
podobne: Hygrocybe coccinea is most similar to Hygrocybe punicea, which, however, is larger and has whitish flesh in the cap.
There is also a whole group of smaller red waxcaps, e.g. Hygrocybe reidii, Hygrocybe helobia, Hygrocybe miniata.

kapelusz: Diameter 1–3 cm, shape at first arched with an inrolled margin, later flat-arched, finally flat with a slightly depressed centre.
Margins slightly striate.
It is weakly hygrophanous; in wet weather it is coloured from orange to scarlet, in dry weather it is matt, ochre-orange.
With time it gradually fades to orange (starting from the margin).
A characteristic feature is the presence on the surface of scales coloured from brown to black, especially in the centre of the cap.
spod: Distant, broad and broadly attached, decurrent with a small tooth, or rounded.
In young specimens they are white, later cream or waxy yellow.
trzon: Height 1.5 cm, diameter 1.5–4 mm, cylindrical, hollow inside, narrowed at the base.
Surface smooth, in colour from orange-red to scarlet, only paler at the base – cream or ochre.
miazsz: Thin, the same colour as the cap, not changing colour when damaged.
Taste and smell indistinct.

kapelusz: Diameter 1–3(6) cm, young – sharply conical, later bell-shaped convex, finally spread out, radially cracked, with a sharply pointed umbo, sticky in wet conditions, silkily shiny during drought, in colour saturated yellow, red-yellow, scarlet-red, turning black when pressed and with age.
spod: At first almost free, later free, broad, bulging, thick, pale yellow to lemon yellow.
trzon: Height from 6 to 8 cm, diameter from 0.5 to 1 cm, cylindrical, hollow, longitudinally fibrously cracked, yellow, orange-yellow, often with a greenish tint, turning black when pressed and with age.
miazsz: Brittle, yellow to orange-yellow, blackening.
Smell fruity, taste astringent.
wysyp: Spores (on 4-spored basidia) 7–9 × 4.5–6 µm in size or (on 2-spored basidia) 8–12(14) x 6–7.5 µm.
podobne: There are several red-coloured species of waxcaps in Poland, including: Hygrocybe coccinea, Hygrocybe coccineocrenata, Hygrocybe helobia, Hygrocybe insipida, Hygrocybe miniata, Hygrocybe punicea, but the strongly conical shape of the young fruit bodies and their blackening make it easy to distinguish the blackening waxcap from them.

kapelusz: Diameter 0.8–2.5 cm, shape at first arched with an inrolled margin, later flat-arched, margin bent downwards, centre of the cap slightly concave.
Margins wavy in some places, but without striation.
Surface matt, dry, rough, scarlet-orange in young specimens, yellow-orange in older or drying ones.
A characteristic feature is the protruding scales of the same colour as the cap or lighter, especially numerous at the top of the cap.
spod: Broad and broadly attached or decurrent with a small tooth.
In young specimens they are white with a pink tinge, later pale yellow.
The edges of the gills may be wavy.
Some sources state that crumbled gills have a smell of garlic.
trzon: Height 2–4 cm, diameter 2–4 mm, cylindrical, brittle, hollow inside, sometimes bent or flattened.
Surface smooth, dry, orange-red at the top, paler at the bottom – yellow-orange.
miazsz: Thin, brittle, yellow-orange, not changing colour when damaged.
Taste and smell indistinct.
wysyp: Spores colourless, ellipsoid, smooth, with several droplets, non-amyloid.
podobne: In Poland there are several species of waxcaps whose common features are a red colour, small size and a scaly cap.
The main morphological features that make it possible to tell them apart are: the gills, the small scales of the cap and subtle differences in colouring.
Hygrocybe coccineocremata.
The small scales of the cap are darker than it: they are coloured from brown to black,
Hygrocybe miniata.
Cap scales of the same colour as the cap, or paler, gills orange-red,
Hygrocybe coccinea.
On the cap radially embedded fibrils, gills in colour from red-orange to yellow-orange,
Hygrocybe cantharellus.
Cap orange-red, scales of the same colour as the cap, or paler.

kapelusz: Diameter from 1.5 to 2.5 cm, shape at first hemispherical, later arched, finally flat and slightly depressed in the centre.
Margin sharp, slightly wavy and paler than the rest of the cap.
Surface dry and finely scaly, especially in the centre.
The colour of young fruit bodies is cinnabar or blood-red, then gradually ever paler – orange-red.
The scales are the same colour as the cap.
During drying, or with age, the cap fades and becomes orange-yellow.
spod: Broad and broadly attached, decurrent on the stem with a small tooth.
They are orange-red in colour and have paler (yellow) edges.
trzon: Height 2–4.5 cm, thickness 2–5 mm, cylindrical in shape.
It is brittle and hollow inside.
Surface smooth, dull, dry.
It is coloured from orange to red, paler at the base – whitish or light orange-yellow.
Under the cap usually dusted with white.
miazsz: Thin, orange-yellow under the skin, otherwise orange, without distinct smell and taste.
wysyp: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, colourless, non-amyloid, with several droplets.
podobne: The characteristic features of the purple waxcap are the small fruit bodies, the dry cap and stem, and the finely scaly surface of the cap.
Similar, also small and red fruit bodies with a finely scaly surface are found in:
Hygrocybe helobia.
It has white gills and occurs in peat bogs and wetlands,
Hygrocybe coccineocremata.
It has scales darker than the cap, gills distant, at first white, then cream.
Hygrocybe cantharellus.
It has a paler colour, decurrent gills, a more slender shape and a dry cap surface

kapelusz: Diameter from 5 to 12 cm, conical-bell-shaped in young fruit bodies, spread out in older ones, always with an umbo.
Surface bare, sticky and slippery.
In young fruit bodies it is scarlet, then fades to blood-red, finally in older fruit bodies to yellow-red.
spod: Brittle, at first adnate, later free, distant, thick, bellied.
They are coloured from yellow through cream to grey-yellow.
Edges smooth.
trzon: Height from 6 to 10 cm, diameter from 1 to 2 cm, cylindrical, narrowed at the base, solid when young, hollow in mature specimens.
Surface longitudinally delicately fibrous, in colour red, orange-red, red-yellow, whitish-yellowish at the base.
miazsz: Thin-fleshed, juicy, white when young, later yellow-orange, dark grey-red under the cap skin.
Taste and smell indistinct.
podobne: Hygrocybe splendidissima is more slender, has a tomato-red cap, a stem orange-fibrous on a yellow background, and vivid orange flesh.
Hygrocybe coccinea has a cherry-red cap, red flesh, and gills broadly attached to the stem.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–8 cm, conical in young specimens, then flat-conical, finally flat, with a low, blunt umbo.
Surface smooth, slightly moist and slightly hygrophanous, intensely orange-yellow, sometimes with an olive tint, orange in the centre.
Older specimens fade to a cream colour.
spod: Distant, thick, up to 12 mm high, with anastomoses, sulphur-yellow or yellow-orange, but paler than the cap, salmon-reddish in mature specimens.
trzon: Height 4–6 cm, diameter 6–18 mm, hollow, brittle, flattened at the bottom, often twisted or asymmetrical.
Surface intensely orange-yellow at the top, paler towards the bottom, even whitish.
miazsz: Very thin, brittle, hard in the stem, coloured from yellow to orange.
It has a mild taste and an unpleasant smell.
It does not turn black when damaged.

kapelusz: Diameter 2 to 7 cm, in young specimens thin-fleshed with an inrolled margin and fawn-coloured, later funnel-shaped sunken in the centre, with wavy or crinkled margins.
Colour from yellow through orange-yellow and orange to red-orange.
Skin smooth, slightly matt, dry, felty in some places.
spod: Thin, crowded, forking, decurrent on the stem, sometimes wavy.
Colour orange-yellow or orange.
trzon: Height 3–5 cm, thickness 3–10 mm, cylindrical at the bottom, higher up widening conically and passing smoothly into the cap.
Solid in young individuals, hollow in older ones.
Colour the same as the gills, blackish only at the base, skin felty.
miazsz: White or cream, juicy and soft.
Taste and smell mild, bitter-sour.
wysyp: Spores elliptical, with a smooth surface and measuring 6–7 × 4 μm.
podobne: Cantharellus cibarius, from which it differs in its more crowded gills and darker, more orange fruit bodies; it usually also has a thinner stem.
Cantharellus friesii.

kapelusz: Diameter from 3 to 7 cm, young – hemispherical, later convex to spread out, margin inrolled for a long time.
Its surface is smooth, strongly slimy in wet conditions, silkily shiny during drought.
Colour white, later ivory, then cream.
spod: Thick, fairly distant, decurrent along the stem, 3 to 5 mm wide.
They are always pure white.
trzon: Height 4 to 11 cm, diameter 5 to 12 mm, cylindrical, tapering towards the base, firmly rooted in the ground, solid.
Under the cap dry and covered with fine scales and fibrils.
Its surface is slimy, white or ivory in colour.
miazsz: In the cap soft, springy and juicy, in the stem fibrous.
It is white and has a weak taste and smell.
It does not change colour after damage.
wysyp: Spores ellipsoid, with a smooth surface.
podobne: There are several white-coloured species of wax caps.
Distinguishing them is difficult even for mycologists.
Sometimes microscopic examination is necessary.
Very similar, for example, are Hygrophorus piceae growing under spruces and Cuphophyllus virgineus, but the latter is smaller and grows in meadows.

kapelusz: Diameter 1–6 (up to 10) cm, olive-brown, olive-brownish, slightly darker in the centre, in mature fruit bodies in places discolouring yellowish, covered with a slimy skin.
The shape of the cap is hemispherical or bell-shaped in young fruit bodies, then convex or spread out, usually with an umbo in the centre.
In older individuals the slime on the skin dries up or is washed off by rain.
Sometimes (rarely) a variety with an orange-yellow cap can be found.
spod: Gilled, gills at first cream in colour, then yellow, broad and distant, soft and slightly decurrent on the stem.
trzon: Cylindrical, sometimes narrowed at the base, 5–7 cm long, 0.3–0.7 cm in diameter, yellowish, in young fruit bodies covered with a thick layer of slime below the ring zone.
The cracking slime may form a striped pattern.
miazsz: Yellowish in colour, soft, rather bast-like in the stem, with no or a slight fruity smell.
podobne: The fruiting time of the late waxcap (Hygrophorus) limits the possibility of confusing its fruit bodies with other species.
The following species are given as similar:
Hygrophorus olivaceoalbus, which has an olive tint on the cap, and the stem is zigzag-banded.
Hygrophorus lucorum.
It is lemon-yellow, less slimy and grows only under larches
Clitocybe brumalis.

kapelusz: Diameter 6–13 cm, hemispherical with an inrolled margin when young, later arched, finally spread out with a blunt and broad umbo.
At first they have a white surface or one with an ivory tinge, then cream with an ochre-orange tinge, in old age they become white or creamy again.
spod: Decurrent, distant, thick, at first white, then cream-yellow.
trzon: Thick, solid, cylindrical, slightly thicker below the cap, base pointed, surface smooth, dry, in colour from white to cream.
miazsz: Thick, compact, with an indistinct smell and a pleasant taste.
podobne: Most similar is Hygrophorus eburneus.
It is entirely white or ivory-coloured, without cream and ochre tints, and moreover has a slimy stem.
Tricholoma columbetta differs by its white, non-decurrent gills and its silky-fibrous cap.
Most similar is Hygrophorus eburneus.
It is entirely white or ivory-coloured, without cream and ochre tints, and moreover has a slimy stem.
Tricholoma columbetta differs by its white, non-decurrent gills and its silky-fibrous cap.

owocnik: Very thin, attached to the tree only by the central part, slightly bell-shaped, standing away from the substrate by up to 2 cm, densely overlapping like roof tiles; dark, red-brown with a narrow black band.
inne: Red-brown; smooth, with sharp bristles on the surface visible only under high magnification, mostly covering a large area of wood and fusing together with small caps; some specimens have no cap margins.
miazsz: Dark brown, fibrous-tough.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–7 cm, hemispherical when young, then flat-convex, quite often with an inconspicuous, small umbo, finally flat.
Margins of the cap mustard-yellow to ochre-yellow, centre darker – rusty-yellow.
Cap margin smooth, in young specimens joined to the stem by a cobweb-like veil.
spod: Fairly crowded and broadly adnate, whitish when young, later grey-violet, in older specimens dark violet-brown.
trzon: Height 4–8 cm, thickness 3–5 mm, cylindrical.
Its colour is from pale cream-yellow to yellow-brown, but without green tinges.
Darker at the base (rusty-yellow to rusty-brown).
In young specimens it is covered with faintly visible, white fibrils.
miazsz: Pale brown, in the stem a little darker than in the cap.
Taste mild, smell mushroomy.
podobne: Galerina marginata.
Poisonous.
It has smaller fruit bodies, brittle and rusty-brown.
Hypholoma fasciculare.
Poisonous.

The most characteristic feature making it possible to distinguish these two species is the colour of the gills; in Hypholoma fasciculare they are greenish, in the mild one bluish and the colour green never occurs.
If in doubt, you can also try the taste; Hypholoma fasciculare has an acrid taste (it should be spat out after a careful tasting), the mild one has a mild taste.
Hypholoma radicosum has grey-olive-brown gills, bitter flesh and a rooting stem.

kapelusz: Diameter up to 7 cm, semicircular in young specimens, then convex to flat, with a small bulge in older ones.
The surface of the cap is dry and smooth.
Colour yellow or sulphur yellow, centre of the cap orange to rusty brown.
spod: Crowded, rounded at the stem.
Colour from sulphur-yellowish in young ones, through dirty greenish, to violet-black in older specimens.
Covered by a thin veil in very young fruit bodies.
