No stem; sometimes in its place there is only an elongated part of the cap covered with white bristles. Surface felty or velvety, margin rolled under, felty.
When dry it is pale ochre-yellow, when moist orange-yellow.
spod: Radiating and eccentric, broad, decurrent.
They are orange to rusty-yellow in colour and have smooth edges.
miazsz: Thin, springy, yellow in colour.
Smell mild, taste indistinct or slightly mushroomy.
wysyp: From very pale pink to pink-brown.
Spores elliptical, elongated, smooth, non-amyloid, measuring 5–8 × 2–4 μm.
podobne: Tapinella panuoides does not have such an intense orange colour,
Sarcomyxa serotina has a small stem, is olive-green in colour and occurs only on broadleaved trees; it also has larger fruit bodies.

kapelusz: At first rolled under (inrolled), later spread out, finally funnel-shaped.
Shape circular, shell-shaped or kidney-shaped.
It reaches a width of 5–10 cm, but sometimes even 20 cm.
It is thin – 1–3 mm thick – and has a sharp and usually wavy margin.
Sometimes 2 or more caps grow from one stem.
Skin gelatinous, since it is built of hyphae stuck together, smooth and bare, shiny in dry weather.
Upper surface in young fruit bodies olive or olive-brown in colour, in older ones becoming purple-brown, chestnut, black-brown, even black, especially in the centre of the cap.
spod: Tubular.
The tubes run slightly down the stem.
They are 0.5–2.5 mm long and form a single layer.
In young fruit bodies they are white, in older ones they change colour to cream or nut-brown.
Pores round and very small, with 4–7 of them per one mm.
trzon: Short and fairly thin (in relation to the size of the cap).
It is 2–2.3 cm long and 0.5–1.5 cm thick.
It is usually eccentric, less often lateral or central.
It is entirely black and suede-like, covered with an easily falling-off tomentum.
miazsz: Fleshy-leathery in young fruit bodies, hardening in older ones.
After drying it becomes brittle.
podobne: Polyporus melanopus, occurring on buried wood of deciduous trees.
Cap of the young fruit body pale, ochre or grey-brown in colour, shortly hairy,
Cerioporus varius.
It has a black stem only in the lower part, and a cap of a colour from yellowish to brown.

kapelusz: Convex in young specimens, but quickly spread out.
Diameter 6–10 cm, white or pale grey, felty-fibrous or scaly, with membranous remains of the veil at the margin (especially in young fruit bodies).
spod: Distant, forked near the stem, decurrent on the stem.
At first they are whitish, then turning yellow.
trzon: Height 1–3 cm, thickness 1 cm, mostly eccentrically placed relative to the cap.
It is whitish and velvety-felty, at first also with membranous remains of the veil.
It has a non-persistent ring.
miazsz: Whitish, turning yellow, bast-like.
podobne: Pleurotus ostreatus, in which there are no remains of the veil and the flesh does not turn yellow.
Edible.
Pleurotus calyptratus, which however has a smooth cap.

kapelusz: Diameter from 5 to 25 cm.
Shape at first arched, with a long inrolled margin, later shell-shaped, fan-shaped or funnel-shaped.
It is attached to the substrate sideways.
It is soft and springy, surface smooth and bare, covered with white felt only near the stem.
Colour quite variable; it may be in various shades of brown, ash-grey, grey-brown, steel blue and violet.
spod: Crowded and deeply decurrent on the stem, coloured from whitish to grey, in older specimens even violet.
trzon: Short, thick, 1 to 4 cm high.
Colour white or grey.
It is bare, covered with bristles only at the base.
miazsz: In young specimens soft in the cap, springy in older ones, in older ones the stem becomes corky and woody.
Colour white, taste sourish.
wysyp: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, 8–11 × 3–4 µm in diameter.
podobne: Pleurotus dryinus has a paler, whitish cap with a somewhat villose surface,
Pleurotus cornucopiae has a trumpet-shaped cap and a grooved stem.
Pleurotus pulmonarius has a light cap, an aniseed smell and occurs from early summer to autumn,
Sarcomyxa serotina is smaller and often has greenish tinges.
Moreover, its stem is yellow, and the gills do not run down it as deeply as in the oyster mushroom, but form a distinct boundary between the cap and the stem in its upper part.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–12 cm, spatula-shaped, oyster-shaped in younger specimens, with a bent, sometimes tattered margin, soft, thin-fleshed, light, cream, pale brown, yellowing at the margin, grey-brown with age, attached sideways to the substrate.
Margin of the cap inrolled.
spod: Crowded, narrow, springy, deeply decurrent on the stem, unforked, narrow, springy, whitish or light cream.
They turn yellow while drying.
trzon: Height 1–6 cm and thickness 0.6–1.5 cm, eccentric, sometimes lateral.
It is conical in shape (thinner at the base).
Surface smooth, whitish, felty at the base.
miazsz: With an indistinct smell reminiscent of aniseed and a sweetish taste, at first springy, delicate, hard and whitish with age.
podobne: The edible Pleurotus ostreatus, but this one occurs only in late autumn, and Crepidotus, which are distinguished by the clay-brown colour of the gills.

owocnik: It consists of a cap and a short stem, sometimes there is no stem.
The cap is up to 2 cm wide.
Bell-shaped when young, later irregularly shell-shaped or hanging cup-like; at first delicately felty; with yellow or reddish-brown stripes; very thin and bast-like.
Cap margin paler.
spod: White, somewhat vein-like folded.
However, these are not true gills, but only forked folds.
inne: Soft, flexible.
Colour white, taste mild.
podobne: Plicatura nivea.
Older specimens also have a similar colour, but are distinguished by the hymenophore

some species of Crepidotus, especially Crepidotus mollis, but Plicaturopsis crispa is distinguished from them in that it has no gills but folds, and by its white spore print (in Crepidotus it is brown).

kapelusz: Diameter 3–15 cm, hemispherical in young specimens, then arched, in older ones flat-arched to flat, sometimes also shallowly concave.
It has a low, broad umbo or papilla, the surface radially fibrous, delicately scaly in the centre.
The margin sometimes extends beyond the gills.
Colour dark to tobacco-brown, paler at the margin, brown-grey.
spod: Broad, bellied, free, at first whitish, then light pink, finally pink-brown to brown-pink.
Edges dark brown.
trzon: Height 4–16 cm, thickness 0.6–1.7 cm, cylindrical with a base widened to 2.5 cm, solid.
Surface grey-whitish to light brown, covered lengthwise with dark brown fibrils.
miazsz: White in the cap, watery in the stem, grey-marbled.
Taste sweetish-mushroomy, smell unpleasant.
podobne: The characteristic features of this species are the large fruit body, occurrence on conifers and the dark edges of the gills.
Pluteus pseudorobertianii is very similar in colouring, but the edges of its gills are not blackish.

kapelusz: Diameter 1.5–5 cm, in young specimens, then arched with a blunt umbo, finally spread out, not hygrophanous.
Margin even, only slightly crenate in older specimens.
Surface smooth or slightly wrinkled, orange.
Orange-red in the centre, matt when dry.
spod: Free, ventricose, at first white, then light pink.
Edges white and fibrillose.
trzon: Height 3–8 cm, thickness up to 0.6 cm, cylindrical, at first solid, later hollow with a club-like widened base.
Surface white to yellow-white, longitudinally fibrous in young specimens.
Base in colour from dark yellow to orange.
miazsz: White in the cap, yellowish in the stem, with an indistinct smell and a bitter taste.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–12 cm, sometimes even up to 15 cm, at first hemispherical, later convex, finally flat.
Sometimes it has a blunt umbo, sometimes the centre of the cap is wrinkled or knobbly.
Surface silky or with fine, embedded fibrils.
Cap colour in various shades of brown and grey; from light grey-brown to blackish-brown, there are also albino individuals with an entirely white cap.
In wet weather it is shiny.
spod: Free (not reaching the stem).
In young specimens cream-white, then salmon-pink, fairly crowded, bellied.
trzon: Height 5–10 cm, thickness 0.5–1.5 cm, but sometimes there are specimens with a stem thickness of up to 3 cm.
It is cylindrical, less often club-shaped.
Surface dirty white with darker fibrils forming longitudinal streaks.
When young the stem is solid, in old specimens hollow.
miazsz: Whitish, elastic in the cap, fairly brittle in the stem.
Taste mild, slightly musty or earthy, smell fairly strong, similar to radish or potato sprouts.
podobne: Megacollybia platyphylla.
It has sparser but broader gills, always white and attached to the stem, and numerous rhizomorphs at the base of the stem.
The spore print is white.
Pluteus atromarginatus has dark brown or black gill edges and grows on the wood of conifers.
Pluteus salicinus has a grey-blackish cap without brown tinges.
It grows on willow wood.
There are still several similar species of scalycaps (Pholiota).
A reliable distinction between them is possible only by microscopic examination.

kapelusz: Diameter 1.3–7 cm, at first convex, later broadly and flatly spread, usually slightly raised in the centre.
Surface silky shiny, covered with fine, thread-like fibrils closely bound to the skin.
These fibrils are arranged radially, and at the top of the cap their spreading ends form small hairs resembling scales.
Surface smooth; only in wet weather may the margin be shortly striate.
The cap is mouse-grey in colour, sometimes darker at the top, with a greenish tinge.
The mouse-grey colour sometimes shifts to olive, or even beige-pink.
Entirely white specimens occur very rarely.
spod: Crowded, free, fairly broad, bulging.
White in young specimens, then with a salmon-pink tinge.
Edge even, slightly cottony-villose and of the same colour.
trzon: Height 2–7 cm, thickness 0.3–0.7 cm, with a slightly thickened base.
At the base somewhat darker streaks are visible, and in the upper part it is silky shiny.
miazsz: In the cap and the upper part of the stem whitish, in the lower part of the stem ivory-coloured.
Smell and taste musty.
podobne: The greenish-grey species is easily recognised by its mouse-grey cap and by the pleurocystidia on the gills.
Similar are Pluteus atromarginatus and Pluteus pseudorobertii.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–12 cm, shape most often funnel-shaped, sometimes spread out.
Skin dry felty, light brown, covered with darker (ochre-brown or red-brown) scales.
spod: Tubular.
Tubes white and decurrent on the stem.
Pores large (diameter 1–2 mm), angular, white in young specimens, yellowish in older ones.
trzon: Height 3–8 cm, thickness 0.5–1.5 cm, cylindrical, straight or crooked, mostly attached in the centre of the cap.
Surface whitish or pale ochre, slightly hairy.
miazsz: Elastic in young fruit bodies, fibrous-tough in older ones, whitish, without smell.
podobne: Similar fruit bodies are produced by Cerioporus squamosus, but it does not have a sclerotium.
A similar hymenophore is found in the much more common Lentinus brumalis, which also does not produce a sclerotium.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–4 cm, irregular, with a fibrously suede-like and scalily cracked surface.
Scales ochre-brown to grey-brown.
spod: 1–1.5 mm long, straw-yellow, running far down onto the stem.
trzon: Whitish, sometimes cream, irregularly joined to neighbouring stems, growing from a branched fleshy base – a sclerotium, taking up nutrients from the substrate.
miazsz: Whitish, fleshy; smell pleasant, resembling dill; taste pleasant, with an astringent aftertaste.
podobne: The edible Grifola frondosa.
Its individual caps are spatula-shaped, fan-shaped, wedge-shaped, without centrally attached stems.

owocnik: Perennial, of the bracket-fungus type.
It grows singly, or in groups of several fruit bodies, which usually fuse together.
It is attached to the substrate sideways.
At first bracket-shaped or semicircular, then hoof-shaped, and in cross-section usually triangular.
It reaches a width of up to 20 cm and a height of up to 8 cm.
Surface concentrically zoned, covered with lumps and furrows, quite often radially, deeply cracked.
Colour at first brown or green-brown, later almost black.
Sometimes it is overgrown with algae and then the surface has a celadon-green colour.
Margin usually sharp and even, chestnut-coloured in young specimens.
Over a width of about 0.5–1 mm it is sterile.
It has fawn hairs, which fall off in older fruit bodies.
spod: Tubular, in young individuals grey-yellowish or yellow-olive, in older ones rusty.
Tubes are 3–10 mm long and the fruit body may have several layers of them separated by flesh.
They have irregular oval, angular, elongated or slightly maze-like pores, usually 0.2 to 0.7 mm long, but sometimes up to 3 mm.
Pore edges entire, mossy in young specimens.
It gives off a strong mushroomy smell.
miazsz: Homogeneous, with a corky-woody consistency and very hard.
It is 5–15 mm thick and coloured from rusty-cinnamon to chestnut.
podobne: Similar fruit bodies are formed by Phellinus chrysoloma, but it does not occur on pine, but on spruce, fir and larch.

kapelusz: Diameter 8–14 cm, young hemispherical, later convex to almost flat, round or oval in shape.
Pale grey when young, early darkening brown to grey-brown; surface dull and delicately mossy, not slippery.
In most cases it is dark and looks as if smoked.
The skin cannot be peeled off, in old age it sometimes cracks.
spod: Young ones light, grey-yellow, early grey-brown, staining when damaged; shorter around the stem; pores most often small, sometimes also relatively large, and then reaching all the way to the upper side of the cap.
trzon: Height 4–16 cm, thickness 1–4 cm, at first barrel-shaped, later cylindrical.
Like the cap it is umber-brown to tar-brown, delicately suede-like; relatively slender and thin.
miazsz: White or dirty grey-whitish, when cut faintly turning greenish-blue (above all above the tubes), and slowly turning red, especially under the cap skin.
Without smell, with a mild taste.
wysyp: Spores oblong elliptical-spindle-shaped, smooth, 14–20 × 6–8 µm in diameter.
podobne: Hard to confuse with other fungus species.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–9 mm, the shape of young fruit bodies bell-shaped, convex or hemispherical, with an indistinct umbo and a margin at first adhering to the stem.
As it matures it partly straightens out.
Margin translucent, radially striate.
Surface at first dusted, then bare, red in young fruit bodies, then fading, and in mature fruit bodies bright orange-yellow only in the centre, becoming yellowish at the margin.
spod: Attached.
Gills 10–14 in number, reaching the stem or ending just before the stem.
Besides these there are 2-3 tiers of lamellulae not reaching the stem.
Gills moderately broad, pale orange to whitish, often yellowish at the base and whitish at the edges.
trzon: Height 1 to 6 cm, thickness up to 1 mm.
It is pliable, with a base covered with sharp, straight and stiff white hairs.
The surface is at first densely white-dusted, but soon becomes bare, and then changes colour to orange-yellow or lemon-yellow.
miazsz: Very thin, translucent, cream, without smell or taste.
podobne: The most similar is Mycena oregonensis, but its cap is more yellow than orange, the gills are broadly adnate or decurrent with a short tooth, the edge of the gills is orange to pale yellow, and the stem is dry, not sticky.
The hyphae of the cap skin are smooth and not embedded in gelatinous matter, and in European collections the basidia are two-spored and have no clamp connections.
Atheniella adonis is similar, but larger.
The orange bonnet can also be confused with small waxy caps (Hygrophorus).

kapelusz: Diameter from 2 to 5 cm (exceptionally up to 7 cm).
At first bell-shaped, later increasingly spread out, finally flat.
Surface bare, never sticky.
On young fruit bodies there are whitish, delicate remnants of the veil, sometimes hanging from the cap margin.
It is hygrophanous: when moist it is red-brown or dark brown, when dry ochre-beige.
When wet the cap margins are finely striate (the gills showing through).
spod: Crowded, light beige when young, then brown-black (without a violet tinge).
Cystidia are located on the edge and on the surface of the gills.
trzon: Height up to 8 cm, thickness 4–8 mm.
It is hollow, very brittle, sometimes slightly wavy, uneven.
Surface bare, sometimes with whitish fibrils that are remnants of the veil.
Ring absent.
In young fruit bodies the stems are pale, in older ones they darken.
miazsz: White and very brittle, with an indistinct smell and taste.
wysyp: Spores oval or ellipsoid, measuring 4.5–6.5 × 3–4 µm, without a germ pore.
podobne: Kuehneromyces mutabilis, which has a two-coloured cap of similar shades, differs in its brown stem with a ring.
Edible,
Psathyrella candolleana, which is honey-yellow, paler even when wet.

kapelusz: Diameter from 2 to 6 cm.
At first semicircular, later cushion-shaped, finally flattened.
Surface in colour from dirty yellow through greenish-ochre to olive-brown, dry, suede-like, sometimes cracked into small patches (especially during dry weather).
spod: Attached or slightly decurrent, angular, yellow when young, later brown-olive or brown-yellow.
trzon: Height 3–7 cm long, thickness 0.4–2 cm.
Solid, yellow to yellow-brown or olive, narrowed below and usually strongly bent.
It has a fibrous structure.
miazsz: Yellowish, lemon yellow above the tubes, brownish in the lower part of the stem, turning slightly blue on a cross-section.
Taste mild, smell mushroomy.
wysyp: Spores oval-spindle-shaped, pale yellow to honey-yellow, measuring 12–18 × 4.5–6 µm.
podobne: A similar-looking mushroom is the so-called Boletus subtomentosus, but the peculiar habitat of the parasitic bolete virtually rules out a mistake.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–10 cm, goblet-shaped or deeply funnel-shaped with inrolled margins.
It is hygrophanous and slightly shiny.
In dry weather the skin is smooth and light coffee-coloured or flesh-coloured; in wet weather from dark umber through coffee-brown to chocolate-brown.
spod: Thick, distant, fairly deeply decurrent on the stem, forked.
They are coloured from whitish through light brown to red-brown.
trzon: Height 5–12 cm, thickness 0.5–1.2 cm, cylindrical, club-like thickened at the base.
Colour brown, with a felty surface covered with fibrils or reticulate.
miazsz: Watery and soft, brownish in colour, with an indistinct smell and taste.
podobne: Pseudoclitocybe expallens (the odourless funnel cap).
It is smaller, only very young specimens have a rolled-under margin,
Cantharellula umbonata.
Its flesh and gills turn reddish when pressed,
Infundibulicybe gibba has a pale ochre cap.

owocnik: Tremelloid, containing a great deal of water.
After drying only a thin flake remains of it.
It consists of a spatula-shaped (tongue-shaped, shelf-shaped) cap and an eccentrically attached short stem.
It may also be attached to the wood by its side (without a stem).
Colour whitish with a bluish tinge.
Upper surface granular or warty.
The width of the fruit body at the top is 1–8 cm.
Besides white specimens there are specimens with grey or pink-brown colouring of the upper side of the cap.
spod: Spiny, the colour of the fruit body.
Spines fairly crowded, up to 3 mm long.
miazsz: Whitish with a pale bluish tinge, of jelly-like consistency, watery, slightly translucent (glassy), without taste and smell.
wysyp: Spores almost spherical, smooth, measuring 3.5-6.5 × 5–8.5 μm.
podobne: Hyalodon piceicola.
It has a flatly spread-out fruit body and in Poland its occurrence has been reported only in the Bialowieza Forest.
it cannot be confused with other white and gelatinous fungi occurring in Poland, because it has a spiny hymenophore.

owocnik: An annual bracket fungus, growing singly or in overlapping groups of a few specimens.
It has a hemispherical, bracket-like or shelf-like shape and is 10–25 cm wide.
Margin blunt and mostly even.
It is attached to the substrate sideways.
Upper surface velvety or rough, uneven, pitted or lumpy, at first cream, then orange-brown, ochre, rusty or tobacco-coloured.
A characteristic feature is the presence on the surface of numerous drops of red-brown liquid.
After drying, brown depressions remain.
Flesh watery and spongy in young fruit bodies, dry, fibrous and corky in older ones.
Its colour is from fawn to rusty-red and it is indistinctly zoned.
Hymenophore on the lower surface, tubular, at first white-grey, then yellow-brown.
The tubes form a single layer.
They have round, white, frosted pores 5–20 mm long.
2–5 fit into 1 mm.
In older fruit bodies they are often overgrown with a whitish-yellowish layer of mycelium.
The fruit body has a fairly strong and unpleasant smell.
Its taste is mild, slightly sour.
podobne: Inocutis dryophila is more common.
It is distinguished by smaller, hoof-shaped fruit bodies, which have a hard, darker, yellow-veined and granular insert in the central part of the cap.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–8 cm, conical-convex in young specimens, usually conical with a distinct sharp umbo in older ones, sometimes flatly spread with an umbo.
Margin straight, radially cracked, sometimes with remnants of the veil on it in the form of white fibrils.
Surface silky, covered with radial fibrils.
It has a colour from olive-lemon to brown.
The top is usually darker.
spod: Notched with a sinus at the stem, thin with a light edge.
They are from lemon-olive to dirty olive in colour.
trzon: Height 4–12 cm, thickness 0.5–1.5 cm, cylindrical in shape, with a small bulb at the base.
Surface white, sometimes with an olive tinge.
In the top part it is distinctly frosted, in the lower part fibrillose.
In older fruit bodies the surface becomes scaly.
Sometimes the stem is smooth, only delicately frosted at the very top.
miazsz: White with a satiny sheen.
It smells of semen, no distinct taste.
wysyp: Spores elliptical-bean-shaped, sometimes with a small beak; irregular spores also occur.

kapelusz: Diameter 1–2 cm, hygrophanous, when moist olive to light brown in colour, also with dark olive or blue-green spots (especially on the periphery), when dried it takes on a colour from pale straw to ochre.
Surface smooth, moist, slippery, slightly sticky.
Shape at first bluntly conical and usually with a sharp papilla in the centre, with age conical to bell-shaped, but never spread out.
spod: Broad, narrowly attached to the stem.
In young fruit bodies light brown, in older ones darker – tobacco-brown.
The edges are paler.
The number of gills is 15-27.
trzon: Thin, 3–15 cm high and 1–3 mm in diameter.
It is flexible, cylindrical and hollow inside, sometimes only widened at the base, usually bent.
Surface pale ochre, smooth or longitudinally fibrous.
miazsz: Beige when dry, grey-brown when moist, without taste and without smell.
podobne: There are many similar species of Psilocybe, small hooded-cap species and other fungi.
Characteristic of Psilocybe semilanceata are: dark gills, a pointed umbo at the top of the cap and an elastic, long and strong stem.

kapelusz: Diameter 5-30mm, hygrophanous, when moist coloured from nut-brown to dark brown.
Surface smooth, moist, slippery, slightly sticky.
Shape convex and usually without the sharp papilla typical of P. semilanceata.
spod: Broad, narrowly attached to the stem.
Cream in young fruit bodies, darker in older ones – dark violet-brown.
trzon: Thin, 4–10 cm high and 2.5 mm in diameter.
Surface pale ochre.
miazsz: It has the smell and taste of flour, and turns blue.
podobne: It is closely related to Psilocybe semilanceata and Psilocybe pelliculosa.
The marsh Psilocybe is commonly confused with Psilocybe semilanceata and can be distinguished by its cap without a papilla and of convex shape.

owocnik: Annual.
It is attached to the substrate sideways.
Fruit bodies grow singly or in few clusters.
A single one is up to 10 cm in diameter, cushion-shaped or semicircular.
Surface hairy, white in young fruit bodies, turning brown in older ones.
spod: Tubular, it arises in the lower part of the fruit body, rarely and late, but disintegrates quickly, so it is rather difficult to observe. The tubes are brittle and short, their pores are torn, 2–4 fit into one mm.
miazsz: Juicy in young fruit bodies, harder only at the base.
It consists of radially arranged fibrils separated by pits, which are filled with chlamydospores.
It is concentrically zoned.
podobne: Postia stiptica does not have such a hairy surface and is bitter in taste,
similar, hairy fruit bodies of the imperfect form also occur in other species of the genera Postia and Tyromyces, but rarely and they are smaller.

owocnik: A bracket fungus with an annual fruit body that is attached to the substrate by its side, sometimes spread out and reflexed.
Fruit bodies occur singly or in groups of several, often arranged one above another like roof tiles.
A single fruit body is semicircular, fan-shaped or bracket-shaped, up to 10 cm wide and up to 3 cm thick.
Its base is often narrowed.
Surface uneven, wavy and radially wrinkled.
Young specimens are felty and rough, older ones bare and usually matt.
Colour orange or brick red.
miazsz: Spongy and juicy in young specimens, fibrous in older ones.
After drying it becomes light, corky and brittle, and also changes colour to apricot-orange.
Under the action of KOH it darkens and becomes raspberry-coloured.
spod: Tubular, consisting of a single layer of tubes 3–5 mm long.
The inner walls of the tubes are often covered with a white bloom.
Pores of the tubes angular, of irregular or labyrinth-like shape.
They are 0.4 to 1 mm in diameter.
In young specimens the pores are orange-brick, in older ones fawn, brittle, torn and toothed.
Taste sour, acrid, smell unpleasant.
podobne: Pycnoporus cinnabarinus.
It has a similar colour, but differs in the consistency of the flesh and in the pores – they are smaller and regular.
Climacocystis borealis.
Its flesh is always elastic, soft and has a pleasant smell.

owocnik: Bushy, from 6 to 20 cm high and from 6 to 30 cm wide.
They are fleshy masses resembling a cauliflower, with a stem that divides into several main branches, which branch further.
The stem is short and thick – from 1.5 to 6 cm in diameter – and narrows downwards.
At first white, with age both the stem and the branches become pale yellow to fawn-brown. Old fruit bodies may fade and become almost white or take on an ochre colour because of fallen spores.
The branching pattern is irregular, with few and thick primary branches – usually 2–3 cm in diameter – and the terminal branchlets are slender (2–3 mm), and usually end in five to seven branches.
The tips of the branches are pink to violet-red.
Melzer's reagent applied to the stem tissue reveals a weak amyloid reaction; a correct result of the reaction is obtained only after at least 30 min.
This reaction can be used to distinguish R. botrytis from other similar fungi.
miazsz: The flesh of the fungus is compact, white and has a smell described variously as indistinct or pleasant.
inne: The variety R. botrytis var. aurantiiramosa differs from the more common variety by the orange colour of the upper branches.
Variety compactospora tends to show a more distinct wine, violet or red colour at the tips of the branches and has smaller spores measuring 9.2–12.8 by 4–5.4 µm.
podobne: The characteristic features of the red-tipped coral fungus include: large size, orange, reddish or purple branchings, striate spores averaging 13.8 by 4.7 µm and a weak amyloid reaction of the parent tissue.
R. rubripermanens has reddish terminal branches, a similar silhouette and striate spores, but it can be distinguished from R. botrytis by its much shorter spores.

Other species with which R. botrytis may be confused include: Ramaria formosa, which has branches pinker than R. botrytis and tipped with yellow; R. caulifloriformis, occurring in the Great Lakes region in the United States, whose branch tips darken with age; R. strasseri, which has yellow to brown tips; R. rubrievanescens, which has branches in which the pink colour fades after picking or in mature fruit bodies; and R. botrytoides, which is most reliably distinguished from R. botrytis by its smooth spores.

The European species R. rielii, often confused with R. botrytis (sometimes the species are considered synonyms), can be distinguished by microscopic features: R. reilii has no clamp connections like R. botrytis, and its spores are longer and wider, and instead of stripes they have warts.

The North American species R. araiospora, although superficially similar to R. botrytis, has several distinguishing features: it grows under hemlocks; it has branches reddish to purple with tips from orange to yellowish; it has no perceptible smell; it has warty, somewhat cylindrical spores of average size 9.9 by 3.7 um; and it has non-amyloid trama.
Uniformly coloured pale pink to reddish; R. subbotrytis has spores measuring 7–9 by 3–3.5 µm.

owocnik: Bushy-branched, 6–15 cm wide and 8–20 cm high.
It grows from a fleshy base 2–3 cm thick.
This base branches 2–3 times into many branchlets with forked or toothed tips.
The terminal branchings are U-shaped, which distinguishes this species from most coral fungi, which have V-shaped branches.
The base is pale pink in young fruit bodies, the rest of the fruit body is salmon pink or orange with lemon yellow tips.
The mature fruit body changes colour to ochre-yellow.
miazsz: Fleshy, pinkish in young fruit bodies, whitish in older ones.
After drying it becomes chalky and cracked.
Slightly bitter in taste.
wysyp: Spores ellipsoid, ochre-yellow, slightly warty or smooth, measuring 9–12.5 × 4–5 µm.
podobne: Ramaria formosa can be confused with many other coral fungus species.
It differs from them in that its lower branches form large arches (like the letter U, not V as in most species).
Besides, the dried flesh has a consistency as brittle as chalk, not horny.

Older specimens of coral fungi (Ramaria) lose their characteristic colouring after a short time and can then be identified only microscopically, so special caution should be exercised when collecting them for eating.

owocnik: Young fruit bodies cauliflower-like, older ones bushy, 8–18 cm tall and 5–18 cm in diameter.
They have a base up to 4 cm thick, which branches several times into increasingly thinner twigs.
The branchings are V-shaped, and the branches are usually wrinkled.
At first the fruit bodies are pale pink, then flesh-pink, finally they take on the colour of coffee with milk and have brown spots on the surface.
The base is paler; at first whitish, later cream, the tips of the branches are coloured from pink-violet to red.
miazsz: Soft, brittle and white.
It does not change colour after damage.
Taste bitterish, smell somewhat similar to that of Maggi seasoning.
podobne: Besides Ramaria botrytis, old specimens of the very similar and poisonous Ramaria formosa can also be found. In beech forests the more ochre Ramaria flava occurs, never having branches with lilac-coloured tips.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–7 cm, arched in young individuals, spread out with a small umbo in the centre in older ones.
It is very water-absorbent.
In wet weather, after soaking up water, it is in colour from grey through rusty-brown to red-brown, in dry weather from pale ochre to grey-white.
The cap margin and the umbo are usually darker.
Skin smooth.
spod: Gills white, shortly attached only at the top and therefore looking almost free.
trzon: Light brown to reddish-brown, covered with white, hairy fibrils.
The base often looks swollen, hollow, longitudinally grooved on the outside.
A very characteristic feature is the cartilaginous nature of the stem: the outer layer is elastic and rubbery, the inner one has cottony-foamy flesh.
miazsz: Flesh thin, watery, soft.
In the cap it is elastic, inside the stem cartilaginous.
In wet weather it is brownish in colour, in dry weather whitish.
Taste and smell indistinct, reminiscent of the smell of rancid butter.
wysyp: Spores ellipsoid, smooth, 6–7.5 × 3–3.5 µm in diameter.
podobne: Rhodocollybia butyracea shows great variability, and for this reason it can be confused with many other species.
Young and dark-coloured individuals can be confused with Tricholoma saponaceum, older ones with Myochromella inolens.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–10 cm, hemispherical in young individuals, arched in older ones, finally spread out with a blunt umbo.
Cap margin inrolled for a long time.
It does not absorb water.
Cap skin smooth, white to yellowish-cream in colour.
A characteristic feature is the presence of rusty spots on the skin, and with age there are more and more of them, so that in older specimens the whole skin becomes uniformly rusty brown.
spod: Narrow, crowded and decurrent with a small tooth on the stem.
They are white in colour, but when pressed they change it to reddish-brown.
Gill edges weakly toothed, in older specimens covered with rusty speckles.
trzon: Height 6–10 cm, diameter 1–2 cm, cylindrical, hard and often curved.
Sometimes it widens at the base, whereas below it it is pointed.
It is solid, becoming hollow inside only in old specimens.
It has a colour similar to the cap and likewise with time becomes rusty-spotted, and rusty in older specimens.
miazsz: Springy, whitish, gradually darkens when damaged.
Smells of sawdust, taste bitter.
podobne: It can most easily be confused with other species of Rhodocollybia, but it differs clearly from them in its bitter, even burning taste and very crowded gills.
It may also be confused with Gymnopus fusipes, but that one is dark, reddish-brown.

kapelusz: Bright pink-salmon in colour, the gelatinous skin in young fruit bodies is covered with a very distinct network of white veins, diameter 1.5–9 cm.
spod: Adnate to notched, crowded, up to 11 mm wide, unforked, pale reddish, non-staining; edges even, gills in 2 to 4 tiers.
trzon: Short, measuring 1.5–3 × 0.4–1 cm, usually eccentric.
Surface dry, covered with a very thin layer of short, vertical, delicate, white hairs, which are easily rubbed off.
miazsz: Solid, light pink to cream, not staining, up to 8 mm thick.
Taste bitter.
Smell not characteristic, somewhat fruity, slightly sharp-aromatic.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–15 mm, at first bell-shaped-arched, then arched, finally with a concave centre.
Margin wavy, grooved and toothed.
Surface sticky, in colour from orange-yellow to orange, faded in older specimens, even to whitish.
spod: Distant and decurrent on the stem, with short lamellulae, at first whitish, then yellowish, finally light orange.
trzon: Height 2–5 cm, thickness 1–1 mm, thin, cylindrical.
Surface under a magnifying glass delicately spotted, yellowish in young specimens, orange-brown in older ones.
podobne: Mycena acicula, which has a yellowish stem, non-decurrent gills and occurs on rotting plant remains.
Xeromphalina campanella is also similar, but its fruit bodies form numerous clusters on rotting wood, and moreover it has no gills decurrent on the stem.
Hygrocybe cantharellus is larger and has a more intense colour.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–15 cm, shape at first hemispherical, then flat-arched with a flat large umbo at the top.
In young fruit bodies grey-white, then brownish-brown-olive, after damage pinkish or the colour of "old rose".
spod: Free at the stem.
In young specimens they are yellow, then olive-yellow.
Pores coloured from carmine-red to wine-red, fading in older specimens.
trzon: Height 5–8 cm, thickness 3–5 cm, shape at first barrel-shaped, then club-shaped.
Surface pale yellow, covered with a very fine reddish reticulum, disappearing under the cap.
miazsz: Pale yellow, turning blue (young fruit bodies) or green (older ones) when cut.
It has a smell of chicory.
podobne: It resembles Rubroboletus satanas, which differs from this species in its unpleasant smell and is also more strongly poisonous.

kapelusz: It has a diameter of 5–20 cm.
Hemispherical when young, then arched, finally flat, cushion-shaped.
Surface colour from whitish yellow to yellow-brown, at first felty, then bare and smooth.
spod: Tubular.
Tubes notched at the stem, at first yellow, then yellow-green.
When damaged they turn blue-green.
Pores small, yellow in young specimens, carmine-red in older ones, finally dirty olive.
trzon: Height 5–12 cm, thickness 3–5 cm, barrel-shaped in young specimens, club-shaped in older ones.
Surface yellow at the top with a purple reticulum (net), at the bottom coloured from blood-red to purple and covered with a purple reticulum (net).
miazsz: Pale yellow, changing colour to blue-green when cut.
Taste and smell indefinite.
podobne: Rubroboletus legaliae has white flesh that turns blue over the whole surface of the section.
Rubroboletus rubrosanguineus differs slightly in colours, occurs only in coniferous forests, and its flesh is like that of the borowik legalowej (Polish name).
Satan's bolete occurs in similar environments, but has a different cap colour, a different type of reticulum and also turns blue throughout the whole section.

inne: Fruit body thick, firm.
Its cap can reach a diameter of up to 20 cm.
In young fruit bodies it is hemispherical, with time convex, in older fruit bodies flat.
A characteristic feature is the pinkish cap margin.
Pores of the tubes red.
Flesh in the cap and in the upper part of the stem yellow, turning slightly bluish when damaged.
Stem cylindrical or bulbous.
The upper part of its surface is yellow and net-patterned in red or orange, the lower part orange-red or pink, without a reticulum (net).
Fresh fruit bodies have a mushroomy smell, dried ones smell of hay.
Rubroboletus legaliae is very similar.
That one, however, lives in symbiosis with broadleaved trees.

kapelusz: Diameter 6–30 cm, grey, in mature individuals with a yellowish, greenish tinge, brown-ochre when pressed.
Hemispherical, later bent and flattened, thick.
Skin matt, dry or suede-like, does not separate from the flesh.
spod: At first yellowish, then blood-red, with age taking on a brown-olive colour.
When damaged they turn blue.
Pores in young ones at first orange-yellow, later carmine, in old specimens becoming olive.
trzon: Height 5–15 cm, thickness 3–8 cm.
Solid, massive, at first spherical or cylindrical, then barrel-shaped.
Beneath the cap it is yellowish, lower down it is carmine-red.
miazsz: Whitish, fleshy, slowly turning blue when cut.
Taste mild, smell faint, old individuals have a smell somewhat resembling carrion.
podobne: Rubroboletus rhodoxanthus.
It is also rare, has a red stem and its flesh turns blue (but only in the cap).
It differs in the pink tinge of the cap, and has a cylindrical stem covered with a characteristic reticulum.
Caloboletus calopus.
It is common, has yellow pores, bitter flesh.
Suillellus rubrosanguineus.
Occurs in coniferous forests.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–10 cm.
Young fruit bodies have a spherical cap, in older ones it becomes broadly spread out and concave in the centre.
Surface smooth, dry and matt, crenate at the margin.
In rain it becomes slippery.
Colour from green through olive green to yellow-green.
Usually darker in the centre.
The skin can be peeled from almost the whole cap.
spod: Broad, crowded and of different lengths, not attached at the stem, or only slightly.
White in young individuals, cream in older ones.
trzon: Smooth and cylindrical, white, rusty-spotted at the base, pointed, without a ring.
Height 4–8 cm, thickness 1–2 cm.
Solid in young specimens, spongy inside in older ones.
miazsz: In young specimens hard, white and brittle.
It has a slightly burning taste, especially the gills.
Under the action of FeSO4 it becomes greyish-pink.
wysyp: Spores ellipsoid or inversely egg-shaped, covered with fine warts.
The warts are up to 0.6 μm high, with blunt tips, some of them joined by single, delicate connectors.
Cystidia blunt or with a broad tip at the top, dermatocystidia cylindrical, blunt.
podobne: It is sometimes confused with the deadly poisonous death cap (Amanita phalloides).
Russula heterophylla is also similar, but it does not have a biting taste and its skin can be peeled off only to one third of the cap radius.

kapelusz: Diameter 4 cm, hemispherical in young specimens, later flat-arched with a depression in the centre.
The margins are often wavy, sometimes lobed.
Skin smooth. In dry weather it is shiny, in wet weather slippery.
It can be peeled off to half of the cap diameter.
Margin of the cap not moderately blunt, wavy and uniform, only in older specimens sometimes slightly notched.
The cap skin is characterised by vivid colours and a great variety of colour forms.
In typical cases the cap is dark red, blood-red, crimson, purple-red, even red-black.
However, there are forms with a strongly pink, red-violet, dirty lilac or grey-olive-brown cap.
spod: Narrow, crowded and brittle.
They are coloured from white to light cream, in older mushrooms they become rusty-spotted.
trzon: Height 4–6 cm, thickness 1–2.5 cm, cylindrical.
At first it is hard and compact, with time it becomes spongy.
It is white and slightly greyish, only at the base faintly rusty.
miazsz: White, hard, reddish-violet only directly under the skin.
In taste it is burning, especially in young mushrooms.
podobne: Russula brunneoviolacea – has ochre gills and an unfolded cap,
Russula vinosopurpurea – is smaller, has no red tinges on the cap and its flesh is not acrid

kapelusz: Diameter 3–8 cm, flat, later concave, sometimes with an umbo.
Margins blunt and smooth, slightly crenate in older specimens.
Surface matt, in colours from violet-amethyst through brown-violet to pink-violet, with olive tinges.
In the centre it is darker.
Sometimes, especially after prolonged rain, it fades to a yellowish and whitish colour.
Skin smooth, dull, thin and can be peeled off almost to the middle of the cap.
spod: Brittle, white, free.
trzon: 3 to 6 cm high and up to 1.5 cm thick.
It is cylindrical, solid in young specimens, hollow in older ones.
Colour white.
miazsz: Without a distinct smell or taste.
It is less brittle than in the brittle russula.
podobne: Russula lilacea.
It grows only in deciduous forests and often has a reddish stem.
Russula turci.
It differs in its characteristic smell of iodoform and has yellow gills.
Russula amethystina.
It differs in its yellow gills and yellow spore print.

kapelusz: Diameter 2.5–9 cm, at first convex, then spread out, sometimes with a small umbo.
Margin thin, rather blunt, smooth or crenate.
Skin very thin and smooth.
Sticky in wet weather, shiny in dry weather.
It can be peeled completely off the cap.
It is lilac, pink-lilac or blue-lilac in colour, in the centre brown-olive with purple-brown, yellowish or grey-greenish spots.
In general this is a russula with a small cap (up to 6 cm in diameter) and variable colouring – completely violet forms are also found.
spod: Crowded in young specimens, later distant.
Sharp at the cap margin, sometimes (rarely) forked at the stem.
At first white, later chalky-whitish.
Deep wrinkles often occur on them.
trzon: Height up to 7 cm, thickness up to 2.5 cm.
Shape inversely club-shaped or spindle-shaped.
Surface smooth and white, yellowish at the base.
Only in young fruit bodies is it solid, it quickly becomes cottony, even chambered.
miazsz: Brittle.
It is entirely white, even under the skin, but shows a tendency to turn yellow.
It gives off a characteristic smell, the taste is acrid.
podobne: The characteristic features of the chambered brittlegill are: occurrence under conifers, small size, a usually blue-lilac cap, an always white, cottony or chambered stem and a white spore print.
Under the action of ammonia it immediately turns pink (especially the gills).
Russula violacea is the most similar.
Some forms of Russula fragilis may also be similar.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–10 cm, hemispherical when young with an inrolled margin, then flat, with a depression in the middle, hard and fleshy.
Surface shiny, uniformly coloured, lemon yellow to chrome yellow.
The skin can be peeled off to half of the cap.
spod: Thick and rather distant, sometimes forked or forming anastomoses.
At the margin they are rounded, at the stem narrowed, free, or slightly decurrent with a small tooth.
At first they are white, later yellow-ochre.
trzon: Height 4–7 cm, thickness 1.5–2.5 cm, cylindrical, sometimes slightly widened in the middle, at first solid, then cottony.
Surface white, sometimes slightly lemon-coloured, almost smooth or suede-like.
Turns grey when touched.
miazsz: Thick and firm, white in colour.
When cut it turns blackish-grey.
In taste at first astringent, later mild and sweetish.
Smell faint.
podobne: Russula decolorans, especially forms with yellow tinges.
They always have a more orange cap, however, and grow in spruce forests,
Russula ochroleuca does not turn blackish-grey and grows in coniferous forests,
Russula fellea.
It has a burning taste.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–15 cm.
Young hemispherical with a turned-under margin, later convex, old concave to funnel-shaped.
Skin mostly without gloss.
In wet weather the skin is sticky, in dry weather shiny.
There is great variability in the colouring of the cap.
It is coloured in various shades of violet, blue, pink, ochre, olive and grey-blackish.
The whole cap may be uniformly coloured, but it may also be a combination of the colours listed.
spod: Gills white, fairly crowded, of different lengths (short gills mixed with longer ones). They are pliable (they do not crumble when touched with a finger) – which is an exception among russulas.
This species is the only Russula whose gills on older mushrooms do not become brittle but stay flexible.
trzon: Height 5–12 cm, thickness 2–3 cm, cylindrical, at first hard, later spongy.
White, rarely tinged lilac-red.
miazsz: Permanently white, fairly firm.
Taste mild.
Unlike other Russula species, the flesh does not stain flesh-pink under the influence of ferrous sulphate.
podobne: Russula heterophylla is similar.
It differs in its more crowded gills, forked and fused near the stem, and in the predominance of olive-green on the cap.
It can also be confused with the edible Russula ionochlora, which is small and has crumbly gills.
Compare also with the edible Russula parazurea and Russula grisea.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–12 cm.
At first almost spherical, later flattened, usually orange or brick-red.
Older caps fade and become ochre and sometimes have slightly striate cap margins.
The cap surface is smooth, sticky in wet weather, dry in dry weather.
spod: Free, crowded, broad, bellied and somewhat brittle.
At first white, later yellow in the shade of butter.
Older ones turn black on the surface, and turn grey after damage.
trzon: Cylindrical, 2 to 8 cm long and 1 to 3 cm thick, white.
Old stems become dark grey or blackish.
They turn grey when damaged.
miazsz: Whitish, sometimes slightly yellowish under the cap skin.
At cuts or with age turning grey or black.
It has no smell, taste mild.
podobne: Russula ochroleuca.
It has an ochre-yellow cap and does not turn grey when broken.
Russula maculata.
It has pink-purple patches on the cap and stem, and when broken it does not turn grey either,
Russula paludosa Britz.
Cap shape and colour similar, but the flesh does not turn grey when broken.

kapelusz: Diameter usually 4–8 cm, exceptionally up to 11 cm.
In young specimens it is convex, in older ones flattened and usually concave.
Skin smooth, shiny and sticky in wet weather.
It can be peeled off almost completely.
Its colour is vermilion, blood-red or almost cherry, the centre is bright red.
Sometimes it fades and becomes pale pink.
Margin blunt, weakly turned in
spod: Pure white, thin, crowded, brittle, slightly attached at the stem.
trzon: Height 3.5–6 cm, thickness 0.8–1.3 cm, cylindrical, sometimes club-shaped in the lower part.
Surface white, delicately mossy.
At first solid, but it quickly becomes cottony.
miazsz: White, usually pink right under the skin.
It has a pleasant, delicately fruity smell, while the taste is bitter, burning and long-lasting in the mouth.
podobne: In Europe there are hundreds of Russula species with a red cap, and telling them apart without more detailed microscopic and chemical examination is sometimes impossible.
Some of them are:
Russula paludosa.
It has a larger stem, is not burning in taste and is edible.
Russula noblis.
Grows only under beeches.
Russula rhodopus.
It has a stem with purple colouring.
Russula sanguinaria.
It has a pink-reddish stem.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–8 cm, arched when young, flat in mature specimens with smooth or shallowly grooved margins.
Skin thin, can be peeled off only at the margin.
Surface matt, in colour from straw-yellow to honey-brownish, sometimes with an orange tinge.
In wet weather the cap is moist and sticky.
Rusty-brown spots appear on the cap when pressed.
The centre is darker than the margins.
spod: Fairly thin and crowded, of equal length, with few lamellulae, rarely forking.
They are narrow and rounded at the margin, narrowing towards the stem and shortly attached.
Colour at first whitish, later pale ochre.
trzon: Height 3–7 cm, thickness up to 2 cm, cylindrical, club-shaped in the lower part.
Solid in young specimens, hollow in older ones.
Colour slightly paler than on the cap.
miazsz: Brittle, white in young specimens, later straw-ochre.
Taste burning, very acrid, smell resembling the smells of mustard, fruit or pelargonium (geranium).
podobne: Russula claroflava.
It grows only under birches and specimens with an acrid taste do not occur among members of this species.
Russula ochroleuca is larger, has no distinct smell and is not as acrid in taste.
Morphologically it is difficult to distinguish Russula fellea from these two similar, yellow-coloured russulas, especially Russula ochroleuca.

A clue may be the stronger colouring of the cap centre in Russula fellea, and the fact that Russula fellea is characterised by a small difference in colour between the cap margin and the gills (in Russula ochroleuca it is distinct).
This can be definitively settled by a taste test; Russula fellea causes an unbearable burning in the mouth.

kapelusz: Diameter from 2 to 5(7) cm, small and brittle, lighter or darker violetish, with an admixture of reddish and greenish shades, also with a greater share of red.
Centre both almost blackish and fading to yellowish to olive-ochre.
The skin soon loses its gloss.
Margin shortly grooved in old age.
The skin can be peeled off to half the radius.
spod: Fairly crowded, sometimes forked, almost free at the stem.
Pure white when young, later cream-yellowish, with a delicately notched edge.
trzon: Height 3 to 5 cm and thickness 7–20 mm.
It is thick, cylindrical, sometimes slightly club-shaped.
Solid in young specimens, hollow in older ones.
White, yellow with age or after damage.
miazsz: Invariably white, with a pleasant fruity smell.
Taste burning and acrid.
podobne: This is a species with great morphological variability.
For this reason many varieties and forms of it have been distinguished.
According to Index Fungorum, all of them are now regarded as synonyms of Russula fragilis.
Similar are: Russula versicolor, with a not very acrid taste, Russula azurea, Russula turci, Russula ionochlora.

kapelusz: Diameter 4.5–7 cm, convex, in older specimens flat-convex, fleshy.
Surface greenish-violet, often green in the centre, with time fading to pale olive with a small number of ochre speckles and a darker bloom.
spod: Almost free, crowded, later more distant, up to 8 mm wide, thin, brittle, with lamellulae, forked here and there, white, pale cream in older fruit bodies, turning slightly yellow while drying.
trzon: Height 3–6 cm, thickness 1.3–2 cm, cylindrical, massive, at first solid, then hollow.
Surface slightly tinged violet.
miazsz: Fairly thick, white, turning slightly yellow when damaged, and pinkish in places eaten by worms.
Taste mild, smell weak, sourish.
Under the influence of iron sulphate, in the stem it turns pink-red or greyish, and in the cap grey-olive-pinkish.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–8.5 cm, 3–8.5 cm, brittle, at first convex, then flattening and very early broadly depressed in the centre, and often even almost funnel-shaped.
Margin rounded, turned in, at first smooth, then fairly broadly grooved, often irregular or lobed, wavy.

Surface irregularly bumpy, colour from blood red to pinkish red, not very dark but intense, fading very strongly in rain; in older specimens with numerous pale, cream or whitish areas, sometimes even completely white at the margin.
spod: From moderately crowded to very sparse, thick or thinner depending on the specimen, sometimes fused, almost always clearly decurrent, 3–8 mm wide, white but with a slight cream tinge, turning yellow when squeezed or damaged.
trzon: Height 2–7 cm, thickness 0.6–1.6 cm, very variable (sometimes eccentric or even lateral), at first mostly club-shaped, later narrowing towards the base, spindle-shaped, less often cylindrical or bellied, sometimes curved or irregular, at first fairly hard, then somewhat spongy.

Surface white, often tinged pink, at least in the places that may turn yellow spontaneously at the base; when scratched it turns light lemon yellow, but sometimes only after several hours, because the colouring is not very distinct.
miazsz: Brittle, fairly compact to hard, white, with a tendency to turn yellow spontaneously, in coloured forms reddish under the skin.
Smell slightly fruity; taste astringent.
A very strong and rapid reaction with guaiacol, no reaction with ammonia.
podobne: Very similar are Russula nobilis and Russula sanguinea, but it differs from them by the yellowing of the stem and gills where cut.

kapelusz: It is 10–20 cm in diameter, arched when young, then spread out and depressed in the centre.
It has inrolled margins, is very hard and thick-fleshed.
Young specimens are whitish in colour, then whitish olive-grey, later dark brown, finally black.
spod: Distant.
Very thick, brittle, plate-like and slightly attached to the stem.
Like the cap, they are white when young, then gradually change colour to black.
When damaged they turn grey, and even black.
trzon: Height 2–7 cm, thickness 1–3 cm.
It is thick, cylindrical, solid and very hard.
Compared with most species of the genus Russula, it is short.
Like the cap, it changes colour during development from white to black.
It turns red when pressed.
miazsz: It is very hard, when cut it first turns red, then black, smell very faint and somewhat bland, taste mild.
podobne: There are many species of brittlegills that turn black immediately when damaged.

Russula densifolia may be similar, but has denser gills; Russula albonigra has a bitterish-minty taste; Russula adusta has a cap that is paler at the margins and its flesh turns red when cut, but does not turn black.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–9.5 cm, shape at first hemispherical, then spread out, even slightly concave.
Margin fairly sharp, smooth and slightly crenate (at most up to 5 mm).
Surface smooth, in colour from pink to carmine.
After rain it fades and becomes dirty yellowish or light pink.
In dry weather the skin is matt, in wet weather slightly sticky; it can be peeled off only right at the margin.
spod: Fairly crowded and fairly thin.
They are 5–8 mm wide, forked, attached with a sinus at the stem, blunt at the margin.
Lamellulae occur between them.
They are white, or with a yellowish tinge.
trzon: Height 2.5–4 cm, thickness 1–1.5 cm, cylindrical, solid.
Surface smooth or delicately rough, without pink colouring, at most with a faint pink tinge.
It is white, yellow or brownish in colour.
miazsz: Hard and compact, white, coloured pink only under the skin.
Smell slightly fruity, taste acrid.
podobne: Russula vesca, whose flesh-pink cap skin does not reach the margin, exposing the white flesh.
Edible.
Russula luteotacta, which has a bitter and acrid taste, and whose cap turns chrome yellow when pressed.
Inedible.
Russula emetica, whose cap is also glossy red, with white but large and ornamented spores.
Poisonous.

kapelusz: Diameter 4-8(10) cm, when young hemispherical, later flat, wavy and slightly bent over.
The skin can be peeled off to about half of the diameter of the cap.
In wet weather it is sticky, in dry weather dry.
Colour yellowish-ochre to lemon.
Cap skin smooth.
Margin blunt and slightly curved under, in older fruit bodies it may be slightly crenate and lumpy.
spod: Brittle, in young fruit bodies moderately crowded, later more distant.
They are free, and sinuately notched at the stem, rounded at the margin, sometimes forked.
At first they are white, with time they become light cream and ochre spots appear on them in places.
trzon: Cylindrical, 5.5–7 cm high and 1.5–2 cm thick, strong, at first solid, later cottony.
Surface smooth and slightly shiny, white, often with a pale ochre tinge, never, however, ochre.
Sometimes it may have ochre spots
miazsz: White or whitish, turning grey near the stem, fairly soft.
Smell very faint.
Taste mild or, in most specimens, tolerably hot.
podobne: Russula fellea.
It is honey-yellow, smells of geranium, has a burning, acrid taste and is inedible.
Its characteristic feature is a small difference in colour between the cap margin and the gills (in Russula ochroleuca this difference is distinct)
Russula claroflava.
It grows only under birches and specimens with an acrid taste do not occur among members of this species.
Russula solaris.
It has a burning taste and grows only under beeches.

kapelusz: Massive, up to 12 cm in diameter, sometimes even up to 20 cm, at first hemispherical, then flat-convex, finally completely flat with a broad depression in the centre.
Surface smooth, moist, matt, as if slightly suede-like, in colour from olive to grey-olive, sometimes shading into brown or with a carmine bloom, especially at the margin.
Margin blunt, rounded, slightly curved under and not crenate.
The skin can be peeled off almost to the middle of the cap.
spod: Free or slightly attached, thick, 4–10 mm wide, fairly distant when mature, blunt, rounded at the margin of the cap, narrowed and slightly forked at the stem, at first white but fairly quickly cream with an ochre tinge, sometimes with a purple tinge on the edges
trzon: Height 4–10 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, sometimes even up to 4 cm, cylindrical or inversely club-shaped, slightly narrowed at the base, at first solid, later cottony, finally hollow.
Surface smooth, matt or silky, white, but usually flushed pink in the upper part.
miazsz: Thick, brittle in older specimens, white, but after cutting quickly changing to pale beige, without a distinct smell or taste.
Under the action of phenol it turns purple-wine in colour, and under the action of FeS04 grey-pink.
podobne: Sometimes confused with Russula viscida.

kapelusz: Cap diameter 10–15 cm.
At first hemispherical, later spread out, finally mostly depressed.
Margin curved under and blunt, even in young fruit bodies, later slightly crenate.
Surface moist, shiny and sticky.
Colour brick-red, blood-red, sometimes with a purple tint, there are also paler fruit bodies, ochre-orange or olive in colour.
The skin can be peeled off to half the radius of the cap.
spod: They stay white for a long time, later butter-yellow, on the edges sometimes reddish.
trzon: Height 7 to 15 cm, thickness 2.5–5.5 cm, cylindrical, equally thick over its whole length, at first solid, later cottony.
White, sometimes with a red bloom.
miazsz: Brittle, not changing colour after damage, white, slightly pink only under the skin, turning slightly grey in old age, without smell, with a mild taste.
podobne: Very similar is Russula emetica, but it is distinguished by its very acrid and burning taste.

The marsh brittlegill can be confused with the edible Russula decolorans – both fungi occur in the same habitat – as well as with the inedible Russula badia, which has an acrid taste, or with the edible Russula velenovskyi.

kapelusz: Diameter 3.2–8 cm, fairly fleshy, at first convex, then widening and finally depressed in the centre, sometimes even navel-like.
Margin narrowing fairly abruptly, not furrowed or almost not furrowed (rarely fairly distinctly and only in old specimens).
Surface at first dark green-grey, olive-grey, sometimes with brown tinges in the centre, ochre or violetish spots.
After cooking the skin turns pink or lilac.
spod: Moderately crowded, fairly thick, often forked here and there or divided in two at the base, sharp at the edge, moderately broad (3.5–9 mm), brittle, at first white, then pale cream or yellow-cream, with lamellulae
trzon: Height 3–5.5 cm, thickness 0.7–1.8 cm, almost cylindrical or slightly widened under the gills, less often slightly thickened at the base, sometimes curved, at first solid, later spongy, pure white, only sometimes with a few brown or yellow-brown spots at the base;.
Surface very delicately dusted, shiny, smooth or finely wrinkled.
miazsz: Brittle, fairly compact but never very hard, white, coloured like the cap only slightly just under the skin.
It has a very faint smell, barely noticeable when fresh, and a sweet or slightly peppery taste after prolonged chewing.
FeSO4 stains it a dirty brownish-pink, usually fairly quickly.
podobne: Macroscopically similar are Russula atroglauca, Russula anatina and Russula cyanoxantha.
The latter often has a very similar colour, but is distinguished by a white spore print and extremely pliable gills (compared with other brittlegills).
Russula azurea has a bluer colour and grows mainly in mountain forests under spruces.

kapelusz: Diameter 8–10 cm, at first convex, later hemispherical, finally spread out and concave in the centre.
It is sometimes wavy, even crenate.
Margin not very sharp, blunt in older specimens.
The surface in wet weather is smooth, shiny and sticky, in dry weather dull.
It is dark red, purple-violet, brown-purple or wine-red in colour.
In older specimens, or in wet weather, these colours fade, but coloured patches remain.
During rains the cap, especially at the margin, loses its colour and takes on a white-grey colour, even with a greenish tinge.
The skin can be separated at most to half of the cap.
spod: Crowded in young fruit bodies, less so in older ones.
They are thin and fairly narrow, broadened at the cap margin.
First whitish, later cream, but without a lemon tinge.
Intermediate lamellae few.
trzon: Height 2-5 (8) cm, thickness 0.5-2 (2.5) cm, cylindrical, but often narrowed at the base and at the top.
It is solid, in older specimens cottony, brittle and fragile.
Surface smooth, slightly mealy, pink-lilac or light carmine, sometimes with dirty wine-coloured stains.
In older fruit bodies the colours fade and the stem becomes cream.
miazsz: Fairly firm and compact, with time it becomes soft and brittle.
It is white, reddish only under the skin of the cap and stem.
It does not change colour after damage.
Smell faint, taste bitter and burning, lasting.
podobne: The edible Russula sardonia, however, has lemon-coloured gills and reticulate spores.
Russula torulosa, which also has an acrid taste and occurs under pines, but is warmth- and lime-loving.
Russula sanguinea also has a red cap and stem, but paler, without a purple tinge.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–8 (11) cm, thick, fleshy, at first spherical, then strongly convex to flat-convex, with the centre at first only flattened, then very slightly concave, finally shaped like a shallow saucer, more rarely with an umbo or a depression limited to the centre only.
Margin at first strongly inrolled, then more or less straightened.

Surface shiny, as if varnished, at first dark red, somewhat coppery, then redder, finally blood-red, but still with darker parts, between Moroccan red and burgundy brown, rarely with a large area discoloured dirty yellowish.
The skin separates well from the flesh, except for the very centre.
spod: Fairly crowded, but thick, with many large lamellulae and quite a number of forks, narrow (4–6 mm), rather blunt at the front, at first ivory-coloured (at the beginning less white than the flesh), then ochre-cream, but always very pale.
Edges of the same colour.
trzon: Height 3–7 cm, thickness 1–2.5 cm, often dented and deformed, sometimes eccentric, often narrowed upwards, though widened at the end directly under the gills, bulging and club-shaped at the base, at first solid, then spongy.

Surface sometimes white, but usually with a pink tinge, more rarely red, often in irregular areas or in the lower part or on one side only slightly coloured yellow or dirty reddish yellow, finely dusted, mealy under a lens, then delicately wrinkled.
miazsz: Thick, hard, then firm but brittle, white, slightly yellowed at the edges;.
It has a very weak fruity smell, the taste is at first mild, then moderately acrid, then takes on a slightly salty taste; but not bitter.
wysyp: Pale ochre when fresh, but fading after drying.

kapelusz: Diameter 3.7–10 cm, 3.7–10 cm, fleshy, even hard, at first convex, then flattening and often depressed in the middle, less often saucer-shaped or with a small umbo.
Margin at first more or less sharp, later more rounded, sometimes slightly wavy, but most often regular, generally smooth, only in old specimens slightly striate, and always inconspicuously.

Surface blood-red, dark violet or pink-red, with the centre sometimes darker, to brown-navy, more or less fading, often spotted whitish or with an ochre spot in the middle, but rarely entirely white or dirty white.

The skin can be peeled off only at the margin, elsewhere it adheres strongly, is slightly sticky and a little shiny only when wet, but quickly dries and becomes dull, finely wrinkled, under a hand lens with small nodules or spots.
spod: In young specimens fairly crowded, in older ones fairly distant or distant, often with a few short gills, generally with fairly numerous forkings, 2–6 mm wide (sometimes less than the thickness of the flesh!), at first whitish, then pale ochre-cream, cream with a pale yellow tinge, often turning yellow after quite a long time when crushed, sometimes with a pinkish or reddish margin near the edges.
trzon: Height (2)4–7 cm, thickness 0.8–23 cm, strong, almost cylindrical, less often slightly narrowed or thickened at the bottom, sometimes slightly spindle-shaped, long, solid and not spongy, but in older age empty chambers may appear in it.
It is dusted and densely longitudinally wrinkled.

Surface usually pink or pink-red, jasper-pink, wine-orange, often more intensely coloured at the bottom than at the top, sometimes in older specimens or when touched yellow or saffron-yellow-brown, less often entirely white.
miazsz: Thick in the centre, but strongly thinned at the margin, firm, even hard, then somewhat brittle, white, pink only under the skin (especially when wet), sometimes with a tendency to a yellowish tinge or with rusty-yellow spots.
It has a faint and atypical fruity smell, the taste quite variable, more or less astringent (never strong), and also more or less bitter.
With guaiacol it changes colour to light blue, darkening fairly quickly; it reacts very weakly with ammonia, but sometimes with a fleeting pink effect when fresh.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–10 cm.
Hemispherical in young specimens, then spread out, finally concave.
In the centre it may have a small umbo or depression.
Skin smooth, dry, shiny, slimy in wet weather.
Colour red-violet or purple-violet, darker in the centre – even blackish-purple.
Faded specimens may be brownish, ochre or greenish (usually in the form of faded patches).
The skin can be peeled off only right at the margin.
Margin sharp, smooth, rolled under in young specimens, straight in older ones and sometimes slightly crenate.
spod: Fairly narrow and crowded, with short gills (lamellulae), often forked.
Sharp at the margin, attached at the stem or slightly arched-decurrent.
In young specimens light cream, then cream with a lemon tinge.
trzon: Height 3–8 cm, thickness 1–2.5 cm.
It is cylindrical, solid and smooth.
Colour at first white, later purple-violet colouring appears.
miazsz: Lemon-yellow, like the gills.
After damage it changes colour to orange after some time.
Taste strongly burning, smell fruity.
podobne: some colour forms of Russula atropurpurea
among the violet Russula species, Russula torulosa and Russula queletii are similar.
Both have a burning, or at least bitter, taste, but neither of them has lemon-yellow gills.
Russula turci – grows in similar habitats, sometimes together with the red-violet Russula.
It is distinguished by a smell of chloroform and ochre gills.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–7.5 cm, fleshy, firm.
Convex when young with a small umbo, later spread flat, finally concave.
Surface purple-violet, purple-red, beetroot, sometimes dark red, sometimes pale with an olive tinge in the centre.
Margin fairly sharp, slightly turned under.
Skin shiny when wet, peelable up to 1/3 of the cap radius.
spod: Crowded, fairly narrow, with lamellulae, partly forked, running down the stem somewhat or sinuately, at first whitish, then white-cream, but never lemon-coloured.
trzon: Height 2–6 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, squat, thick, solid in young specimens, cottony in older ones.
Surface dull in colour from bright violet-purple to pale grey-lilac, whitish or straw yellow at the base.
miazsz: White, hard, with a characteristic smell of apples.
Taste bitter and acrid, more burning in the gills.
podobne: Russula sardonia has a similar colouring, but it has lemon-yellow gills, a very acrid taste and is more delicate.
Russula gueletii smells of gooseberry and has a blackish cap centre.

kapelusz: Usually 5–8 cm in diameter, at first convex, but it quickly becomes spread out, finally concave.
Margin blunt, and notched in older specimens.
Surface sticky in wet weather, especially in the centre, matt in dry weather.
Colour dirty violet, violet-red, wine or fawn, often violet at the margins.
The skin can be peeled off up to one third of the cap radius.
spod: Moderately crowded, somewhat forked near the stem and rounded near the margin.
At first they are cream, later ochre and yellow.
trzon: Height from 3 to 7 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, shape cylindrical.
At first it is solid and fairly firm, later cottony and hollow.
Surface smooth, matt, white, more rarely slightly lilac.
Sometimes it is tinged with pink.
miazsz: Firm, white, turning slightly yellow.
Lilac only under the cap skin.
Taste mild.
Sometimes a smell of chloroform can be detected, though not always.
podobne: Russula azurea is very similar.
These species are often confused with each other or not distinguished.
The azure russula always has white gills and does not have a chloroform smell.
It is also distinguished by the ornamentation of the spores.
Russula fragilis has a cap with green and blackish tints and a strongly burning taste.
It grows mainly under broadleaved trees.

kapelusz: Diameter 2–4.5 cm, brittle, at first convex with an even and rounded margin, but quickly flattening with a crenate margin, finally with a small depression in the centre.
It is usually multicoloured; pink-lilac, purple-yellow, in older specimens yellowish-olive to dark olive-blackish in the centre.
Skin smooth, sticky and shiny in wet weather, peelable fairly far.
spod: Thin, fairly sparse, free, sometimes with a few lamellulae, forked here and there, rounded at the cap margin, with wrinkles, cream to light ochre.
trzon: Height 2–6 cm, thickness 0.5–1 cm, cylindrical, wider below, brittle, at first solid, then cottony to chambered.
Surface smooth in young specimens, slightly ribbed in older ones, white, but turning yellow after a few hours.
miazsz: Brittle, fairly thick only in the centre, white, slowly turning yellow.
It has a weak, fruity smell, in taste at first mild, but after a longer time and in old specimens acrid.
Under the action of FeSO4 it usually quickly changes colour to flesh pink.
podobne: Somewhat similar is Russula puellaris, which differs in its mild taste and paler, whitish spore print.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–12 cm, pale ochre, reddish or brown-red, often with pink or violet patches, at the margins at first smooth, then slightly furrowed.
Semicircular when young, then convex, finally flat, usually with a depression in the centre.
Skin dull, not quite reaching the edge of the cap.
spod: Brittle, fragile, white when young, mature with rusty spots on the edges, rounded at the margins of the cap.
trzon: Cylindrical, narrowed at the bottom, solid, hard, white, yellowish or rusty-ochre at the base.
miazsz: Brittle, white, in cross-section it stains rusty-brown in places.
Taste slight, mild, reminiscent of hazelnuts.
A fresh fruit body smells indistinct, an old one like herrings.
Under the action of FeSO4 it becomes orange-pink.
podobne: A red or pink cap is also found in the slightly poisonous, acrid-tasting Russula emetica and Russula mairei.
In contrast to them, the bare-toothed brittlegill is always less shiny, and its flesh is firmer.
A good identifying feature is the cap skin, which falls 1–2 mm short of the margin.
Compare also with the edible Russula velenovskyi.

kapelusz: Diameter up to 5 cm, convex in young specimens, flat with a shallowly depressed centre in older ones.
Surface in colour from greenish to dark violet, paler at the margin.
Margin blunt, sometimes wavy and lobed.
Skin moist, sticky and partly peelable.
spod: Sinuate, in young specimens fairly crowded, in older ones more distant, slightly forked near the stem, blunt at the edge, at first white, then cream.
trzon: Up to 5.5 cm high and up to 1.5 cm thick, cylindrical, narrowed at the top or widened at the bottom, pliable or brittle, at first solid, then cottony.
Surface silky-shiny, white, with time yellowish or brownish.
miazsz: Fairly compact, white, slightly yellowish or brownish in places, with an acrid taste and a strong pelargonium (geranium) smell.
podobne: Characteristic features of the violet Russula are the greenish colour of the cap at least in its central part, a tendency of the flesh to yellow in the stem and cap, and broadly egg-shaped, almost spherical spores.
Similar is Russula fragilis, but it has a less violet colour and toothed gills.

kapelusz: Diameter about 6 to 15 cm, spherical in young fruit bodies, later hemispherical-arched, finally spread out.
Margin blunt and quite often knobbly-notched.
A characteristic feature is the cracked surface divided into small fields, but this occurs only on older fruit bodies, especially in dry weather.
Colour grey-green to blue-greenish, verdigris, the cap fading yellowish in places or entirely.
Skin scaly, always matt and without gloss.
spod: Thick, up to 10 mm wide.
White in young individuals, pale cream in older ones, with brownish edges.
trzon: Height from 5 to 12 cm.
White, solid, becoming spongy with age.
Base often with rusty spots.
miazsz: Thick, fleshy, white, hard in young fruit bodies, brittle and porous in older ones.
When damaged it turns slightly brown.
Taste delicate, smell nutty.
wysyp: Spores with warts either separately distributed or partly connected in a net-like way, measuring 6–8.5(10) × 5–7 µm.
podobne: It has such a characteristic cap surface that fully grown fruit bodies basically cannot be confused with other mushrooms.
However, young specimens can be mistaken by inexperienced mushroom pickers for the deadly poisonous Amanita phalloides.
It is essential to check the stem; the death cap (Amanita phalloides) has a bulb with a volva at its base.
It can be confused with Russula aeruginea, but this mistake is not so dangerous, because that species is also edible, but has a much worse taste.
Several other species of green brittlegills also grow in Poland, but none has such a characteristic 'checkered' surface and such a shade of colour as Russula virescens.

kapelusz: 8–12 cm in diameter, fleshy, at first convex, soon spread out flat.

Surface at first very sticky and shiny, in dry weather matt, wine-red, buff-ginger with a brownish tint, ginger with a pink margin, in the centre usually ochre, ginger or yellowish-green, exceptionally grey-violet.
Margin long inrolled, shortly striate, often irregularly lobed.
Skin that can be peeled off only at the margin.
spod: Fairly distant with few lamellulae, some forked, narrowed both at the margin and at the stem, whitish with a greenish tint.
trzon: Height 4–9 cm, thickness 2-3, exceptionally up to 5 cm, hard and firm in young specimens, cottony in older ones.
Surface white, tinged fawn or reddish-brown towards the bottom.
miazsz: Thick and hard, white, then yellowing in places or with a greenish tinge.
It has a mild taste, but in the cap of older specimens it may be acrid.
Smell faint. It turns red with FeSO4.

kapelusz: Diameter 5–10 cm, when young semicircular, with time becoming flat, depressed in the centre.
It may have different colours, depending on which tree it grows under: in coniferous forests purple, in oak forests pink, brown-red, under birches yellow, yellow-green.
Surface first slimy, then dry and suede-like.
spod: In young individuals cream-white, then becoming yellowish-cream.
When pressed they turn brown.
trzon: Height: 4–8 cm, thickness: 15–30 mm.
Smooth or slightly wrinkled, red or white with a red tinge.
miazsz: Cream, in places brown-yellow.
Taste somewhat acrid when young, later almost imperceptible.
The smell of a mature specimen resembles the smell of herrings.

kapelusz: Thick-fleshed, 6–25 cm in diameter, flat-convex, depressed with age, at first with rolled-under margins, later becoming lobed and bent.
Colour brownish with a slightly reddish tint.
Covered on the surface with thick, concentrically arranged scales of dark colour.
spod: Decurrent on the stem, whitish, grey to brownish.
They are crowded and brittle.
trzon: Cylindrical, 3–6 cm high and 1–3.5 cm thick, thickened at the base.
At first whitish, later turning brownish, velvety or with adpressed fibres.
miazsz: Springy, dry, at first whitish, later grey-brown, brownish at the base of the stem.
It has a pleasant taste and a spicy smell.
wysyp: Spores roundish with numerous nodules, measuring 6–8 × 5–5.5 μm.
podobne: Sarcodon squamosus – has finer scales that stand out less from the cap and grows under pines.
Morphologically it is so similar that it is key to determine under which tree it grows
Hydnellum scabrosum – has a smaller cap (up to 12 cm) and smaller, adpressed scales.
The flesh has a bitterish taste and a blue-green colour at the base of the stem.
Hydnellum joeides also has a brown colour, but its flesh slowly changes colour to violet when cut.

kapelusz: Thick-fleshed, up to 6 cm in diameter, flat-convex or flat, covered with thick scales in colour from brown to dark brown, almost black when wet, dark brown to black after drying.
spod: 0.2 cm long, crowded, in fresh condition cream to brown in colour, dark brown in dried specimens.
trzon: Cylindrical, up to 5 cm tall and up to 1.5 cm thick, central or eccentric, solid.
Surface when fresh coloured from cream to light brown, dark brown after drying.
miazsz: Brittle, whitish in young specimens, grey-brownish in older ones, with a spicy smell and a pleasant taste.
podobne: The pine and the spruce Sarcodon were not distinguished from each other for a long time.
They are almost identical morphologically.

The biggest difference is the size of the fruit body (the spruce Sarcodon is larger) and the scales on the cap; in the pine Sarcodon they are darker and more protruding; these species also differ in habitat, areas of occurrence and genetic features.

kapelusz: Diameter 4–11 cm, shape spatula-shaped, kidney-shaped, shell-shaped or fan-shaped.
It is attached to the substrate sideways or by a very short stem.
It is arched or flat.
Skin dry and smooth, and beneath it there is an elastic, gelatinous thin layer.
Young fruit bodies at first are dark green or green-brown, later ochre-brown, yellowish ochre, flesh brown.
trzon: Height 0.8–1.4 cm, thickness 1–2 cm.
In relation to the size of the cap it is very short and relatively thick (sometimes there is no stem at all).
Conical in shape, surface delicately scaly, colour from pale yellow to ochre.
