podobne: The half-free morel is distinguished by having a head attached for 1/3 to 1/2 of its length.
Verpa conica has smaller fruit bodies, and the surface of the head is not folded.

kapelusz: Diameter 8–20 cm, white or yellowish.
Egg-shaped to bell-shaped when young, then convex, almost flat with age.
Whitish and delicately yellowish in the central part in older fruit bodies.
Margin of the cap not inrolled.
Surface dry, covered with delicate, silky, cream or light brown fibrillose small scales hanging from the cap margin.
spod: Gills white, taking on a flesh-pink colour with age, broad, mixed, bulging.
Crowded and not attached to the stem (free).
trzon: Solid, 6–20 cm long and 0.7–2 cm in diameter.
More or less even, but usually narrowing slightly towards the apex.
Often curved in order to set the cap in a horizontal position, because of lateral growth on wood.
Surface dry, white or yellowish, smooth and without a ring.
The base of the stem is surrounded by a thick volva reaching to half its height.
At first it is whitish, with age it turns yellow and brown, smooth, dull.
miazsz: Compact but delicate, soft, white, does not change colour after damage.
With a slight smell of radish.
Taste mild, pleasant.
podobne: The characteristic features of this species are: large size, light cream, silky-scaly cap, deep volva, occurrence on decaying broadleaved trees.
The subspecies Volvariella bombycina var. flaviceps has a yellow cap.

A similar species, also occurring on broadleaved trees, is Volvariella caesiotincta, which has a grey-olive colouring (sometimes with a bluish tinge), an unpleasantly astringent taste, and its flesh has a smell reminiscent of Geranium.

kapelusz: It reaches a diameter of 5–12(15) cm.
Whitish, ivory with a grey, grey-brownish centre.
Young egg-shaped, then spread out with a bulge in the centre.
Skin bare, rarely with white remains of the veil, slimy in wet weather
trzon: Dirty whitish.
Of equal thickness, long, slender, deeply embedded in the soil.
Without a ring, dry and smooth.
Base with a skin-like, white volva.
spod: White, salmon pink with age.
Fairly broad and crowded, free.
miazsz: White, soft.
Smell resembling radish, taste mild.
podobne: Because of a certain outward resemblance to white, deadly poisonous amanitas (for example Amanita virosa), this species may be collected only by mushroom pickers who know its features well.

Volvariella species are distinguished from Amanita species by the pink colour of the spore print (and of mature gills), whereas Amanita species are characterised by a white spore print and mature gills of the same colour.
In addition, Amanita species have a ring, which Volvariella species lack.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–10 cm, at first convex or hemispherical, later slowly flattening and sometimes slightly sunken in the centre.
Skin dry, dull, delicately mossy, brown, yellow-brown, often with an olive tinge, ochre-grey, red-brown or dark brown.
During drought it cracks into patches and the flesh in the crust is exposed, from whitish to reddish.
spod: At first pale yellow, later green-yellowish or olive-greenish.
They turn blue when pressed.
Pores of the same colour as the tubes, broad and angular, sometimes stained brown, turning blue under pressure.
trzon: Height 4–8 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, mostly cylindrical, narrowing towards the base, often slightly bent.
Yellow under the cap, otherwise mostly coloured red or brown, often with longitudinal fibrils.
miazsz: Hard in young specimens, later delicate, soft, watery and quickly decomposing.
It is often attacked by mould.
In the cap it is yellow, when damaged it first turns blue and later red; in the stem of adult specimens it is brownish-red.
It has a faint smell and a slightly sourish taste.
wysyp: Spores narrowly ellipsoid or egg-spindle-shaped, smooth, measuring 12–14 × 4–5 μm.
podobne: There are several similar bay boletes, usually not distinguished by mushroom pickers and called by the common name 'little hares'.
These include, among others:
Xerocomellus porosporus, which does not have a reddish colour in the cracks of the skin and whose stem does not have a red colour.
These two very similar species can be distinguished reliably only by examining the spores,
Boletus subtomentosus.
It has brighter yellow pores, its cap in older specimens does not crack into small fields and its flesh does not turn blue when pressed.
Xerocomellus pruinatus.
It has a darker cap, harder flesh and grows only in autumn.
It has greater culinary value than the golden-pored bolete.

kapelusz: Up to 7 cm in diameter, at first hemispherical, then convex.
Surface ochre, pale brown, grey-brown, olive-brown, dark brown to blackish-brown, sometimes with a reddish tinge; it may also be entirely red.
When dry it is velvety, but it cracks very quickly and pinkish flesh shows through the cracks.
spod: At first lemon yellow, later pale yellow with an olive tinge, turning blue when crushed.
Pores the colour of the tubes.
trzon: Height 4.5–8 cm, thickness 1–1.5 cm, cylindrical or slightly club-shaped, often curved and usually tapering at the base.
Surface light yellow at the top, gradually becoming bright red towards the bottom.
It turns blue when damaged.
Mycelium at the base of the stem white.
miazsz: In the cap cream to yellowish in colour, in the stem brownish, turning blue after damage, especially in the stem.
Smell and taste indistinct.
podobne: It can be hard to tell apart from Xerocomellus chrysenteron.
Xerocomellus chrysenteron is less prone to cracking, has slightly larger spores, and the base of its stem does not turn blue as intensely.
Xerocomus pruinatus very rarely has a cracked cap surface, and moreover has somewhat larger spores than the two preceding species.
The riverside Xerocomellus is clearly distinguished by its habitat; it occurs in wet riparian forests and alder carrs under willows and poplars.
In the stem it has thick-walled and amyloid hyphae.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–10 cm, shape flat-arched or cushion-shaped.
Skin velvety, dry and uniformly coloured reddish-brown or dark brown.
Damaged places change colour to red-brown.
A characteristic feature of this species, distinguishing it from other similar ones, is that its cap does not crack into small fields in old age and in dry weather.
spod: Pale ochre in young specimens, later pale yellow, when damaged they turn blue.
Pores at first whitish, later yellow or yellow-green.
trzon: Height 5–10 cm, thickness 1–2 cm, cylindrical, solid and hard.
Skin longitudinally fibrous, on a yellow background with red-brown colouring, except for the upper part under the cap, where it is always yellow.
miazsz: Yellow, juicy and fairly hard, fibrous in the stem.
When damaged it turns slightly blue, taste fruity, smell pleasant.
podobne: Xerocomus subtomentosus – has an olive-brown cap cracking into small fields.
Xerocomus ferrugineus – does not have such a red stem, its cap is lighter and cracks into small fields in dry weather.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–10 cm, in young specimens hemispherical, later becomes arched, finally flat and slightly depressed in the centre.
Skin felty, dry and uniformly coloured yellowish-olive, olive-brown, reddish-brown to dark brown.
Damaged places change colour to red-brown.
spod: In young specimens intensely yellow or golden yellow with round pores, later brown-yellow or yellowish-greenish with angular pores.
The colour of the pores is the same as that of the tubes.
trzon: Height 3–10 cm, thickness 0.5–2.5 cm, cylindrical, solid and compact.
Skin smooth, in colour from cream through light brown to pale red-brown.
Hyphae of the mycelium at the base of the stem lemon yellow in colour.
miazsz: Whitish or yellowish with an indefinite taste.
Dry fruit bodies give off an unpleasant smell of urine.
podobne: Boletus subtomentosus.
It may have similar colour varieties, but its pores turn blue when pressed, and the flesh when cut has a similar colour in the cap, but the stem is pinkish in the lower half.
It also has a different colour of the hyphae of the mycelium – white.
Xerocomellus pruinatus, but its cap does not crack into small fields, and the places damaged and nibbled by slugs are red-brown.

kapelusz: Diameter 3–10 cm, semicircular in young specimens, more flattened in older specimens.
Margin rolled under for a long time.
Skin velvety or felty, dull and not peelable.
In dry weather it is cracked into small fields.
Colour most often olive-brown, sometimes yellow-brown or grey-brown.
It forms several colour forms, for example with a light yellow cap (X. subtomentosus var. luteolus) or a brown-reddish cap (X. subtomentosus var. rubrotinctus).
spod: 5–20 mm long, yellow, darkening with age to green-yellow and olive-brown, at first attached and slightly decurrent, then free.
Pores large, angular, irregular, light yellow then greenish yellow, they do not change colour when damaged, in older fruit bodies they may turn grey.
trzon: Height 5–13 cm, thickness 1–3 cm, slender, cylindrical, solid, narrowed at the bottom, crenate at the top.
Colour from yellow through yellow-brown to red-brown.
Longitudinal, darker streaks or a reticulum with very elongated meshes may occur.
The mycelial hyphae at the base of the stem are white, which is an important identifying feature.
miazsz: White or cream with a yellow tinge, darker above the tubes.
In the cap soft and fleshy, turning blue when pressed; in the stem fibrous and tough, pink or red in the lower part.
The smell may be unpleasant, especially at the base of the stem it resembles iodoform.
wysyp: Spores large, spindle-shaped to ellipsoid, measuring 10–15 × 4–5.5 μm.
Under the electron microscope an ornamentation resembling scattered rod-shaped bacteria is visible on the surface.
podobne: It is variable in the colour of the fruit body, especially the cap surface.
Very similar are:
Xerocomellus chrysenteron, which has a more cracked cap, lighter pores and a stem with a reddish tinge.
Xerocomus ferrugineus has an olive-brown cap and yellow mycelial hyphae at the base of the stem, visible after twisting the fruit body out of the soil, which in the suede bolete are white.
Xerocomellus pruinatus, whose pores turn blue when pressed.

kapelusz: Diameter 0.5–2 cm, at first bell-shaped-convex, later depressed.
Margin striate.
Surface in colour from yellow to brown, dry and smooth.
spod: Arched decurrent on the stem, sometimes joined by anastomoses.
They are the same colour as the cap, or slightly lighter.
trzon: Height up to 1–1.5 cm, thickness 0.1 cm.
At first it is solid, later hollow.
It is red-brown in colour, at the base covered with brown hyphae of the mycelium.
miazsz: White.
Very thin in the cap.
Does not change colour when pressed.
Taste and smell mild.
podobne: Xeromphalina campanella is hard to confuse with other species thanks to its tufted growth on conifer stumps.
Numerous Galerina species are similar in habit and cap colouring, but they do not have a dark brown stem, only a light brown one, and moreover they have a dark spore print.

inne: It forms fruit bodies on the surface of the bark in the form of a smooth or finely dotted, cracked, grey-brownish coating.
Context hard, brownish.
Spores ellipsoid (3.5–7 × 2.5–3.5 µm), smooth, amyloid.

owocnik: The fruit bodies are hollow inside, 15–30 cm tall.
kapelusz: Cap conical to egg-shaped, often flattened at the sides.
It is deeply pitted and ribbed, ochre, brown to grey-brown in colour.
The ribs on the cap are usually distinctly crowded, irregularly twisted to toothed, and usually form many deep pits of irregular shape.
The edges of the longitudinal ribs are usually flattened and black-brown, darker than the rest of the cap.
Short transverse ribs are usually paler, twisted, lower, and therefore set deeper in the cap.
trzon: Stem cylindrical, whitish, bent.
podobne: It is easily confused with other morel species, which are also edible.

It is also very similar to the edible Morchella conica, from which it differs mainly in its typical habitats transformed by humans and a different arrangement of the ribs on the cap – in Morchella pragensis they are much denser, more twisted and irregular.

kapelusz: Cap 7–12 (15) cm in diameter; convex, with an inrolled margin, spread out after ripening, with a blunt umbo.

Surface from whitish to cream-brown, flocculose, with longitudinal fibres; the centre is covered by a large brown scale, usually star-shaped; between the star and the margin of the cap there are usually large brown scales, very weakly attached, so they fall off easily.
trzon: The stem is 8–15 (18) cm long and 0.8–1.5 cm thick, with a slightly thickened base, and is usually longer than the width of the cap.
It is finely reticulate (net-like) and after scratching the skin of the stem it may turn red, but does not have to.
It has a thick, strong, woolly ring with a ragged edge, movable on the stem and not fully double, because it consists of remnants of the partial and universal veil.
The ring may, however, be somewhat thinner and the distinct groove between the two veils is not always visible.
spod: Gills narrow, widely spaced, whitish, often with a pinkish tinge when the spores mature.
They are separated from the stem by a circular collar (collarium).
miazsz: Flesh white, does not turn red or at most slightly under the skin of the stem; it has a weak mushroomy smell.
In the stem it is woody and strongly fibrous.
wysyp: Spore print pale cream with a reddish tinge to distinctly pink.
podobne: It is often confused with Macrolepiota procera.

Macrolepiota procera is larger and stronger, has smaller, more numerous and thicker scales on the cap, which do not fall off near the margin, more distinct stripes on the stem and a whiter spore print.
The rare M. olivascens looks like a somewhat darker parasol mushroom and can be distinguished by the same features, but with age it turns red and green.
Other Macrolepiota species, such as M. mastoidea and M. excoriata, differ in a thinner, single (not double) ring and a very faint reticulum (net) on the stem.
Shaggy parasols (Chlorophyllum) differ in a smooth stem without bands and in flesh that turns red throughout the fruit body (not only under the stem skin).
Fungi of the genus Leucoagaricus (some suspected of poisonous properties) also differ in having a smooth stem and/or distinct reddening of the flesh when damaged.
Other species, including Lepiota, are distinctly smaller, have different scales and/or do not have a strong ring on the stem.

kapelusz: It is often smaller and shorter than Rhodocollybia butyracea, and its cap is light grey and hygrophanous.
owocnik: It is also rarely albino (white).
podobne: However, there are several differences between it and Rhodocollybia butyracea in structure and habitat.
It is often smaller and shorter than Rhodocollybia butyracea, and its cap is light grey and hygrophanous.
It must be distinguished from the inedible Clitocybula platyphylla, which is larger, brownish-grey and strongly fibrous.
Another similar species is Gymnopus dryophilus, which, like it, is edible.
